blocks.html: My dear children, and the children who will come after you,

I have written this book first and above all to give God the glory, and to tell of the wonderful things He has done in our family. I did not want any of it to be lost. The God who heard the plea of a young woman in a convent, who lifted our family up and carried it across the world, is the same God who is watching over you. As you read this, I want you to know Him the way we came to know Him.

I have written it, too, to leave behind. For my son, my grandchildren, and for all the generations that come after them, if the Lord has not yet returned. I want you to see how far back the gospel goes in the roots of this family, and how deep the love of God has run through our lives, from one generation to the next. You are not here by chance. You were planned, and wanted, and part of a design God began generations before you were born, and you were prayed for long before you came.

I have written it, too, to encourage you. If the circumstances of your life ever get hard, I want you to hold on and keep strong, because His plan is always the best plan, even when you cannot yet see it. I have lived long enough to tell you that it is true. As the Bible says:

Blessed is the one who perseveres under trial, because, having stood the test, that person will receive the crown of life that the Lord has promised to those who love Him. James, chapter one, verse twelve.
So I leave you with this. I love you. From the past, with a pen in my hand, I am praying for you now, for those of you here and those of you yet to come:
The Lord bless you and keep you; the Lord make His face shine upon you and be gracious to you; the Lord turn His face toward you and give you peace.

Stay connected to the vine. Jesus said that He is the vine and we are the branches, and that apart from Him we can do nothing. So remain in Him, and let your roots go down deep into Him, because a branch joined to that vine is a branch that cannot be shaken loose. The storms will come and go, but you will not be uprooted, for you will be held in the one thing that can never be moved, the Lord Jesus Christ Himself.
Hold on to Him, and He will hold on to you. He always has.
With all my love, and all my faith that God will be as faithful to you as He has been to me,
Moses Campisi
My mother nearly did not live to be my mother.

She was just a small girl. It was the cool of the evening, in the hills of Calabria, and her father was out working the family land. In the late afternoon her mother would gather up the children and go out to the little shack they had in the grove, to prepare dinner for the family over an open fire outside. Her father would see the sun dropping low toward the hills and know it was near time to finish for the day. When dinner was ready her mother would call across the grove, and they would come in and eat together as the light dimmed.

The children crouched in a ring around the flames, close to the warmth and the smell of the food. My mother, Rosina, was among them. One of her sisters, a child herself, not understanding what she was doing, took a burning log from the edge of the fire and slipped it under Rosina where she crouched.
Her dress caught.

It was her mother who saw it first. She did not stop to think. She snatched Rosina up off the ground and ran to an animals' drinking trough close by and plunged her daughter down into the water. Her mother's quickness saved her life. The fire had taken hold only where she had been crouching, and the water put it out before it could spread and do worse. But the burning she had already taken marked her, there, for the rest of her days. She was still a very small girl, and she carried that mark out of childhood and kept it her whole life.

One fire almost killed my mother when she was a little girl. But another fire was about to give her life. When the Holy Spirit came down, they saw what seemed to be tongues of fire that separated and came to rest on each of them, and that fire would one day catch hold of her and give her back far more than the first one ever took.

She did not know that yet. Years later, when she had grown into a young woman and the girls of her village were beginning to think about marrying, my mother turned instead toward God. The love she had for Him had always been in her, and it carried her all the way to the convent door, because the convent was the only place she knew where He was. I have also wondered if that scar played a part in her choosing the convent. Perhaps she could not bear the thought of standing before a man and uncovering that old shame. With God there was nothing to hide, for He had seen the fire and the scar and loved her anyway.
Either way, she wanted God, and she lived in a country that was certain it already had Him sorted.

It was Calabria, 1946. The toe of southern Italy, where the mountains come down hard to the sea and the villages cling to them like they are holding on for their lives. One of those villages, further inland, was called Fabrizia, and it was there, at eighteen, that Rosina entered the convent near her village, and settled in there, looking forward to a life poured out for God and for others, full of His love.

She would often tell me the stories of those two years, and there was real joy in some of them. She loved the habit and the headpiece. She shared a room with her best friend. In time they put her in charge of the grocery storeroom off the convent kitchen, her and one other nun, and it was there that one of her happiest memories was made, the day of the olives.

They had laid a whole crop of olives out on sheets of paper to dry in the sun, and when the olives were ready to be brought inside for seasoning, the two of them went out to carry them in. My mother took two corners of the paper. The other nun took the two corners on the far side. They lifted together, and the paper tore straight down the middle. Every olive they had dried went up into the air at once and came raining down across the floor. She was still laughing about it decades later, placing her hand over her mouth the way she did, the picture of the two of them standing there with a torn sheet of paper and a whole harvest rolling under the benches.
But there were other things she saw in that place, and those she did not laugh about.

The novices were taught that obedience came before understanding, that to lay down your own will was itself a way of giving yourself to God. The mother superior told them plainly that they would see and hear things they would not understand, and that it was not their place to understand them, only to obey. If they were told to plant the cauliflowers in the garden upside down, then upside down was how the cauliflowers went in, and not a word about it. I have no doubt the ones who taught this believed it, and meant it well, as a way of breaking the young of their pride. My mother understood the intention of it. She simply found that the more she was told not to ask, the more her own heart wanted to.

Then there was the matter of the meat. In the Catholic tradition of those years, no one was to eat meat on a Friday, out of reverence for the day the Lord was crucified. Yet week after week my mother was sent to carry the lunch and the dinner in to the priests on Fridays, and on the tray were meatballs, or some other meat. She did not understand it, and it was not her place to ask. There may well have been reasons she was never told, allowances made for the old or the unwell that a young novice was not meant to know about. I cannot say. She only knew that she was asked to keep a rule that others at the same table seemed free of, and that no one would explain to her why. She carried the tray. She kept her mouth shut. She kept her eyes open.

The thing that troubled her most was the Bible. In that convent, in those years, the novices were not permitted to own one. Bibles, she was told, were for the priests and the men of the cloth who had risen high enough to be trusted with them. When she asked what a person had to do to come into the Grace of God, the answer she was given was that it came only at the top of a long climb, rung by rung, year by year, through obedience and holiness, until one had at last been found worthy of it. I want to be fair to the ones who taught her this. They had come to God by that same road themselves, and they were handing on the only path they had ever been shown. But something in my mother could not rest under it. She did the arithmetic in her head, and her heart sank. I might be an old woman before I reach the top of that ladder. And who is to say God will even take me after all of it?

She had come to the convent to find God for herself, to know Him the way you know someone you love. She was beginning to fear that in this place He would always be Someone she was told about by others, and never Someone she was allowed to meet on her own.
Then a man died, and the door opened.

One of the older priests passed away, and a maintenance man was given the job of emptying the dead man's room and burning everything in it. He had built a pile of clothes and belongings near the doorway, ready to take out and set alight. My mother happened to be walking past that morning, and something in the pile caught her eye. A thick black book.

She knew exactly what it was. She asked the man, as evenly as she could manage, whether she might have it. He shrugged. He was about to burn the lot, so what did it matter to him. Take it, he said. She slid the Bible inside her cloak, thanked him, and kept walking, her heart slamming against her ribs the whole length of the corridor. A novice was not allowed to so much as touch one of these. She had just hidden one against her own body.

From that day she read it every moment she could steal, and what she was looking for was simple. She wanted to know what a person had to do to be in the Grace of God. But the stolen minutes were few, and the guilt of hiding the book sat heavy on her, and the more she read, the more she felt a gap open between the words on the page and the life she was living inside those walls. After two years she finally let herself ask the question she had been circling. Was she any closer to God than the day she had walked in? She was not. If anything she felt further away, not because the people around her were unkind, for they were not, but because the thing she had come for, God Himself, near enough to touch, seemed always to be kept one more rung up a ladder she could not climb.
So one day she went into the chapel, knelt down in front of the crucifix, and prayed the most honest prayer of her young life.

"God, I came here to be close to You. To know You for myself. But here I am not even allowed a Bible of my own, and I am told that only those who have climbed high enough into Your Grace are fit to read it and understand it. What must I do to come into Your Grace? If You are not to be found in this place, and I am not meant to be here, then please, take me out of it."
She finished in tears, and left it with God.
That very week, He answered.

A pain came up in the lower part of her stomach so fierce she could barely stand. The infirmary took one look and sent her straight to hospital, where they found an uncommonly inflamed appendix and operated on her at once. In those days the rule was firm. Any nun sent to hospital had to recover at home, under the care of her own family, until she was well enough to return. So, with her stitches still fresh, my mother was sent back down the mountain to her parents' house. She did not yet understand that the appendix bursting in her side was the first piece of a puzzle God had already begun to lay out across her whole life.

Her parents, Salvatore and Maria Rosaria, owned a small home just outside the village, with their fields around it, which they worked themselves and sometimes hired men to help with. They grew olives among other things, and pressed them, and sold the oil from the house, so that people from the village and travellers passing along that road would stop in to buy from them. My mother spent her recovery in an upstairs room, and from its window she could see across to where a team of young men were labouring in the fields. She noticed something strange about them. Every so often, for no reason she could see, one or other of them would stop, lift his hands into the air, shout out a few words she could not make out, and then bend straight back to the work. It happened again and again. It got under her skin. She could not figure out what they were shouting.
So she asked her father.

Yes, he had noticed them. In fact, he said, there was a story behind those boys. Earlier that month a couple had come through the village on a horse and cart, on their way to a town further on, and they had needed somewhere to spend the night. Her father had taken them in. By morning they had become friends. While they were under his roof the couple had seen how badly the family needed labour for the fields, and to thank him for his hospitality they had promised to send their eldest son and a few of his friends for a week to help bring the harvest in.

That was who the young men were. As for the lifting of hands and the shouting, well, her father said, it had something to do with their religion. While they were staying, the couple had tried to share their faith with the family, and the strange thing was that everything they said could be opened up and shown straight from the Bible they carried with them. One thing in particular her father could not get out of his head. They had shown him a verse, and made him read it with his own eyes, from the book of Leviticus.

Do not make idols or set up an image or a sacred stone for yourselves, and do not place a carved stone in your land to bow down before it. I am the Lord your God. Leviticus, chapter twenty-six, verse one.

"After I read it for myself," her father admitted, "I did not know what to say to them. Our own religion has us doing the very thing this Book forbids. No wonder we are not encouraged to read it. I was almost ashamed." He thought the couple were called Evangelists. He told his daughter that he and her mother were taking what they had heard very seriously, because these were people who lived clean and godly lives, who were generous to a fault, and whose every word and action seemed to revolve around God and the Bible.
That was all my mother needed to hear. She asked her father if he would invite the young man in for lunch. He agreed, and went to fetch him.

The young man came in, introduced himself, and thanked them for having him. His name was Vittorio. They settled around the table, and before they had so much as picked up a fork my mother asked the question that had been burning in her since she first saw the men in the field. What was all that, the lifting of the hands, the shouting?

Vittorio told her they were praise breaks. Moments he took, right in the middle of the work, to give the glory back to God for the Grace that had been given to him, freely, for his salvation and the forgiveness of his sins. Then he began to tell her, plainly and without any ceremony, of the things he had seen God do, and the encounters he had had with Him.
My mother nearly fell off her chair.

I have been in a convent for over two years searching for God, she thought, and here is a labourer at my father's table speaking about God as though He were his own Father. Telling me He is near. Telling me He gives His Grace to anyone who comes to Him by faith in His Son, Jesus Christ. The ladder she had been told to climb for the rest of her life, and here was a young man already standing at the top of it, talking like he lived there. That is the God I have been looking for.
Then Vittorio paused before the food, and looked at her habit.
"I can see you are a nun," he said. "I take it you are a woman of prayer. Are you going to give thanks to God for the food?"
She faltered. "I have not brought my prayer book. I left it at the convent."
"Well then," he said, "may I pray? I do not need a prayer book."
Again she was stunned. She looked to her father, who nodded for her to let him. Vittorio rose to his feet, lifted his hands toward heaven, and prayed.

"God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, we come before You today to lift Your name above every name, together with these dear children of Yours. My prayer is that You would reveal Yourself to them as You revealed Yourself to me." He said a few more things she would never afterward be able to recall, and closed by thanking God for the food, and sat down.

By the time he said amen, my mother was undone. The fire had found her at last, the other fire, and this time it did not burn her. It warmed her, all the way through, and it left no scar. She never could remember a single thing she ate at that table. What she remembered was that she had found the God she had been searching for, and she had found Him in the prayer of a poor, unschooled shepherd boy. In that moment she understood that getting sick, and being sent home, had not been bad luck at all. It had been the first piece of a divine plan, the opening move in a puzzle God was quietly assembling so that she would come to know Him.

By the end of that lunch the whole family had given their lives to Jesus. They repented of their sins and were born again, just as the Bible says: Very truly I tell you, no one can see the kingdom of God unless they are born again. John, chapter three, verse three.

But my mother was not finished with Vittorio. She kept him there the whole afternoon, soaking up everything he knew, question after question, until at last he told her his dream. One day he wanted to become a pastor. He wanted to build a church for God.

Something turned over inside her. This is where I belong. With a man who loves God enough to want to build Him a house. She never went back to the convent. She had walked out of that place with nothing but a hidden Bible and a broken heart, and within the space of a single afternoon God had handed her two things at once. The God she had crossed her whole young life to find, and the next piece of the puzzle. The young man at her father's table. Vittorio, the man she would marry for the love they both carried for God.
Vittorio was the man who would one day become my father.

He went home that week and made sure of something. His own father was a pastor, and Vittorio had him send an elder down to my mother's parents' house to hold meetings every week. That is how the first evangelical church in that town was born, in the front room of my grandparents' house. The elder they sent was a man named Maiolo, and they say he was meek and gentle as a dove. As soon as the family had been baptised in water and in the Holy Spirit, the little group did not just grow. It caught fire.

My mother caught fire with it. She told me that when the Holy Spirit fell on her, the shyness she had carried her whole life simply burned away. The timidity, the fear of what people thought of her, gone. In its place came a boldness she had never known. The girl who had crept down a convent corridor with a Bible hidden in her cloak now stood up in her own village and preached, and many believed.

Word got around fast, because in those meetings things were happening that people could not explain. The sick were healed. Men and women were baptised in the Holy Spirit and spoke in tongues, exactly as the Bible had promised: And these signs will accompany those who believe: in my name they will drive out demons; they will speak in new tongues. Mark, chapter sixteen, verse seventeen. The little nun who had walked away from the convent was now causing the priests of her village a great deal of trouble.

When the convent finally understood that she was not coming back, that she had, in their words, changed religion, the priests were furious. To lose a nun to another faith was a public shame for the Catholic Church. So they began sending nuns my mother had befriended inside the convent down to her parents' house, one after another, to talk her into returning and to put a stop to what she was doing.

It did not go the way they planned. Each time a nun came to win my mother back, my mother used the visit to preach to her instead. She told them what she had found. That the Grace of God was not a prize reserved for priests and vicars at the top of some ladder, but a free gift for every single person who would believe in Jesus. That the only way to the Father was through His Son, not through the Church and not through any man, just as the Bible says in John, chapter fourteen, verse six. She had found the one true road to heaven, and it was paved with nothing but the unconditional love of God and His free gift of salvation. When the nuns carried those words back to the convent, the priests realised they were losing the battle. Worse, they were losing nuns. They stopped sending them, for fear of how many more they might lose to those simple biblical truths.
So they tried something harder.

This was just after the Second World War, and in those days it was still unlawful to hold unregistered gatherings, public or private. The priests knew it. They began sending children to throw rocks at my mother's windows during the prayer meetings, to break them up, knowing that since the meetings themselves were illegal there was nothing she could do in reply. But the rocks did not stop the meetings, and they did not scatter the people. So the priests went one step further. They took my mother to court, piling up every accusation they could think of, the illegal gatherings chief among them, hoping a judge would shut the whole thing down and choke the movement before it could spread.

Word of the court case ran through the town like a fever. It had the feel of David going up against Goliath, one young woman standing alone against the might of the Church, and half of Fabrizia turned up to see it. On the day, the room was packed wall to wall, and the air in it was tight with expectation.

The priest opened with both barrels. He stood and threw every charge he had at my mother. What an unfaithful, disgraceful woman she was, a traitor to the Catholic Church. How she was dragging the whole town off into some new religion. How she was performing miraculous healings without the Church's permission, holding meetings without a permit, on and on it went.

When it was her turn, my mother did not deny the one thing she was guilty of. She told the judge plainly that no, she did not have a permit for the meetings in her house. But she wanted him to understand what those meetings actually were. They were not political. They taught people to pray, and to respect the government they had elected. Most of all, they brought eternal hope to people's souls and healing to their bodies.

Then she told the judge one more thing. That the priests had been sending children to smash her windows while she and her people were at prayer. She knew she had been in the wrong not to seek permission, she said. But that did not give the priest the right to break her windows.
The judge turned to the priest. Was it true?
The priest knew some of those very children were sitting in the room. To deny it was to be caught in a lie in front of the whole town. He admitted it.
The judge rose to his feet.

"You brood of vipers," he said. "Your souls are as black on the inside as your garments are black on the outside." He turned to my mother. He found that this young woman had done no wrong to the community whatsoever. He did not stop there. He granted her the authority to hold gatherings in her house freely. As compensation for what had been done to her, he ruled that she could also hold meetings in the town square itself, as often as she liked and for as long as she liked. "And if anyone gives her any trouble," he said, "they will answer to me."
The hammer came down on the desk. Case closed.

You can imagine the roar that went up in that courtroom. The crowd erupted, cheering and shouting for the sheer joy of it, and the whole place was charged with a feeling of freedom, because something had just broken open. A door had swung wide for the Gospel to be preached out in the open in that corner of Italy. From then on there were not only meetings in my grandparents' house. There were open-air meetings in the town square, and many more came to the Lord.

That is where it began. A girl who wanted God, a hidden Bible, a shepherd boy's prayer, and a judge who threw the doors of a whole town open. None of them knew yet what God was building. They only knew He had started.
There is a footnote to my mother's story, and it did not reach me until forty years later, on the other side of the world.

One day in 1990 I met an Italian pastor in Sydney by the name of Charlie Fazio. I asked him where in Italy he was from, and he told me he came from a village in Calabria called Fabrizia. I said my mother was born and raised in that very village. He asked her name. I told him. Rosina Iacopetta.

"No," he said. "No way." He asked me a few more questions, turning it over, and then he was sure of it. "I know your mother," he said. Then he asked me something that made the hair stand up on my arms. "Did she ever tell you a story, from when she was a young woman in Fabrizia, about being persecuted by the priests? About some boys who used to come and smash her windows while they were at prayer?"
Yes, I told him. She had.
"My brother and I," he said, "were two of the rascals the priests sent to smash your mother's windows."

I could not take it in. The boys who had thrown stones at my mother's prayer meetings were now pastors of the very Gospel she had been on her knees praying for. I said to him, why don't we ring her right now and let her know what you have become. So we did. When my mother heard the news, she was so delighted she invited Charlie and his wife to come up and stay a few days with her on the Gold Coast, where she was by then living. They came, and they sat and reminisced, and as they pieced it all together we discovered that the Fazio family had been saved in the very church my grandfather had pioneered in those days.

The stones had been thrown. The boys who threw them grew up to preach. That is the kind of God my mother found at her father's table, the God I am going to spend this whole book trying to tell you about. The God I thought I knew.

Every so often, in my father's family, a child is born with the wrong colour eyes. Not brown, the way a Calabrian's eyes are supposed to be, but blue, the kind that catches a stranger in the street and holds them a second too long. The colour skips along the bloodline as it pleases, surfacing in one child and not the next, turning up a generation later in a face nobody expected. In a family of dark-eyed southerners those eyes have no business being there at all. They came into the family the way a great many things came into my family. Through a scandal that God turned into a blessing.
It begins around the turn of the twentieth century, with a young woman newly married in Calabria, and a husband with his eyes already fixed on the horizon.

In those years the land could not feed its own people, and a man who wanted a future for his family went looking for it across the ocean. So the day after the wedding, my great-grandfather left for America, the New World, to make his fortune and build a life. The plan was simple. He would go ahead, get himself established, and send for his wife once everything was ready. They would begin their life together over there.
He reached America. Then the letters stopped before they ever started.

His wife waited. A year. Two. She heard nothing. Whether he could not write, whether he would not, whether something had happened to him on those far streets, she never knew. People were illiterate in those days, and perhaps that was all it was, a man with a heart full of words and no way to put them on paper. But a silence is a silence, and after eight years of it, the hope of ever hearing from him again had gone out of her like a lamp running dry.

It was then, with her husband eight years gone and as good as dead to her, that she gave herself one night to another man. He was married. He was handsome. He had blue eyes, and a surname, Monteleone, that the town would never hear spoken in connection with hers. She fell pregnant at once.
Less than two months later, her husband came home.

He came home rich. He had made his fortune in America after all. But the New World had been too lonely a place to spend it in, and he had found that he missed his wife and his family more than he wanted any dream, so he had packed up his fortune and sailed back to Calabria to claim the life he had left behind. What he found waiting for him was a wife carrying another man's child.

A lesser man would have turned on his heel. He did not. He had been gone eight years without a word. He understood what his silence had done to her, and he loved her still. He asked her, simply, whether she still wanted him. They sat together and talked their way toward a reconciliation neither of them had any right to expect, and at last she said yes. Yes, but. But what about the baby?
What he did next is the reason I am able to carry the name I carry.

No one in the town yet knew she was pregnant. So before anyone could count the months, he did a bold and selfless thing to save his wife's honour. He claimed the child as his own. He would tell the town the baby had simply come early, born premature. He gave the newborn his own surname, Campisi, and declared the boy his son in front of everyone.

The boy was my grandfather. He was born carrying the one thing his adoptive father could not hide and would not explain. The blue eyes of the man who had fathered him. The first blue eyes the Campisi family had ever seen. From that child on they were in the blood, surfacing here and there down the generations, in this child or that one, a quiet mark that still turns up in the family to this day, the visible memory of a scandal that a good man chose to cover with his own name.

I have thought about that man a great deal. A husband who came home to a wife carrying a child that was not his, and who chose to give that child his name rather than his shame. I did not understand, when I was younger, why a story like that belonged at the front of a book about God. I understand it now. The whole gospel my family would go on to preach across three continents is hidden in it already. A father who claims a child not his own by blood, and gives him a name and a future as though he had been his all along. We did not invent that idea in our little churches. We inherited it. It was in the family before the family ever knew God.

There is something else in it too, something I have come to see runs all through the Bible. God has always been willing to use the very things the world would throw away. When He set out to bring His own Son into the world, He did not run the bloodline through spotless people. He ran it straight through the broken and the scandalous. Judah, who fathered his line through Tamar, a woman everyone had wronged and written off. Rahab, who had sold her body in Jericho. Ruth, a foreigner who did not belong. David, who took another man's wife. The blood was tampered with at every turn, and yet out of that very line, in the fullness of time, came the Messiah. So when I look at the tampered blood in my own family, and the blue eyes that should never have been there, I take heart. Not because the wrong was any less wrong, but because it shows me that a broken line is not something God turns away from. It is something God still uses.
They named the boy Domenico Campisi.

He grew into a force of nature. By the time he was a young man, Domenico Campisi was the kind of name people in the district said carefully. Strong-willed, stubborn, afraid of nothing. They said of him that he had a horse, a gun, and a fierce heart, and the order of those three depended on who was telling it.

At eighteen, in 1927, that fierce heart went and fell in love. Her name was Eugenia, and she was seventeen. Domenico's mother was against the match from the start, with all the reasons mothers give. The girl was too young, and she was poor. But love has never once in the history of the world stopped to take advice. Domenico and Eugenia ran off together and eloped, without troubling anyone for the vows of marriage, and that was that.
Eugenia fell pregnant almost at once, and in the spring of 1928 she gave birth to a son. They called him Vittorio. He was my father.

More children followed, year after year through the 1930s, until there were five of them filling the house. Then, early in 1938, God walked into the Campisi family the way He so often did with us, through a side door no one was watching.
A distant cousin came home to Calabria from Argentina, and he brought the gospel back with him.

He shared it with the whole family, and it did not just touch them. It overturned them. Domenico Campisi, the man with the horse and the gun and the fierce heart, was born again, and so was Eugenia, and the change in them was so total that the first thing they wanted to do was put right the one thing they had never bothered to make right. They had eloped eleven years and five children earlier without ever marrying. Now, suddenly, they could not rest until it was done properly, made holy and respectable before God and before the town. So Domenico and Eugenia were finally, formally married, with their own children old enough to attend the wedding. My father told that story all his life, and the detail he always landed on was this. He remembered, as a boy, eating spaghetti at his own parents' wedding.

From the day he gave his life to Christ, my grandfather never turned back. The fierceness that had made him a man others feared simply found a new master. He began to preach. He pioneered the first evangelical church in his home town of Nardodipace, and in the years that followed he planted others across the province of Catanzaro, one village at a time, one front room at a time, until he had planted seven churches in all. One of those villages was a place further up the mountains called Fabrizia.

blocks.caption: The members and family of my grandfather Domenico’s home church in Calabria.

blocks.html: That is where the two halves of this book come together.

You have already heard about a certain evening in Fabrizia. You heard it in the last chapter, from my mother's side of it. A couple passing through the village on a horse and cart, needing a bed for the night, taken in by a family who sold olive oil. A couple who turned out to read everything they said straight from the Bible, who showed my grandfather Salvatore the verse in Leviticus that left him almost ashamed of his own religion. A couple who, before they left, promised to send their eldest son and a few of his friends to help bring in the harvest.
That couple was Domenico and Eugenia. That eldest son was my father.
Here is how the same evening looked from the road.

Domenico and Eugenia were on one of his evangelistic outreach journeys, headed for a village a long way from home, when they realised the dark would beat them to their destination. So they stopped in Fabrizia. Seeing a house on the road that sold olive oil, they pulled up there, and they asked only for directions, whether the owners knew of anywhere nearby where two travellers might find a bed for the night.

That is not what they were given. Those were hard years, and people were poor, and doors did not open easily in that country. Theirs did. Salvatore and Rosaria would not hear of sending two strangers back out into the dark to go looking. Our daughter left us two years ago to join the convent outside town, they said. You can have her room. They put the horse away for the night, sat the two travellers at their own table, and gave them the bed of their own daughter.

My grandfather never let an open door go to waste, and this one was wide open. He preached the gospel under that roof that night, and again the next day. When the time came to settle up, for the room, for the food, for the oil he had bought, Salvatore would not take his money.

"You have given us more than money can buy," he told Domenico. "The joy of knowing that God loves us, unconditionally, like a father, has set us free from every insecurity and every judgement we carried. I only wish our daughter were here to hear everything you have said about the Bible."
My grandfather pressed him to take the payment. Salvatore would not hear of it. So Domenico, who could not abide owing a debt he had not repaid, looked out at the property and found another way.

"In that case," he said, "I can see your olive groves are ready for the harvest. Let me send you my eldest son and a few of his friends to help bring the olives in. They will be fine sleeping in the manger."

That eldest son was my father, Vittorio. Back home he was a goat shepherd, tending his own father's goats on the mountainside, but he was a boy who did whatever his father asked of him, and if that meant leaving the goats to go and pick another man's olives, then that is what he did. So he was sent.
Salvatore gave way at last, and gladly, because labour was scarce in those days and a strong young man's hands were worth more than coin.

Neither father knew what he had just set in motion. One was lending out his son. The other was opening his home to the very young man who, within two weeks, would sit at his table, pray over his food without a prayer book, and before long carry his daughter out of the convent and into a marriage that would carry the gospel across two more continents. The daughter sleeping somewhere up in that convent, the son sleeping out in the manger. Two strangers, two fathers, one ordinary night in a mountain village, and God laying the pieces down one beside the other, the way He always did, so quietly that no one in the room felt the floor of history move beneath them.

But it had moved. Salvatore's daughter came home from the convent to recover from her appendix. The boy from the manger came to lunch. Not long after that, my mother Rosina and my father Vittorio were married, the Iacopetta line and the Campisi line bound into one, two families who had each gone looking for God on their own and found, at the same table, that He had been arranging to introduce them all along.

They did not stay long in that mountain country. They could not. The land that had made them could no longer feed them. All across the south, the fields were emptying of young people, every one of them turning the same direction, north, toward the cities of Europe and the promise of real work and real wages. My father felt the pull as strongly as any of them.

Six months into the marriage, he kissed his new bride goodbye, and went looking for a new world of his own. He did not go alone. Her father went with him, my grandfather Salvatore, the same man who had opened his door to two strangers on a horse and cart, leaving his own wife and his own fields behind. The two of them, father-in-law and son-in-law, set out together.

My father left for the new world six months after his wedding, the way the men of the south all left in those years. With a cardboard suitcase, a wife he was leaving behind, and a child on the way he would not be there to meet.

There was no choice in it. The land that had raised them could no longer keep them. The fields stood half worked because there was no one left to work them, and every young man with a strong back was turning the same direction, north, away from the sun and toward the grey industrial cities of Europe where the money was. The Campisi family scattered to the four winds in those years. Some went to Germany, some to the north of Italy, some all the way to Australia, and a few stayed behind in Calabria with their parents. They left at different times, by different roads, and most of them never came home for good. That is what it cost to survive in those days. A family scattered into pieces and posted across continents.

My father took the road to Belgium, and so did my mother's father, my grandfather Salvatore. The Belgian government had thrown its doors open to any man willing to go down into the coal. The wages were high, the benefits were real, and for a young couple with nothing, it was a door marked future. They were given their permit for the French-speaking part of the country, and my father went, leaving my mother in Italy carrying their first child, the two of them knowing he would not be there when it came.
He went down into the earth to build a life on top of it.

A coal mine is not a place a man from the Calabrian hills is built for. It is a kilometre of dark, a roof of rock over your head and the weight of the whole world pressing down on it, the air thick with black dust that settles in your chest and does not come out. My father spent his days down there in that dark, hewing out a future one shift at a time, and he had no way of knowing that the coal he was breathing in would remain inside him for the rest of his life. But that is a story for further on.

Five months into that dark, the word reached him. On Christmas Day, the 25th of December 1948, my mother had given birth to a baby girl. They named her Gesuina, a name made from the name of Jesus, given to a child born on the very day the world remembers His birth. My father was two thousand kilometres away in a cold country, and his first child had come into the world wrapped in the name of his Saviour, on Christmas morning. He would not lay eyes on her for a year.
It took that long. A year after Gesuina was born, around Christmas of 1949, my father had finally built enough of a life to send for my mother, and she came up to Belgium to join him.

My grandfather needed another year still to gather the means to bring the rest of the family across, and it was in that year that he and my grandmother made the decision that closed the door behind them. They agreed together to sell the land, the fields he had worked all his life and she had cooked in on those summer evenings, and the money from it paid their way north. The house itself they did not sell. They gave it away. They handed it over to the evangelical church in Fabrizia, the same front room where the first meetings had been held, so that it would go on being what it had become. Then, on the 11th of January 1951, my grandmother arrived in Belgium too, with her son and three of her daughters, the whole household pulling itself back together one boat and one train at a time.

Gesuina was a year old before my father and grandfather ever set eyes on her. When they finally did, the joy of it nearly knocked them flat, this little girl who had been only a name in a letter, now real and warm and theirs. My parents understood it for what it was. Another piece of the puzzle, set quietly into place.

They settled into a town called Roux. The government had built rows of little houses for the migrant families who stayed on as permanent residents, three or four homes stuck together in a terrace, and my parents had the end of one row, number 10 Stalingrad Street. My grandparents were further down the same street at number 21. My parents worked themselves to the bone to pay the house off, and slowly, in a country whose language they could barely speak, they began to build a home.

The language gave my mother trouble more than once in those early days, and there was one story she liked to tell about herself for the rest of her life. There was a place a long walk down the road where the families fetched their water, hauling it back in great plastic containers. One day my mother set off with her container, and a man coming the other way looked at her and said something in French, over and over, pas d'eau, pas d'eau. She had no idea what he wanted, and it unsettled her to be spoken to by a stranger she could not understand, so she ignored him and kept walking. But she made a point of remembering the words. That night she repeated them to my father and asked what they meant. He asked her, did you get your water? No, she said, there was none. "That," he told her, "is exactly what the man was trying to tell you. There's no water. He was trying to save you the whole walk." She shook her head and laughed at herself, the nun who had stood up to priests and judges, defeated by a kind stranger and a puddle that was not there.

But the thing that had brought my parents to God in the first place had not left them when they left Italy. It had come with them. Wherever there was a soul to be reached, the two of them reached for it, and in Belgium there were souls everywhere, lonely ones. The migrants had come for the money and found themselves marooned in a strange grey country, a different language, a different food, a different sky, with no one to belong to. My parents had something to offer those people that no wage packet could. A sense of belonging. A family. A God who loved them.
The place my father found them was the one place no one would have looked. Down in the dark.

Most of the men hewing coal beside him were Italians like himself, and in those black tunnels a kilometre underground, between the shifts and the dust, my father talked to them about the Lord. He never let an opportunity pass. Those men, worn down and far from home, were so hungry for it that they began to beg him. Come to our houses. Bring your wife. Talk to our families the way you talk to us down here. So my parents did, gladly, going from home to home in the evenings, and the ones who gave their lives to Jesus they invited back to their own house once a week, for Bible study and prayer.
The group grew, and then it did not just grow. It caught fire.

It grew so fast that the house on Stalingrad Street could not hold it, because the miracles had started, and word of a miracle travels faster than anything else on earth. They split the meeting across different nights of the week, and still it overflowed, until my grandparents had to open up their own house down the street to take the spill. On Sundays the whole family worshipped at a beautiful French-speaking church that had welcomed my father and grandfather the moment they arrived, and my father had become close friends with its pastor. So my father took the problem to him, this flood of new Italian believers with nowhere to put them all. The Belgian pastor did not see a problem. He saw the hand of God. His name was Pastor Vandenabeele, and he was a remarkable man of God. He told my father to start his own Italian church, offered to mentor him, and handed him the use of the church building at hours that did not clash with his own congregation.

He gave my father one piece of counsel that my father never forgot, and that I have never forgotten either. If you want to become a pastor, he said, you must lay yourself down like a doormat at the threshold of your church, and let everyone who comes in wipe their feet on you. It was the whole of servant leadership in a single sentence, and my father spent the rest of his life trying to live it.
Shortly after, my father was ordained, and the Italian meetings began.

blocks.caption: The Italian congregation gathered at the Belgian church, where the kind pastor gave my father the use of his building for the Italian meetings.

blocks.html: Another piece of the puzzle, set into place.

The miracles in those days were not rare events spoken of in hushed tones. They were the weather the church lived in. But there is one that my parents told and retold for the rest of their lives, because of how it ended, and because of the man at the back of the room.
It began with a neighbour pounding on the door.

She was a woman who lived in their street and knew my parents, and she was frantic. Come quickly, she said, please, come now. Five doors down there was a woman about to take her own life. My parents went at once, and when they reached the house they found the woman collapsed on her kitchen floor, crying so hard she could barely breathe. My mother got down beside her and asked her what was wrong. The woman pointed across the floor at her little girl, five years old, lying there too.
"Look at her," the woman said. "I cannot do this any more. I would rather die knowing my daughter could walk than live and watch her drag herself along the ground for the rest of her life."

The child had been born without any muscles in her legs. She would never stand. She would never walk. She would spend her whole life pulling herself across the floor with her arms, and her mother had reached the end of what a heart can carry.

My mother stayed with her. She brought her back from the edge of that floor, settled her, and then she began to speak to her about God. Not a God who watched from a distance, but a God with the power to heal, to save, to restore, to mend a heart broken in two. To give them a crown of beauty for ashes, as the Bible says in Isaiah, the oil of joy instead of mourning. When the woman had steadied, when something like hope had returned to her, my parents asked her one thing. Be ready at your door on Sunday morning, with your daughter. Let the whole church stand with you and believe God for her. The woman agreed.

That Sunday, my father called the mother and her little girl to the front of the meeting. He told the church their story. Then he did what he always did. He built their faith up, taught them to expect the impossible, and asked every soul in that room to stand, lift their hands toward heaven, and receive the child's healing by faith. They did. They prayed and worshipped and pressed into God together, until the air of the place felt heavy with it.
Nothing happened.

The little girl looked exactly the same. But my father had taught his people what the Bible says in Hebrews, that faith is the substance of things hoped for, the evidence of things not seen, and that a believer is not moved by what he can or cannot see, only by what God has said. So not one of them walked out disappointed. They walked out expectant, certain that God had simply not finished yet, and the meeting carried on to its end.

That week my parents went to visit the woman and her daughter, to ask whether anything at all had changed. The mother answered sadly. Not really, she said. Look, she is still dragging herself along the floor. Then, almost as an afterthought, she added one thing. It was the first time she had ever seen her daughter pull herself toward a chair and try to stand up on her own. She had fallen straight back down. But she had tried.

"That," my parents said together, "is wonderful." It might look like nothing to you, but God has begun to move. They opened the Bible again, to Philippians, where it promises that He who began a good work will carry it on to completion. They told her that faith was not only for the saving of a soul but for every corner of a life, and that she could start rejoicing right now, because the trying and the falling were the first sign that God had started a work in the child's legs, and a work God starts, He finishes. Before they left, they asked her to bring the girl to church again the following Sunday. She agreed.
That next Sunday, a stranger came to the meeting.

He was an atheist. He had heard the rumours, that signs and wonders and healings happened in this Italian church, and he had come to see the trick for himself. He hated religion and believed in none of it, and he was not taking any chances. He posted himself at the very back of the room, near the door, arms folded across his chest, where he could watch the whole room at once and nothing could happen behind him, so that the moment anything strange started he would be the first to catch the trick.

In the middle of the service my father stopped to give the church an update on the little girl. Then, as he had before, he asked them all to rise, lift their hands, and believe God to finish what He had begun. The whole congregation stood, hundreds of them, hands in the air, eyes shut tight, pressing into God.
Every eye in the room was closed. Except two.

While the church prayed with its eyes shut, the little girl slipped down onto her stomach and began to crawl, the only way she knew how, out from the front and down the length of the church toward the back, and not a single person saw her go. Not a single person except the man standing at the back with his arms crossed and his eyes wide open, watching this child drag herself across the floor straight toward him.
She reached him. She took hold of his trouser leg. Using his leg, she pulled herself up, steadied herself on her feet, let go, and stood.
Then she ran.

She ran up and down the aisle of that church screaming at the top of her lungs, "Mummy, look! I can walk! Mummy, look! Mummy, look!" The whole room erupted. The prayer turned into a roar, eyes flying open onto a little girl who had never stood in her life, running, running, screaming her joy, her mother somewhere in the middle of it dissolving. Tears and laughter and shouting all at once, the whole place lifted into something there are no ordinary words for. The whole city block must have known that morning that something had happened in that church.

The atheist at the back, the man who had come to prove them frauds, broke down with the rest of them. He pushed forward through the crowd to the front of the church with his hands thrown up over his head, shouting, "I believe! I believe! I believe!" He asked my father if he could say something to the people, and when my father let him, he turned and told them the truth. That he had not believed in God. That he had walked in that morning an atheist, come to make a mockery of the whole thing. That he could not now deny what his own open eyes had just seen. He gave his life to Jesus where he stood.
That was how revival spread in those days. Not only the believers carried the news. The unbelievers carried it too, the loudest of all, the ones who had come to laugh and stayed to weep.

This was the God my family served. A God who thought nothing of straightening a child's legs in front of a man who had come to scoff, because He wanted them both, the girl's body and the man's soul, and saw no reason He could not have the two in a single morning.

This was the God I would be born into, a little over a decade later, into this same family, these same stories, this same certainty. I grew up on these accounts the way other children grow up on fairy tales, except that mine were true, and the people in them were sitting at my own table.

So I never had to be talked into believing. What I saw, from the time I could see anything at all, was a God who did everything, and did it on time. Nothing was too hard for Him, and nothing ever came too late. He was powerful. He was unbeatable. In all my growing up I never once saw Him come off second best to anything that stood against our family. As far as I could tell, He arranged Himself around what we wanted. We asked, and He answered. We needed, and it came. That was simply how the world worked, and nothing in my childhood ever gave me a reason to think it worked any other way.

It would be a long time, and it would cost me more than I can yet tell you, before I learned that this God is also a God who sometimes does not do the thing you are on your knees begging Him to do. But that reckoning was still many years off, on the far side of the world. For now, in a terrace house on Stalingrad Street, the fire was burning, and it was only getting started.

My mother was carrying her second child when the name was already chosen. If it was a son, he would be Moses. She had come to love that story in her convent years, the baby in the basket, the river, the deliverer drawn out of the water, and she kept the name the way she kept everything precious, pressed safe in the pages of the Bible she had carried out of that place under her cloak. My father agreed. The name rested there, between the pages, waiting for whoever would come.
She did not know it yet, but in that family a quiet evening was never safe. God had a habit of walking in without knocking, tipping over every plan in the room. He was about to do it again.

The missionaries came from the Italian church in America. A woman named Sister Zullo and her daughter Ruth, who had come to preach in my father's church, and travelling with them a friend of theirs called Mary, who had crossed an ocean for one reason only, to carry the gospel to her husband's relatives in a far-off town in Belgium. My parents met them at the airport. After a short while of laughing, talking over one another the way Italians do when they have not seen each other in years, they put Mary in a taxi to her in-laws, brought Sister Zullo and Ruth home. Two weeks, then Mary would take the train down to Italy to see her own people. That was the plan. People are always so sure of their plans.

Back at the house Sister Zullo and Ruth unpacked, made themselves comfortable. After a while Ruth came down to the lounge room, picked up her guitar, began to play. She was only humming the song Hallelujah, "Hallelujah, hallelujah," nothing more than that. The presence of God came down on the room the way weather comes down on a valley, fast, with no warning. One by one they were pulled toward her. They gathered around that guitar. The power of God swept through the whole house, they began to pray aloud in tongues, words none of them had ever been taught.
Then Sister Zullo shouted, "Stop. Stop. Everyone, stop."

They froze. She was not a woman you ignored. While my mother was speaking in tongues, she said, the message had come out in English, every word of it clear to her. It was short. Mary had been put out of her in-laws' house, and she was waiting outside it now. "We must go," Sister Zullo said. "She is sitting outside their house."
My mother stood there stunned. She had never heard a word of English in her life, let alone spoken one. Yet it had come through her mouth, clear enough for an American woman to read like a letter.

My father did not waste a second. He had Sister Zullo and my mother in the car before the sentence had finished landing. They knew the house. They had put Mary in a taxi to that very door only hours before, with two happy weeks ahead of her. Now they drove back out to the town near Bruxelles, to the same address, with nothing to go on but a message that had come out of a woman who could not speak a word of English.

They turned into the street, and there she was. Mary. Sitting on her own suitcase on the footpath in front of the house, praying, exactly where the words had said she would be. The in-laws had not wanted the gospel under their roof. They had turned ugly about it, put her out with her case. She did not know the streets. She did not know the French. So she had done the only thing left to her. She had sat down on her suitcase, prayed for God to send her help.

Help came down the road in my father's car, sent by a woman speaking a language she did not know, praying in a lounge room on the far side of the city. That is how God moved among them in those days. He thought nothing of using a guitar, a hum, a pregnant mother who could not speak English, to tell one cast-out woman sitting on a footpath that she had not been forgotten.

Mary stayed only three days, then left for her own family in Italy. When the time came for Sister Zullo and Ruth to go on to their own mission, my mother had just given birth. It was a son. The name she had been keeping all those months was ready at last.

But Sister Zullo stopped her. She felt a nudging from God, she said. This boy was not to be Moses. He was to be called David, because that name means beloved of God, and that is who this child is. My mother loved it, and was glad to give her son a name that carried such a meaning.

It was no small thing she was being asked. Times had been hard, harder than my mother let on, hard enough that she did not believe there would be more children after this one. As far as she knew, this baby was her one chance to give a son the name she had carried out of the convent, the name she loved above every other. To let it go was to bury the dream for good. A quiet grief went through her. But she wanted to please God more than she wanted anything of her own, so she bowed her head and let the name go.

They had all seen what came out of that woman's mouth, what was waiting on that footpath. No one argued with the anointing on her life. So my brother was named David at his birth on the 4th of August 1952.
The name went back into the Bible, where it was discovered.

In those days hardly anyone owned a car, so every Sunday morning before the light came up, my father was already out in his, driving. He would make trip after trip across the town, fetching the people who had no way of getting to church, dropping them at the door, turning the car around, going back for more. He did it because he could not bear for anyone to miss what was happening in those meetings. But it meant that the man who most needed to be on his knees in prayer before the service spent the hours before it behind a steering wheel instead, ferrying his congregation in one carload at a time.
God noticed. He usually did.

There was a man in the Belgian church, a believer named Brother LeBrun, who was wealthy, and who came to my father one day with something on his heart. He felt God had asked him to buy the Italian church a bus. So that my father could give his Sunday mornings back to prayer and to the presence of God, instead of spending them driving in circles round the town. That week they went out and bought a thirty-seater. They allocated a few members of the church who held the right licence to take the bus out, collect the people and bring them to the meetings, and carry them home again afterwards, and my father got his Sunday mornings back.

blocks.caption: The inauguration of the church bus, 20 February 1966. My mother stands by the bus in her red dress. In the centre is my father, and beside him Brother Matteo De Santis, the superintendent of the Italian churches of America.

blocks.html: The bus did more than carry people to the meetings. On a Sunday it would let the people off in the car park inside the church compound for the service. Then, after the morning service was over, a driver would take the people back home, and then drive right back to the town square, where the market was. My father and the allocated team were already there, setting up. They would park the bus among the stalls, and draw the power for the microphone, the speakers, and the guitars straight from the bus battery. The musicians played in front of the bus, and there, in the open square, in the middle of the town, my father would preach, and the music and the crowd would draw people in off the market to hear the gospel.

blocks.caption: An open-air meeting in the town square. The musicians of the church play in front of the bus, and the market crowd gathers to hear the gospel.

blocks.html: One Sunday, at the old French church, the bus I was meant to be on pulled away without me. I was only a small boy. Everyone else had gone home in their cars, and when I looked around and saw that I was alone, my heart dropped. Then I caught sight of the red bus out of the corner of my eye, already moving off down the street. I ran. I ran along the footpath beside it, my legs going as fast as they could, and thank God it had to slow down as it got to the traffic at the end of the street, where the market was. Someone had seen me running alongside it and called out to the driver. The doors opened, and I jumped in, out of breath, and I felt saved. Everyone fussed over me, making sure I was all right.

The bus was used only one day a week. The rest of the time it sat parked along the side of our house, which was the first in its row, doing nothing. It was that idle bus, sitting there quietly through the week, that became the door.

One day the doorbell rang. On the step was an officer from the transport department, who had noticed a brand-new bus parked up beside a house day after day, going nowhere, and wanted to know why. My father explained that it was used for the church on Sundays. The officer thought about that, and then he asked my father a question that would change the course of the whole family. Would he be interested in using the bus on weekdays to do the school runs?
When my father heard the money on offer, he told the man he would think about it and come back to him.

He went inside, talked it through with my mother, and the two of them prayed it over, the way they did with everything, waiting to see whether this was God or just an opportunity. They did not have to wait long. They both came to the same understanding. This was God, swinging open a door of prosperity, laying down another piece of the puzzle they had been watching Him assemble their whole lives. So they set up a proper non-profit organisation in the name of the church, and my father went back to the officer and told him they were ready.
Then he did something that, ten years earlier, would have been unthinkable for a migrant from the Calabrian hills. He gave up the coal.

He walked away from the ten-year mining job that had brought him to Belgium, away from the dark and the dust and the kilometre of rock overhead, and he climbed up into the light to drive a bus for the government. Weekdays now, he collected the children in the morning, carried them to school, and brought them home in the afternoon. As the months went on, everything went from good to better, in the church and financially.

Then the transport officer came back. If my father had a second bus, he said, there was more work, picking up the coal miners and carrying them to and from the pits. So my father bought a second bus, and that one did double duty, hauling miners through the week and bringing even more people to church on Sundays as the revival kept growing. That became the pattern of the next years. The more work the transport department gave him, the more buses he bought. The more buses he bought, the more souls he could carry to church. Later on, as he learned the business properly, he added touring coaches that ran all the way across Europe. He would also hire them out as charters, for weddings and for all kinds of occasions, so the coaches earned their keep every day of the week and not only on the school runs. Over the years that followed the little fleet kept multiplying until it reached around forty buses.
My father took the opportunity, one at a time, to hand out driving positions to men still down in those mine corridors.

For a long time, the family had been only Gesuina and David, born three and a half years apart. But as the buses multiplied and the money came in and the hard years finally loosened their grip, my parents decided they were not finished having children after all. So, eleven years after David, the name that had been waiting all that time was finally lifted out of the pages where it had rested.

I was born on the 26th of November 1963, in Charleroi. A four-kilo baby boy with, by every account, an enormous smile and a steady stream of dribble that kept my bib permanently damp. This time she made certain of it. This time the boy would be Moses.

Six months after I arrived, my mother was expecting again, and this time the family chose the name in a way only my family could have. They wrote out all their favourite names from the Bible, each on its own slip of paper, folded them up, and dropped them into a bucket. Then they asked my sister Gesuina to reach in with her eyes closed and pull one out. She drew one slip, and when she lifted it clear, a second slip had hooked itself onto the first and come up with it. She went to shake the extra one loose, and my mother stopped her. "No," she said. "Don't put it back. It might be twins." The two names that had come up together were Andrew and Philip.
It was twins.

Andrew and Philip were born in Charleroi on the 13th of December 1964, and they came far too early, at seven months, weighing one and a half kilos each. The doctor was honest with my parents. He did not think the boys would live. Their lungs had not finished forming. They were put into incubators and hooked to breathing machines, two scraps of life too small to manage their own air. They were so small my father could have held each of them in the palm of one hand.

To this the doctor got an answer he was not expecting. My father told him not to give up, not to give in to the fear, but to believe the boys would live and to do everything in his power to keep them alive, because that coming Sunday, a miracle was going to happen. Then he did what he always did. He carried the case to his church, laid it before them, and the whole congregation took hold of it together in prayer and would not let go.
Soon after, the doctor came to my parents with the news. Both babies were breathing on their own.
My father loved to tell people afterwards how small the boys had been, small enough to sit in the palm of his hand, and how God had filled their lungs when the medicine had run out of answers.

There was one more thing about the twins. They had each been born with a large, dark birthmark covering one cheek of their little bottoms. My aunt Josephine's husband, my uncle Guy, heard about it, and one day he and my aunt came to visit them at home. He asked my mother whether he might take a look at the birthmarks, and when he saw them, he told her plainly that he believed God was going to take them away. Could he pray? Of course, my mother said. So my uncle Guy laid his hands on the two babies, prayed over them with everything he had, and then left it at that, the way you do when you have handed a thing to God.

The next morning my mother went to bathe the twins, and stopped. The birthmarks were gone. Both of them. Off both babies, clean, as though they had never been there. She called everyone she could think of to tell them that God had done it again.

So that was the family, complete at last. Gesuina, born on a Christmas Day with the name of Jesus. David, named by a prophecy, beloved of God. Me, Moses, the name my mother held in her Bible all those years, finally out. The twins, Andrew and Philip, drawn out of a bucket two at a time and breathed back to life on a Sunday morning.

My father stood at the very height of his dreams in those years. The boy who had slept in a manger to bring in a stranger's harvest, who had gone down into the coal of a foreign country with a cardboard suitcase, now had a growing fleet of buses, a church that experienced real miracles, and a house full of children every one of whom had a story attached to their name. He had come up out of the pit and into the open air, and the air was full of God.
There was only one thing left that he wanted. He had been carrying it in his heart since the day he gave his life to God. He wanted to build God a house of His own.

My parents had only ever wanted one thing for themselves, and it was not for themselves at all. From the day my father gave his life to God, he had carried a dream in his chest. He wanted to build God a house. Not a meeting hall borrowed at off-hours from a kind Belgian pastor. A church. A real one, with its doors open to the street and the name of God over it.
He had confided that dream to a builder friend of his, a man named Jean Baudoux. One day Jean Baudoux came to him with an answer to it.

He had found a block of land in the very middle of the city of Charleroi, and he meant to put up an eight-storey high-rise on it, with two levels of underground parking beneath. But behind the high-rise, he told my father, there would be just enough land left over to build a church. A five-hundred-seater. If my parents wanted it, if they would go ahead, he would keep the entire first floor of the high-rise and give it over to whatever the church needed.
My parents looked at that proposal and saw the hand of God all over it, the way you see a signature you have known your whole life. They went ahead.
What they built was something Europe had never seen.

My father had not asked for five hundred seats. He had asked for seven hundred, and since the ceiling rose five and a half metres overhead, the builder hung a balcony across the back to hold the extra two hundred. The pulpit stood on a raised platform, and behind it, up on the concrete, sat the baptism tank, built above the ground on purpose so that when the time came to baptise, they would lift the pulpit away and the whole congregation could watch through glass bricks, at eye level, as people went down into the water and came up new. An artist had painted the wall behind the tank: a lamb standing on the rocks, with a stream of water running down on either side of it, so that when the tank was full it looked as though the water were pouring down off those rocks and into the font. To the left of the pulpit, a four-tiered podium for the choir. To the right, the same again for the musicians. Over the pulpit hung three cone-shaped chandeliers, and over the choir and the band, four great spheres of light that had been given to my father by the churches in America. Wall-to-wall carpet ran the length of it. It was an American church dropped into the grey middle of industrial Belgium, and there was nothing else like it for a very long way in any direction.

That first floor of the high-rise became its own small kingdom of generosity. There was a reception room fitted out for weddings, so that no member of the church would ever have to pay for a wedding reception again. There was an office for the bus company. There was a three-bedroom apartment with a commercial kitchen big enough to cater a feast, two stoves, two ovens, two sinks, built to house the visiting pastors and missionaries who would pass through to preach.
But a building like that needed a deposit, and a deposit like that needed America.

When my father first shared his vision with the heads of the Italian churches of North America, and showed them how the bus company could carry the weight of it, they encouraged him to do two things. To come to America and take up a mission across their Italian congregations, raising the extra money the deposit demanded. To set his own church alight with the project, sending the people out door to door to gather what they could.

The whole church embraced it completely. Groups were organised and driven out into different corners of the city, each one trying to bring back the most, and they went out into all of it, the cold, the heat, the rain, the snow, and the sun. They were the pillars of the church in those days, ordinary people knocking on strangers' doors to build a church, a house of God that they would love and call their own.

The building was still only a drawing and a debt in those days, and that cost my father something he did not talk about much. He had always hoped that his first daughter would be married in the church he was going to build. But Gesuina and Arthur loved each other, and nobody could say how many years the building would take, and it was not fair to ask two young people to wait on bricks. So on the 12th of October 1968 they were married in the French church, and Brother De Santis, who had come all the way from America with his wife, as he always did, was the one who married them. It was a house of God that was not the one my father had dreamed of, and his own church was still unbuilt, still alive in his heart.

My father agreed to go. In 1969 he left for America, and he was gone nine months. He travelled state to state, preaching, and he made friendships that lasted the rest of his life. I still have the photo album he brought home, full of faces and places from that trip. I do not know a single one of the people in it. Yet I cannot bring myself to throw it away. It would feel like throwing away a piece of him, and a piece of history.

For a boy of five and six, the best of that trip was the parcels. Every so often a great box would arrive from America at our coal-mining home in Couillet, and the day it came was Christmas. We tore them open and gorged ourselves on the clothes and the foods and the gifts, things we had never seen the likes of.
Then my father came home, by ship, and I was six years old.

We all went to the port to meet him, and because he had warned my mother there would be a mountain of luggage, we went in the big red bus. The ship was called Le France, and when I saw it I could not believe a thing that size could float. I had never seen anything so enormous in my life. From where we stood on the dock I could see, up on one of the ship's balconies, a mechanical horse, the kind you put a coin in for a child to ride. I wanted to ride it, and I was a little disappointed when I was told we could not go aboard.
But the most important thing my father carried off that ship was not in any of the chests. It was something he had caught in America and brought home in himself, and it changed our whole world.
He brought home freedom.

In the American churches he had seen people worship the way he had always longed to, free in the Spirit instead of bound up in rules. The congregation was allowed to clap their hands while they sang. They clapped when someone finished an item or shared a testimony. Women cut their hair and wore short sleeves, and were free to groom themselves and look pretty, instead of grey and lifeless. People even watched television in their homes. Every single one of those things, before that trip, we had been taught was a sin. What my father had come to understand was that God does not look on the outward appearance, but on the heart. A person can cover the head and lengthen the sleeve and still carry malice and anger and gossip on the inside, where none of it shows. The rules we had lived under polished the outside of the cup and left the inside untouched. What God wanted was not a covered head but a clean heart. My father went to America a man of the old rules and came home a new man, and what he set down in front of his church was permission to breathe. He brought back freedom, and the church was never the same.
On the 1st of May 1971, we inaugurated the church.

Pastors came from America, from England, from Germany, from France, from Italy. The place overflowed. My mother and father stood together and cut the ribbon, and I looked up at my mother's face and saw it streaming with tears, and I did not understand why a person would cry at the happiest moment imaginable.
