blocks.html: I understand it now.

She was standing in a seven-hundred-seat church in the middle of a Belgian city, and she was remembering a girl on her knees in front of a crucifix in a convent chapel, asking God to intervene. She was remembering a thick black book hidden inside a cloak. She was remembering a young man at her father's table telling her that one day he wanted to build God a house of His own. She was remembering all of it at once, and measuring the distance God had carried her across, and there is no other thing a person can do in the face of that except weep. It was the largest piece of the puzzle they had ever dared dream of, and there it stood, full of people, and they knew every name in it.

There was one more move to make. My parents had built that apartment for the visiting missionaries, and they had every intention of staying out in their coal-mining estate and simply hosting their guests in the city. But when the superintendent of the Italian churches, Brother De Santis, saw the apartment and heard their plan, he told them it was a beautiful, selfless idea, and that he believed God wanted something else. He believed God wanted them to move into that apartment themselves and host the missionaries under their own roof. After much discussion, and days of waiting for the Holy Spirit to confirm it, my parents agreed.

So one of my first clear memories is of the day we left the coal-mining estate of Couillet and moved into the city of Charleroi. I was seven. Two hundred metres to the left of our apartment was the city centre, marked by a tall concrete monument with a bronze angel at the top, high above the street. In front of the monument, the streets were lined with shops of every kind, clothing shops and jewellers, butchers and bakeries. And do not get me started on the bakeries, and the Belgian chocolate. My mouth waters even now, writing this, all these years later. On the right was my school, five doors down and a street to cross, and one block further on, across the road, was the hospital. We had everything close at hand, all within a few minutes' walk. On Sundays the council closed the whole city centre and filled it with a street market. The market came right up to our front door.
We spent the whole week waiting for Sunday.

Every Sunday morning I was woken by the sound of the market stalls going up in the street below, hammering and music drifting up through the window. We would dress in our little suits, shine up our instruments, and get ready. My father was already downstairs in the church, where he had been for hours, praying. My mother was preparing the communion, making certain everything was in its place. Even before the meeting began, you could feel the presence of God in that place. People came in and knelt at their seats to pray before the meeting started. The musicians tuned up, and what a band it was. My aunt Antonia at the piano, her husband Jacque on the mandolin. My sister Gesuina on the accordion, her husband Arthur on the guitar, his brother Maurice on the drums and guitar. My brother David on the trombone. The twins and I on the trumpets, and me on the alto trombone. There were more of us than I can name.

When the meeting got going, the signs and the wonders came with it, and the joy of the Lord filled that place to the rafters. When it came time to finish, nobody wanted to. The band kept playing, the choir kept singing, the children kept bouncing. Those were the hours of my childhood I wished would never end.

blocks.html: We were one of the first churches in all of Europe with a full band playing every Sunday, drum kit and all, and nothing pleased my father more than seeing his own children up there in it.
Which brings me to the trombone.

When the time came for us to take up instruments, my father told us we could choose. The twins both chose the trumpet at once. I asked for the piano. He stopped me before the word was properly out of my mouth. No piano, he said, because you cannot carry a piano from church to church. I was baffled, since there was already a perfectly good piano sitting downstairs that he would not have had to buy or move anywhere, but there was no arguing the point. So I was left to think of something else.

While I was still deciding, he went out with the twins and bought their two trumpets, and he came home that same day carrying an alto trombone. It was for me. Nobody had asked me. I stood there feeling as though my whole life had just collapsed. There was no saying no to my father. Whatever he decided, was. So I learned the thing, and I hated every hour I had to spend with it.

My father wanted us to practise one hour every single day. The first thing he would ask, every time he walked in the door from work, was, "Did you study your hour today?" Weekends included. If we had not, he would send us straight down into the empty church to do it. I noticed something about those hours, though. He never once came down to check on us. He never came down to listen, or to encourage us, or to sit with us. He sent us down, and he stayed up.

So a couple of months before one Christmas, my brothers and I decided to record ourselves playing, over about three weeks, and give my father the tape as a Christmas present. It was meant as a gift, nothing more. But somewhere in the middle of making it, we played the tape back in the empty church downstairs, and we heard how the sound filled the place and carried up through the corridors. That was when the thought arrived that changed my life. Played loudly enough, that tape would sound exactly as though we were practising. From that day on, whenever we did not feel like studying, down we went, put the tape on loud, and my father, hearing the music coming up through the corridors, was satisfied that his sons were hard at work. We had bought our freedom for the price of one cassette.

The truth is, the band was so loud on Sundays that it never mattered what I actually played. No one could pick my part out of the wall of sound. Sometimes, in the middle of a hymn, my brothers and I would catch each other's eye and deliberately play something ridiculous, some honking wrong note, and dissolve into laughter right there in the service, certain that not a soul could hear us.

My father, however, was not a fool, and he could sense that we were not enjoying ourselves, me least of all. So three years later he surprised us with a solution. He came home with five button accordions. A new one for my sister, who already had one. A small one for her daughter. One each for my brothers and me. I looked at my brothers and they looked at me, and we did not know whether to laugh or cry. Out of the frying pan, into the fire.
But of all that happened in that building, the great church, the band, the crowds, the one thing that has never left me had nothing to do with any of it. It was the day God gave me His Holy Spirit.

When I was eight, about a year after we moved into the apartment, my father held a prayer meeting every Wednesday for people who wanted to receive the Holy Spirit. One Wednesday a friend of mine the same age as me, a boy named Federico Parrinello, decided to stay in the meeting with me instead of going off to the children's playgroup. There was a guest pastor that night, an Italian from Germany named Pastor Vozza. He told the congregation that if they wanted the Holy Spirit, they should start glorifying God and say the word "Glory," fast, over and over. I cannot tell you whether that was strictly the right method, but I am certain God was watching our hearts and not our technique.

So we said it. Glory, glory, glory, faster and faster. All at once the two of us, two eight-year-old boys, burst into tears we could not explain, and the word "Glory" broke apart in our mouths and ran together into a language we had never learned, and we went on like that, speaking in tongues, for a good five minutes. The adults around us rejoiced and patted us on the shoulders. My whole body felt as though it were on fire. I knew, with everything in me, that I had received the Holy Spirit.
When the meeting ended I ran upstairs to tell my mother what had happened to me.
She looked at me and said, "That means that from now on you're going to be a good boy?"

It was like a glass of cold water thrown over the fire. I stood there shocked, because it seemed that now something completely impossible was being asked of me, and I half wondered whether the whole thing had even been real. I understand her better now. She had three boys of nearly the same age penned up in a high-rise apartment, and the insurance company on the ground floor was bribing us every week with little matchbox cars to keep the noise down over their heads. She was an exhausted mother seizing a moment of leverage, hoping the fire of God might do what her own voice could not. I do not hold it against her.

Whatever she meant by it, the fire did not go out, not then. From that day on I would go, on my own, into my room, just to be in the presence of God. I cherished it. But I am sorry to say it did not last. We were at school all day, and then there was our school homework to get through, and on top of that the daily hour with the instrument I never wanted. Between the three of them, there was little left of a boy at the end of a day. Slowly that flame was quenched. The thing the Holy Spirit had lit in me was pressed down under the weight of it all, and fell quiet.

But here is the thing I have learned since. What God gives, He does not take back. His gifts are irrevocable. That flame did not die. It only went dormant, resting for a season under the weight of a boy's tired days, waiting. The Holy Spirit He had placed in me was still there, still mine, and in time I would fan it back into flame. God had lit something in that little eight-year-old that no amount of school, or music, or weariness, or years, could ever put out.

As I grew, He never stopped being with me. He was there every minute of my life. If I did something I should not have done, or went somewhere I should not have gone, He would whisper in my ear. I always knew that it was Him. It was not God scolding me. It was God protecting me.

That was the summit. But the summit was never the building. The seven hundred seats, the painted lamb, the chandeliers from across the sea, the buses going out on a Sunday morning to gather the people in, none of that was the dream. Those were only the means. The dream was what came through the doors because of them. A lost world gathered into one place to hear of the love of God. People who arrived not knowing Him and went home knowing Him, Sunday after Sunday, year after year. That was what my parents had given their whole lives for, and that was what God had put into their hands.

My father was not spared the critics. A man who builds something from nothing, a bus business out of one idle vehicle, a church out of a front room, will always draw the eyes of people who have never built anything themselves. My father was an easy target for them. He was an unschooled man. He had finished only the first grade before he was put to work, and there were those who never let him forget it. They saw every wrong turn he made, and he made them, because he was learning as he went, with no one ahead of him to show the way. What they did not see was the courage it took, the weight he carried, the nights he could not sleep. It is an easy thing to stand on the sidelines and judge the man in the game. It is a far harder thing to step onto the field yourself.

I have to confess that in those years, I was not the help to him that I wish I had been. I was a teenager, caught up in my own world, reckless the way the young often are, and I did not have the eyes to see what my father was carrying. I was not old enough, or wise enough, to come alongside him, to encourage him, to help him carry the load. I wish now that I had been. It is one of the regrets I carry to this day.

I have come to believe that God asks something better of us than judgment. He asks us to come alongside the ones who are trying, to carry one another's burdens, to build each other up instead of tearing each other down. The Bible says, "Do not let any unwholesome talk come out of your mouths, but only what is helpful for building others up." My father carried a great deal, more than most. There were many days he was downcast and discouraged, days he needed someone to come alongside him and lift his spirits. But everyone around him was busy with their own load. My mother had the children to watch over, and each person near him was taken up with their own work and worries, and so his need went unnoticed. I only wish I had been the one to encourage him. It is one of the regrets I carry to this day.

I did not know it then, that a man who climbs as high as my father had climbed has only one direction left to travel. None of us knew it. We were standing on the top of everything we had built, with our faces in the light, and the descent had not yet begun.

It started, as these things did with my father, as something smaller than it turned out to be. In 1974 he decided to go to Australia. The reasons he gave were good ones. He had a brother, Natale, and two sisters, Palma and Iolanda, who had settled on the far side of the world and whom he had not seen in years, and there were Italian churches all over that country who would be glad of a visiting preacher. So he wrote to the heads of the Italian churches, who put him in touch with the man over the Italian churches of Australia, a Pastor Roma, and between them they drew him up an itinerary that would carry him from congregation to congregation across the whole continent, with extra time built in around Grafton and Newcastle, where his brother and his sisters lived.

He did not go alone, but he did not take all of us either. My parents left for Australia with my brother Andrew. Philip stayed behind with my eldest brother David and his wife. I was left with my sister Gesuina and her husband. The bus company was left in the hands of my mother's sister Josephine and her husband Guy, who ran it the whole time we were away. We did not think much of any of it at the time. It was only a trip. We did not know we were rehearsing the way our family would soon be cut into pieces and posted across the earth, the same as my father's family had been a generation before.
He preached his way across Australia, visited his brother in Grafton and his two sisters in Newcastle, and then he came to his last stop. The Gold Coast.

There was a little Italian church there in those days, run by a young man on fire for God, a pastor named Rocco Cardillo, who was all of eighteen years old and held up by the strength of his parents and grandparents behind him. My father had come to minister to them. What he had not expected was the place itself. He stepped off into a beauty he had not known existed, and into the arms of the Cardillo and Versace families, who had the gift of hospitality the way other people have the gift of music. They simply could not do enough for you.

My parents did not want to leave. When they said as much, Pastor Rocco's family, who owned a block of holiday units, handed them the keys to one and told them to stay as long as they liked for next to nothing.
So my father picked up the phone and called my brother David in Belgium, and told him to come, and to bring Philip and me with him.
When we landed on the Gold Coast, we thought we had died and gone to heaven.

Everything moved slowly. The cars were enormous and drifted along the wide roads as though no one had anywhere in particular to be. There was hardly any traffic at all. Everyone seemed to be living permanently on holiday, and they were courteous and easy and kind in a way we were not used to. The sun was warm. The air was clean and fresh. The sand on the beach was white. The units had a great blue swimming pool right out the front. It was Paradise, and that is not me reaching for a word. The very centre of the Gold Coast, the heart of where we stayed, is actually named Surfers Paradise.

We fell in with the Italians who had washed up there, and made friends we would keep. The brightest of them was a woman named Filomena, a character several sizes larger than ordinary life. She worked in a bread factory, and every so often she would turn up with whole bags of cream buns for us children. She knew every Italian in town, helped anyone who needed helping, and tore around the place in a little yellow Toyota Corolla, carting us wherever we needed to go. To a boy of ten, she was magnificent.
Then something happened to my father that turned a holiday into a destiny.
He began to cough up coal.

Out of his lungs, in that pure clean coastal air, came small black pieces of the mine. Ten years he had spent a kilometre underground in the dark, breathing the coal dust into himself shift after shift, and now, on the other side of the world, the clean air was drawing some of it back up out of him. It did not empty his lungs of all the coal, though we did not understand that yet. But it helped, and it felt to us like the air of Paradise itself was reaching into his chest. I would hear him talking quietly with my mother about how good it would be, how good for him, if only they could live in a place like this.
I did not understand yet that his body had just made the decision for all of us.

We could not stay, not that time. David had a wife waiting in Belgium and had to go back first, on his own. The rest of us began the long journey home, but we did not go straight back. We stopped in Newcastle and stayed at my aunt Iolanda's house for several months. We even went to school there for a while. I never fully understood the shape of it, but somewhere in there my father went on ahead to Belgium and left my mother and the three of us boys in Newcastle with his sister Iolanda and her family for months before we finally followed him home.

Then we were back in Belgium, and everything went back to the way it had always been, as though we had never left. For the next four years life went on much as before. The church, the buses, the school, the music practice, the Sundays.

But Australia had got into my father the way the coal had got into his lungs, and it would not come out. Looking back, I do not think the thought of moving there ever left his mind for a single day in those four years. He preached about it. He would stand in the pulpit and tell the church how beautiful Australia was, until I think the congregation could have drawn the beach from memory. He was, plainly, obsessed with going back. Australia kept coming to us, too. People we had met out there began turning up in Belgium to visit, Filomena among them, and the Capelli family, and even our schoolteacher from the Broadbeach state school and her husband, who called in to see us while they were making a round trip of Europe. The two countries had started reaching for each other across the gap, and my father stood right in the middle of the pull.
Early in 1978, in my first year of high school, I came home one day to find the whole family gathered, and my father told us we were moving to Australia.

We were thrilled. Of course we were. We were children, and Australia meant the pool and the beach and the cream buns and the sun. I was far too young to understand what I was actually being told. I did not grasp that I was about to leave behind the only life I had ever known, the church, my brother David and his family, my aunts and uncles, my cousins, my friends from school, the whole warm crowded world of people I belonged to, and that I would never get most of them back. A boy cannot weigh a thing like that. He just hears the word beach and starts packing.

My father would go first, he said, with my mother, my brother Andrew, and my brother-in-law Arthur, to buy a house so that there would be a home waiting when the rest of us arrived. He handed the church over to the care of the Italian churches, who sent a good pastor to look after it. He handed the bus company to my aunt Antonia, her husband Jacque, and my brother David. The two great works of his life in Belgium, the church and the company, he simply set down and walked away from, his face turned toward the sun.

The day they left, the red bus was filled with family and friends going out to the airport to see them off, and behind it came several cars packed with church members. It struck me only years later how fitting that was. My father left Belgium in the bus that had begun everything, surrounded by the very people it had been bought to carry.

When he rang to tell us he had bought a beautiful house on the water, my imagination did what a European boy's imagination does. I pictured an enormous hut on the muddy banks of a billabong, crocodiles sliding past the door. Then the photos arrived in the post, and we crowded around them, astonished. It was a beautiful double-storey brick house, sitting on the water, on a canal that ran all the way out to the ocean.

A few days before my birthday in 1978, my sister Gesuina, her daughter Lidya, and I boarded a plane and left Europe for good. We flew into Sydney, where my brother-in-law Arthur was waiting to meet us, and from there the four of us flew on together to the Gold Coast. When we arrived, they stayed at my parents' house until they found a house of their own and bought it. They worked hard in those years, heads down, paying it off, but every Sunday we still ate together, and on birthdays too. The family always came to the one table.

I arrived in Australia with a handful of English words to my name. The school did not quite know what to do with me, so they put me in grade eight to see what I was made of. Two weeks later they moved me up to grade nine. Two months after that they moved me up again, into grade ten at Miami High School on the Gold Coast, and I finished out the year and walked away at the end of 1979 with a grade ten certificate, in a language I had barely been able to speak twelve months earlier.

I did not do it alone. My mother, my brothers and I went to extra night classes that whole year to learn English as fast as we could, and we had a lovely teacher named Mr Allan Day, who would come and collect us in his car and run us home again afterwards, every single time. There was a great deal of kindness shown to us in those first Australian months by people who owed us nothing.

So there we were. The Campisi family, transplanted from a grey city and a great church into a house on a sunlit canal, in a place actually called Paradise. My father had got what his body and his heart had both been crying out for. The air was clean. The sand was white. The cars drove slowly and the people were kind, and a boy could learn a whole new language in a year if he had to.
It looked, in every direction you cared to turn, exactly like the promised land.

But Paradise is the oldest setting in the Bible for a fall. The thing about a garden that looks like heaven is that you stop watching for the forbidden fruit in it. We had crossed the entire world to get to the most beautiful place any of us had ever seen, and not one of us understood that we had carried the trouble in with us, and that it was here, in Paradise, with the sun on the water, that everything my father had built was going to fall apart in his hands.
For a while, Paradise held.

Soon after we arrived, my father did what my father always did. He set about planting a church. But there was already an Italian church on the Gold Coast, the little one run by Pastor Rocco Cardillo, the young man whose family had taken us in so warmly on our very first visit. My father would not dream of setting up in competition with him. So the two of them talked it over, and out of respect my father went right down to the other end of the coast, to Coolangatta, and opened his own church there. By the end of that first year he had bought a restaurant as well, an Italian place right in the mall in the heart of Surfers Paradise, open twenty-four hours a day. He asked the three of us boys whether we wanted to work in it. None of us had ever set foot in a restaurant kitchen in our lives, but that did not matter. He told us to work for free, and that when each of us married, he would buy us a house. We did not doubt him for a second. He was a man of his word, our father, the man who had built a church out of a dream and a bus company out of a donation. If he said a house, there would be a house.

Because I was the eldest of the three, he gave me some good pocket money each week, and said he would do the same for the twins when they reached my age. I agreed, and I saved every single dollar of it, the whole year long.

The church grew to about forty people. My father gave the first jobs to the people who had only just come to the Lord. He employed a woman who had recently been converted, an Italian, a mother of five who knew how to cook, along with three of her daughters. Her husband had not yet come to faith. We ran the restaurant in three shifts around the clock. My brothers and I took the nights. My father took the mornings. My sister and her husband took the afternoons. When we finished our shift at dawn, we would hand it over to our father and go home to sleep.
That was the arrangement. That was the trust. That is what makes what happened next one of the worst things I have ever had to write.
One morning we came home from work at half past seven, having handed the shift over to my father, and found my mother sitting on the lounge, crying.

I asked her what was wrong. She would not say. I pressed her, and pressed her, until at last it came out of her. For some time now, she said, my father had been coming home in the early hours of the morning. That very morning he had confessed the whole of it to her. He was seeing the woman from the church. The cook. The one he had given a job to. He had even told her, my own mother, that he had bought himself a pair of binoculars to watch the woman from the bedroom window. His eyes were set on her, and he had given up hiding it.

I could not make my ears believe what they were hearing. I had noticed, in some dim way, that my mother had not been herself lately, but I was young, and I had not stopped to wonder why. I stopped wondering now.
I think that was the morning I became a man.

The blood went straight to my head. I did not say a word to my mother. I went out to the car, drove to the restaurant, and there they were, the two of them, flirting in the kitchen as though they had not a care in the world. They looked up and saw me and the colour drained out of both their faces, because they could see in mine exactly what I knew. I crossed that kitchen and took my own father by the collar, and I told him that if I ever came home again and found my mother crying, it would not go well for him. Then I turned to the woman and told her to get out.
My father asked me who was going to cook.
I told him no one was going to cook, because I was closing the restaurant.
He told me I couldn't do that.
I said, "Watch me."

The woman's daughters were working that same shift as waitresses. I told them to finish what they were doing and go home with their mother, and to their credit they did not ask a single question. They had heard enough in the tone of my voice, which is something this page, mercifully, cannot reproduce. I closed the restaurant door behind them and locked it. My father said I couldn't do this, that it would send him bankrupt. I told him he had gone bankrupt the moment the thought first entered his mind to sin with that woman. He started reaching for excuses, reasons, the way a drowning man reaches for anything floating, and I told him to go and buy a few of his own sermon tapes and listen to them. He might learn something.
Because one of those sermons, one I had heard him preach with my own ears, went like this. A good captain never leaves his ship. No matter what.

I have thought about that word bankrupt many times since. The ruin in the garden did not begin when the fruit was eaten. It began earlier, in the moment they looked at the tree and let themselves want it. The eating only made public a thing that had already been decided on the inside. My father did not lose everything in that kitchen. He lost it the first time he allowed himself to look.
We drove home, each in his own car. As we came through the door, the telephone was ringing.
It was my brother David, calling from Belgium. The bus company had just gone bankrupt.

There was worse inside the worse. The great church my parents had built, the seven-hundred-seat American church in the middle of Charleroi, with its painted lamb and its chandeliers from across the sea, had been tied financially to the business. So when the business went down, it pulled the church down into the bankruptcy with it. Both of them. Gone. In a single afternoon, on a single day, my father lost his marriage in a restaurant kitchen in Surfers Paradise and his life's work down a telephone line from Belgium, the two pillars of everything he was, falling at the very same hour.
So came the fall of a great man of God.

My parents divorced not long after. The beautiful house on the water, the one I had once pictured as a crocodile hut on a billabong, was sold. After the restaurant's debts and the last of the remaining bills had been paid, my father took his half of what was left and was gone. Pastor Rocco, who had watched this disaster tear through our family, quietly offered me a job in his own restaurant, and I took it.

The divorce broke something in each of us in a different place. My brother Andrew could not bear it, and moved away to Sydney. My mother, who had stood up to priests and judges, who had snatched a Bible from a near-burning heap and preached the gospel in a town square, who had carried it across a continent and helped build a great church on the far side of it, my mother could not survive this. She had never once believed such a thing could happen to her family. What shamed her most was not what it did to her, but what it might do to the Gospel, because thousands of people across Europe knew their names, had been saved under their ministry, had watched them as an example. She made herself sick with grief over it, sick enough that she had to be taken to hospital, where she stayed for quite some time with trouble in her heart.

One good thing about my mother being in the hospital was that she had somewhere to be, a roof and a bed and people to watch over her, while I went and did the thing that had fallen to me to do. I had to find us a home.

We had been left with fifty thousand dollars. The average house on the Gold Coast in those days cost a hundred thousand. I came in contact with an amazing real estate agent. I told him the whole truth of it, that a family had been left without a roof, that all we had in the world was the fifty, that we needed somewhere to live. The man was so moved by what had happened to us that he went to work for us as though we were his own. He showed me house after house, all of them a long way inland, far from the part of the coast where we lived and worked. One night I prayed a bold prayer. I asked God for a miracle. I asked Him for a house near the beach.

The next day the agent rang. There was a place about to come onto the market, a double-storey in a cul-de-sac close to the sea. The owners wanted eighty-nine thousand. We drove in to see it, and as we came up the street the first double-storey house I laid eyes on was an ugly thing made of fibro, fibro walls, fibro roof, and my heart sank, because I thought, that has to be the one, at that price, it could only be that. But the agent drove straight past it. The only other double-storey on the street was a beautiful hacienda, Spanish in style, built of brick with concrete roof tiles and a high fence with Spanish arches running all the way around it. He pulled up in front of it and said, "This is it."

I could not believe a house that lovely could cost so little. He walked me through it. Three bedrooms, a bathroom, a double garage, and a granny flat downstairs at the back. A pretty garden, and a back gate that opened onto the car park of the Mermaid Beach Lawn Bowls Club. Next door stood a caravan park with the very same style of fence around it, and the agent explained why. The house belonged to the caravan park, and the church that owned the whole property was selling the house first, with plans to turn the caravan park into a retirement village later on.

I told him I loved it. I asked him to leave it with me, because I had to put it to my mother before anything could be decided, and she was still in the hospital. He agreed, but he told me to hurry. A property like this, he said, would not sit on the market long.
So I went to her bedside and told her I had found the house I believed God was going to give us. She shook her head. We can't, she said. We only have fifty thousand. We cannot go a dollar over.

The agent offered to take me to the banks to try to borrow the difference, but I told him to push the price down instead. He went back to the church and laid it out for them plainly, that the woman who wanted the house had just been through a divorce, that she had been left with three young boys and nothing, that they were desperate. The church committee talked it over and came back with their answer. The house owed the church sixty-three thousand. That was as low as they could go. So now I had to find the difference, thirteen thousand dollars, and I went to the banks for it. The banks wanted nothing to do with me. I told the agent as much, and he advised me to try the finance companies instead, where the interest would be higher but where they might take a risk on me. So I went to them, one after another, and most of them turned me away as well, because I was just a boy and far too young to be trusted with that kind of money. But one of them said yes. One finance company approved me for the thirteen thousand dollars, and that was enough.
When the church heard we had the finance, they let us move in before settlement day even came.

My brother Philip and I cleaned that house from top to bottom with our own hands. We painted the walls. We bought new carpet, and three small cheap chandeliers for the living room, because a son who grew up under chandeliers from America cannot quite let a home go without them. I bought twenty-two metres of velvet for the curtains, measured it, cut it, and glued the hems, every one of them. I did not know how to sew, and there was no time to learn. It all had to be finished before my mother came out of hospital. By the time settlement day arrived, my mother came out of the hospital and walked into the home that the Lord had provided.

Philip and I worked night and day to pay that loan down, and with God's help we cleared the whole thing in a single year. The year after that, my brother Andrew came home from Sydney. The family was whole again, sheltered, safe, settled into a new life with no father at the head of it, leaning the whole of our weight on God to guide us.

Because that is what I had become. The father. The responsibility for the family had come down onto my shoulders, and from then on, whenever something needed doing, my brothers and my mother came to me. I was seventeen, gluing curtains, signing finance papers, and standing where a father was supposed to stand.

I have spent many years reflecting on the God who allowed all of this to happen. He did not stop the affair. He did not save the marriage. He did not reach down and rescue the church my parents had poured their lives into building. For a long time I could not reconcile that with everything I had been raised to believe. But as I look back now, I see something different. God did not stop the fall. He met us at the bottom of it. He provided for us there, a beautiful house at an impossible price when we were on our knees with nothing left to our name. The deeper thing was this. He did not give us the miracle we had so desperately prayed for, the restoration of my parents' marriage. He gave us a different kind of miracle instead. His presence in the pain. His faithfulness in the brokenness. His way of drawing healing and hope out of what looked beyond repair.

It was the first time in my life I caught the edge of a truth that would take me decades, and a far greater loss than this one, to finally understand. That the God I had been raised on, the God who always came through, who fixed what was broken and handed me the rescue I asked for, was bigger and stranger and harder than I knew. That He is good even when He does not give you the miracle you are on your knees begging Him for. I did not learn that lesson here. Here I only felt the edge of it. The whole weight of it was still years down the road, waiting for me, and when it came, it would come wearing the face of death.

As for my father, the rage I felt in that kitchen did not leave me quickly. It would be years, and another long road, before I could look at him and forgive him. That day, I could not, and I did not try. But that is a chapter still ahead of us, and it ends better than this one does.

We were settling into the new house, the new quiet, the new shape of a family without its father, when my brother Philip picked up his guitar one day in the lounge room and began to worship. As he played, the Spirit of God came over him, and he saw something.

He called us all in. He told us that God had just shown him three young women, from behind, dressed in white wedding gowns. He could not see their faces. But he heard the Lord say, plainly, I am preparing three sisters for you three brothers.

We were far too young, and far too newly wounded, to do anything with a word like that. So we did the only sensible thing. We tucked it away in the back of our minds, three brides we could not picture, waiting somewhere on the far side of all this grief, and we got on with the business of surviving.
I had no idea God had already chosen them. While we carried on with our lives, destiny was quietly unfolding somewhere beyond our sight, preparing a meeting that only heaven could have orchestrated.

blocks.title: The God Who Gave Me Everything

blocks.html: Every January, for years, the three brothers from the Gold Coast made the same pilgrimage.

There was an Italian Christian youth camp held each summer up in the mountains inland of Sydney, in the second week of January, right in the heart of the Australian heat. It was nine hundred kilometres from our front door, and we drove every metre of it, year after year, because that camp was where the whole scattered world of young Italian believers came together. For the three of us it was more than a camp. For one week each year it gave us back something of what we had left behind in Belgium, the congregation, the crowd of friends, the feeling of being among our own people again. We had gone five years running. The sixth year we had to work, and missed it. But the seventh year, which was January of 1991, all three of us had time off at once, so we climbed into my brother Philip's van and drove the nine hundred kilometres south again.

We knew almost everyone there, and almost everyone knew us. The three brothers from the Gold Coast. We dropped our bags and went room to room catching up with our friends, and in one of them we found the people we loved best, our friend Mark Deluca and his parents, Mario and Fina. They had missed us the year before and were overjoyed we had made it. We sat in that room swapping all the news.
Then, confidently, I asked Mark's mother, Fina, whether there were any nice girls at the camp that year for me to marry.

She laughed and shook her head. "They're all either too young or too old for you this year, Moses." But then she paused, and a thoughtful look came over her face. She reached into her bag, took out her Bible, opened it, and slid a photo out from between the pages. She held it up and pointed to a girl standing at the very back of a group of people.
"See that girl there?"
All I could make out was half a face, half hidden behind the others. "Yeah?"

"She was here last year. Her name is Dina." Then Fina set about telling me who Dina was, and the way she said it, you would have thought she was describing treasure. "She is not one of those girls you play around with. She is serious. She loves the Lord. Her father is a pastor, and she has been raised strictly, raised to be serious about her life. You can be certain no one has ever so much as touched her. She is a wonderful cook. Your house would always shine, because she is so clean. She will make a wonderful mother and a wonderful wife."
I loved every word of it. The only trouble was the photo. "She sounds wonderful," I said. "But I can hardly see her face."
I did not know it, but that single sentence set the whole camp in motion.

That very day, without telling me, a few of the older women slipped away from the camp, drove back to their own homes, and dug out every photo and video they had of Dina from the previous year. Then they brought the whole lot back.

That evening they called my brothers and me down to the television room. We came in to find the coffee table covered in photo albums and videotapes. They had gone to all this trouble, they explained, so I could get a proper look at the girl. I was stunned that grown women would go to such lengths over me and a girl I had never met. She clearly meant a great deal to them.
So they showed me. Photo after photo. I found her very pretty. But it was not the photos that did it.
It was the video.

They put on a tape of Dina standing at the front of a church. She was saying her goodbyes, though I did not understand at the time that she was leaving to go back to Italy. She spoke, and then she sang a solo, and somewhere in the middle of that song something in me went still and certain. I cannot explain it any better than that. I watched a girl I had never met sing a hymn on a television screen, and I knew. The words came out of my mouth before I had decided to say them.
"That girl will be called Moses' wife." Then, because it was the truest thing in me and I could not keep it behind my teeth, I said it again, plainer. "I am looking at my wife."

I said it because I felt it, all the way down. The women in that room did not laugh at me. They got excited. "Let's ring her," one of them said, "and see if she's still available." A few of them gathered around Fina and made the call, telling Dina they were at the same camp as last year, that they had been thinking of her, just ringing to see how she was, and, by the way, had she found herself a young man yet, was she engaged to anyone?
Dina's answer came down the line. "No. I don't have anyone, and I don't want anyone."

There was more chatting and laughing after that, and then they hung up and turned to me, pleased. She was free. Then they let slip the detail nobody had mentioned. That phone call had just gone to Sicily.
"What?" I said. "She's in Italy?"

Yes, they told me. She had spent the previous year in Australia, staying with her aunt, which was how she had come to be at last year's camp. After the camp she had gone home. Home to a village in Sicily, on the far side of the world.
The girl who was going to be my wife was eighteen thousand kilometres away, and I had never once stood in the same room as her.

The next morning I went to find the pastor who ran the camp, a man named Pastor Foti. He was no stranger to our family. He had known my father well for years, my father had preached in his church more than once, and there had been a real friendship between the two of them, right up until the divorce. And he knew Dina's family just as well. When they had lived in Australia, for nine years, from the time Dina was a little girl of two until she was eleven, before they went back to Italy, they had been part of Pastor Foti's own church, and Dina's father had preached from his pulpit too. So when I asked him straight out what he thought of the idea of Dina and me as a couple, I was asking a man who knew both sides. He had known both our fathers, both families, from his own congregation. He knew exactly where I had come from, and he knew the family Dina had been raised in.

He thought about it, and then he told me that if I was physically attracted to her, and she to me, he believed it was a match made in heaven, and he listed the reasons like a man counting them off on his fingers. Her father is a pastor. My father had been a pastor. We were both Italian, with the same culture and the same traditions. We had even been raised on the very same hymnbook. Later we would discover something else, that our mothers had been pregnant at the very same time, and that I had been born just three weeks before Dina. We had come into the world within three weeks of one another, I in Belgium and Dina in Sicily. He gave me his blessing.

Then I asked him a favour. Would he be willing to write to Dina, and ask her whether she would be open to writing to me? Because I wanted to get to know her. He said he would, gladly, once he was back at his office in Sydney.

When my brothers and I got home to the Gold Coast, I became, I will admit, a torment to that poor man. I rang him again and again to ask whether he had written the letter yet. He was backed up with work, he told me, but he promised he would write to Dina the moment he had the chance. In time he called to tell me the letter was sent, and that it was all in God's hands now. Still I kept ringing, asking whether Dina had answered. Every single day felt like a year.
At last the word came. She had written back. She did not mind, she said, having a pen friend in Australia.

A pen friend. That was not at all what I had in mind, and I was not going to pretend otherwise. I sat down and wrote her my first letter, and I made my intentions perfectly clear. I did not want a pen friend. I wanted to know whether she could be my wife. I put three photos of myself in the envelope, so she would know exactly who was writing to her. In every one of them, my brothers were standing right beside me.

Then came the waiting again, and the waiting was torture. My mother watched me pacing and fretting for a few days, and then she had enough of it. She picked up the telephone, dropped it in my lap, and said, "Ring her. Now."
I looked at her, shocked. Was it even proper to do such a thing?
"Yes. Ring her."
So I did. My heart was going a hundred miles an hour. It was the first time we would ever speak.
One of her sisters answered, and I asked, as steadily as I could, to speak to Dina. My heart was beating clean out of my chest. She came to the phone.
"Hello, Dina. This is Moses, from Australia. How are you? Did you receive my letter?"
"Yes," she said. "Just this morning."

She told me later what that morning had been like for her. When my letter arrived, she had carried it upstairs to the bathroom for privacy, and before she opened it she had prayed. God, before I open this letter, I need You to help me. If this is not meant for me, please make it clear, and stop it now. But if he is the one, then open the doors, and let everything go the way it should. Then she had opened the envelope, and the first thing to fall out was the three photos, every one of them with my brothers crowded in beside me, so that she had to read the letter to find out which of us was Moses. By the time she finished reading, she told me, she knew. God was taking this to the next step.

On the phone I told her she had beautiful green eyes, and that I found her beautiful. She thanked me, and she said, "I love your voice." It was enough. My heart was sold out. While I was speaking to her I kept thinking, I cannot believe I am talking to my future wife. I told her my intentions were true, and that if things went the way I hoped, I meant to come to Sicily and meet her as soon as I had saved enough for the ticket.

By the time we had each said the things we had wanted to say, and asked the things we had wanted to ask, something quiet and certain had settled over the both of us. Without either of us putting it into words, we already knew. We had just spoken, for the very first time, to the person we were going to spend our lives with. So we made each other a promise. We would write, and keep writing, until the day I could come to Italy and stand in front of her at last. Then we said our goodbyes, and started dreaming.

Dina told me later she was overwhelmed at the boldness of it, a man she had never met talking about marriage and aeroplane tickets in their first phone call. But in her own mind, things were beginning to line up, because she had been carrying some words for a while, and mine sounded like the confirmation of them.

Three different prophets had passed through her father's church and spoken over her. The first had told her that her husband would come from a faraway country. The second had told her the same, that her husband would come from a far-off land, and that her sisters would be blessed through her. She had wondered about that one, whether perhaps he meant the man would be rich and would give them money. The third prophet had told her that her story would be told like the story of Isaac and Rebecca in the Bible, where Rebecca had to leave her own country and go to live in her husband's land, and that God would use her greatly for His glory.

A husband from a faraway country. Sisters blessed through her. A girl who would leave her home and cross the world like Rebecca. She was holding all of that, quietly, the day my letter fell into her lap with three photos and a marriage proposal inside.

I was holding something too. My brother Philip's vision, from years before, of three brides in white that God was preparing for the three of us. When Dina mentioned, somewhere in that first conversation, that she had two younger sisters, I felt the floor of heaven shift very slightly under my feet.
After that, I was the one setting the pace, and the pace I set was a sprint.

I had told Dina I would come in six months, once I had saved enough. But I sat down and did the sums again, and worked out that if I pushed, I could have the money for both our tickets in two. On our next phone call I decided to surprise her. I told her I had a small problem. She asked, worried, what it was. I said I would not be able to come in six months after all. She asked, sadly, why not. I told her, because I could be there in two instead, if that was all right with her family.
She nearly dropped the phone with excitement. She asked her father, and her father said yes. So I booked my seat on a plane bound for Italy, departing the 1st of May 1991.

I should have been nothing but joy, and in the daylight I was. But something had begun working quietly against me, and it had to do with that video. When we left the camp, Fina had lent me the tape of Dina to take home to the Gold Coast, and I watched it every single day. As long as I could see her face and hear her sing, the certainty I had felt in that television room held firm. Then, after some weeks, Fina asked me to send the tape back to her, and of course I did. The moment Dina was no longer there in front of me, with nothing left but a picture of her growing fainter in my mind, the certainty began to slip through my fingers. It is a strange thing about the human heart. You can be utterly sure of something while it stands before your eyes, and watch the doubt come rushing in the instant it is gone.

So as the date drew closer, in the quiet hours, the doubts began to nibble at the edges of my faith. What if she is not the one after all? What if you do not find her beautiful in person? What if she does not like you? You have had girlfriends before, and tired of every one of them. What makes you so sure you will not tire of her too?
I had told the whole world I was flying to the other side of it to marry a girl I had never met. As I packed my bag, I was no longer entirely certain I was not a fool.
I boarded the plane with every one of those doubts boarding it beside me.

I boarded the plane with all my doubts boarding beside me, and for the first while I sat there stewing in them, eighteen thousand kilometres of second-guessing stretched out ahead of me. Then the plane reached its altitude, levelled off, and I got talking to the young man in the next seat.

He was Australian, fair-haired, about my own age, and after a while he must have sensed that something was not right with me, because he turned and asked if I was feeling all right. Was it the flight? Was the plane making me sick?
"No," I said. "It's not the plane." Then, because it was eating me alive and he had asked, I told him the truth. I was on my way to Italy to marry a girl I had never met.
He looked at me for a moment. "Really," he said. "So am I."
"What do you mean?"
"I'm flying to Italy," he said, "to marry a girl I've never met."
I sat there with my mouth open. "What are the chances of that? You're sitting right next to me, doing the very same mad thing I'm doing."
He shook his head. "Unreal."

Just like that, something in me began to loosen. I was not the only one in the sky that day bound for the same kind of madness. The remarkable thing was that this man carried no fear about it at all. He was calm, almost cheerful about the whole adventure, and the longer we talked the more his steadiness rubbed off on me. We started joking about it, two strangers bound for the same insane errand at opposite ends of the same country. I asked him, half seriously, to show me a photo of his girl, just to be sure we were not both flying all this way for the same one. He laughed, because I had already told him mine was in Sicily and his was up in Milano. He showed me his girl's picture, and I showed him mine. "Pretty," I said, looking at his, "but definitely not her."
Then I asked him how old he was.
"Twenty-seven."
"So am I." I asked him what month he was born.
"November."
"No," I said. "So am I." I asked him the day.
We said it at the same time. "The twenty-sixth."

We turned and stared at each other. Two men, born on the very same day of the very same month of the very same year, somewhere in Australia, who had never laid eyes on each other before, now sitting shoulder to shoulder in the same row of the same plane, flying together to the same country on the same day to marry two women neither of them had ever met.

I have thought about that man many times since, and it was only later, when I began telling people this story, that I understood what he had been. God had not left me to make that crossing alone with my fear. He had set a man beside me on the very same journey, with the exact same birthday and the exact same impossible hope, a man who carried no fear at all and did nothing but encourage me, so that I would know, all the way down, that I was being watched over. He shall give His angels charge over you, to keep you in all your ways. That is what the Bible says in the ninety-first Psalm, and I believe with my whole heart that God sent me an angel in the next seat to hold me up over the ocean.

We landed in Rome and said our goodbyes. He went off to catch his plane to Milan, and I went to catch mine to Sicily. He told me his name, but I never held onto it. My whole mind was already racing ahead to the bride waiting at the end of the next flight, and his name slipped straight through me. It is only now, telling it, that I wish I had kept hold of him, that I knew how his own story ended, whether his stranger became his wife the way mine became mine. But that is the way of it. Sometimes God sends you an angel for one leg of the journey, and you do not realise what he was until he is already gone.

My flight to Sicily was only an hour, but the moment I sat down in it the nerves came roaring back. In one hour, I kept thinking, in one hour I am going to see her. And then what? What if it all goes wrong?
The man beside me this time was Italian, and the first thing he said to me, in Italian, was, "Are you all right?"

I had not realised it was written so plainly on my face. But I told him a quick version of the whole drama, and admitted I was frightened something would go wrong. He waved it away. There was nothing to be afraid of, he told me. If it went wrong, well, they would put me on the next plane home and I could count the whole thing as an experience and be no worse for it. Then he said the thing I needed to hear. He leaned in and said, "But think. What if everything goes right?"
It steadied me more than he could have known.

When the plane came down into Sicily, he could see my nerves had got the better of me, so he did something I will never forget. He slipped his arm under mine, the way men do with one another in Sicily, and he held me up and walked me the whole way into the airport, this stranger, carrying me on his arm like a brother.
That is how I came to walk straight past my future wife without ever seeing her.

Dina was there, on the other side of the airport glass, watching the arrivals. But she was searching the crowd for a single man, a man on his own, and what came through the doors was two men walking arm in arm. Her eyes slid right over me. I never saw her at all, because the light was throwing a reflection across the glass and I could see nothing behind it. So the two of us, after eighteen thousand kilometres and three prophecies and a vision and a photo pulled out of a Bible, passed within a few feet of one another, and neither of us knew it.

The Italian man showed me where I should wait, wished me well, said his goodbye, and went off to find his own family in the crowd. Then he too was gone, my second angel, and I was alone at last on the threshold of the thing I had crossed the whole world to do, not knowing that I had just walked right past her.
She had asked me for one thing only.

Not jewellery, not anything from Australia at all. When I had asked her, on one of our last phone calls, whether there was something from Australia she would like me to bring her, something they might not have in Italy, she had thought about it and said that when I stopped in Singapore, she would love some Singapore orchids. I had no idea what Singapore orchids even were. I found out when I landed there on the layover. They are extraordinary flowers, purple and white, shaped like little bells, hanging in rows down a firm stem, and they keep their bloom fresh for a long, long time. The airport was full of shops selling nothing else. I bought her a clear box with twelve stems inside, and carried it the rest of the way like it was made of glass.
She had told me one other thing, so that I would know her in the crowd. She would be wearing the same clothes she had worn in the video where I first saw her. A black skirt and a pink top.

So there I was, at last, leaning against the wall of the arrival bay in Calabria, holding a box of orchids, having crossed the entire planet to meet a woman I had never laid eyes on in the flesh. I looked down at the box in my hands and watched the flowers trembling inside it, and realised it was me, shaking. The harder I tried to hold them still, the more they shook. I stood there fighting my own hands, the orchids rattling in their box like something alive.
Then I saw the pink top.

She came through the crowd at a half-run, scanning every face, and I learned afterwards what she was doing. She had been waiting on the other side, watching the passengers come out, and when she had not found me among them she had decided I must have missed my flight. This was her last desperate attempt, one more look at the arrival gate before she gave me up for lost. She pushed through the people, searching, and I got my first proper look at her in the living world.

My heart slammed into a gear I did not know it had. She was better than the video. She was better than the photo Fina had pulled out of her Bible, better than every picture I had watched for weeks in my mother's lounge room. Every doubt I had carried eighteen thousand kilometres simply lifted off me and was gone. There was not one left. All I wanted in the world was to hold her.
So I walked up behind her and tapped her on the shoulder.
She pushed my hand away without even looking, because she thought it was her father, come to tell her it was time to give up and go.
"Hey, Dina," I said. "It's me."
She spun around. "Moses!"

We looked at each other, one long second, and then we were holding on to each other, and I said into her ear, "Please hold me, or I am going to collapse." Because I meant it. After thirty seconds of that she pulled back just enough to ask me, quietly, whether there was a man with white curly hair watching us. I said yes. "That," she said, "is my father. You had better let go of me now."

But here is the thing I have never been able to explain to anyone. The instant my eyes met hers, my whole spirit went down into a sea of love and something in me said, clear as anything, Ah. I'm home. I could not unlock my eyes from hers if you had paid me. I had flown to the far side of the earth to a woman I had never met, and I looked into her eyes and felt like a man walking back through his own front door.
I gave her the orchids, and she introduced me to her father, Antonino.

On the way to her home we made our first stop at her aunt Natalina's, in a place called Villa San Giovanni, right down near the water where you cross the strait over to Sicily. Aunt Natalina had a son, Salvuccio, who was a doctor, and she welcomed me not like a stranger but like a mother welcoming home a son she had been waiting years for. She threw her arms around me, squeezed the breath out of me, took me by the hand, and dragged me to a table laid out with a spread fit for a king.

After Dina's father gave thanks for the food and for my safe arrival, we ate. Or rather, everyone else ate. I could barely manage a mouthful, because my eyes were fastened on Dina and would not be moved. Dina, the moment she had finished her own plate, would not sit still. She was up and clearing dishes, helping set out the next course, refusing to let her aunt work alone. Part of me wanted her to stay in her seat beside me. The rest of me was quietly delighted, because here was the proof of everything Fina had told me, a home girl, a girl who could not bear to watch her aunt carry a tray by herself. I begged her, once or twice, to sit a little longer so I could go on looking at her eyes, and she would, for a moment, going pink with embarrassment, before she finally said, "I'm sorry. I can't let my aunty work on her own. I have to help her."
After about two hours we had to tear ourselves away to catch the ferry, because Dina's home was on the island, in Sicily, and the only way across was over the water.

We drove the car straight onto the ferry and out across the Stretto di Messina, the strait that separates the toe of Italy from Sicily. It takes about half an hour. The scenery was something out of a dream, the blue water, the mountains rising on the far shore, and me standing on the deck of a ferry beside a girl I was going to marry, on my way to spend three whole weeks on that beautiful island. I could hardly believe it was my own life.
We came off the ferry on the Sicilian side and drove another half hour, until we pulled up at the little grocery shop that Dina's parents owned.

I could not resist. I asked Dina whether I might play a trick on her mother, Angelina, walk in as an ordinary customer and see whether she would recognise me. Dina loved the idea. So I went in, said hello, and asked Dina's mother, very politely, whether she might make me a ham sandwich.
"It's him!" she cried, before I had finished the sentence. "It's him!"

By then Dina and her father had come in behind me, and the whole little shop filled up with joy. I met Dina's married sister, Marianna, and a few of the local customers who had heard what was about to happen and had come to be there for it, because it was a small beach village, and in a small beach village everyone knows everyone. The shop sat on the beach road, right at the foot of the mountain their house was built into. Dina's mother told me to go up to the house, have a shower, and rest, because that evening we would all have dinner at Marianna's place, just four buildings down from the shop.

We drove up a narrow winding road that ran out halfway up the mountain, parked, took my luggage, and walked the rest of the way up a wide stepped path that wound through the village to the top. Every house along it was painted a different colour, blue beside yellow beside terracotta beside white, the whole village stacked up the mountainside like something off a postcard. Halfway up the climb we reached Dina's parents' house, and I was met at the door by her sisters Romina and Natalie, and her grandmother Maria, all of them lit up with excitement.

After we had talked together for a while, they could see the tiredness weighing on my eyes, so they pointed me to the shower and then showed me to my room, a cute little room up in the attic with a bunk bed, a wardrobe, and a small window looking out over a back alley. I was so grateful for a bed that I barely noticed any of it. I lay down, and I think I was asleep before my head finished settling on the pillow.

It felt like one minute later that I heard Dina's voice calling up to me to wake and come down, that it was time for dinner at her sister's. I opened my eyes in that little attic, still half lost, working out where on earth I was.
Then I heard a voice.
It was as clear and as close as if someone were standing in the room beside the bunk, and it said, "Blessed is He who marries in this household."

There was no one there. I lay still in that attic on the far side of the world, in a house I had slept in for a few hours, and I knew exactly Who had spoken. After the orchids and the embrace and the long flight and the longer years, after the photo from the Bible and the two angels and the three prophecies, God leaned down into a tiny attic room in a Sicilian village and told me, in words I could not mistake, that He had blessed this. That I was exactly where He had always meant me to be.
I had crossed the whole earth chasing a feeling. Heaven had just confirmed it was the truth.

Dina's sister Marianna lived in the penthouse of a four-storey building right on the beach. The front of it looked out over the road, and the back looked straight out onto the Mediterranean. By the time we arrived that evening it was dark, and they took me out onto the back balcony to show me the view, and there across the black water I could see the lights of cars moving along the coast of mainland Italy, and the lights of the villages clinging to the mountains above it. I stood there looking at it and could hardly believe it. Postcard after postcard, this whole country, and I had landed in the middle of it to marry a girl out of a video.

They called us in for dinner, and Dina's father gave thanks for the meal, and we began on the good Sicilian food laid out in front of us. We had barely finished the first course when Dina's mother turned to me and asked me, straight out, what I thought of her daughter.
I looked at Dina, sitting beside me, and I said, "I love her, and I find her beautiful."
"That," her mother said, "is a yes." Then she turned to Dina. What did Dina think of me?
Dina said she was very pleased.
"That," her mother said, "is also a yes."

Then she apologised for being so blunt, but she wanted me to understand the situation. This was a small village. The reputation of the gospel sat on this family's shoulders, and she was not about to have people watching a young man come in and out of her house for three weeks with no announcement made. Since it was a small village, with only the one reception room, and since I was only here for three weeks altogether, she had already gone ahead and booked the one day available in that window for an engagement. The twelfth of May. If we were happy, we could get engaged.

I will be honest. My first reaction was to bristle. I had been raised to lead, not to be led, and here was a woman I had met only a few hours before, arranging my own engagement without so much as asking me. How dare she, I thought, take such a step without my permission.
Right in the middle of that thought, the Lord spoke to me, as plainly as the voice in the attic. Moses. I have paved the way for you. You can either complain about it, or you can enjoy the ride.

That settled it. Who cared who had done the organising? I wanted to marry Dina. God had laid the whole road out in front of me, smooth and straight, and here I was complaining about who had paved it. So I turned to Dina and asked her, "Are you happy with this?"
"Yes," she said.
"Then," I said, out loud, "let's get engaged."

The whole table broke into cheers. When the cheering settled, Dina's mother explained to me what it truly meant to them. They would not be able to come to our wedding in Australia. They were not in a position to afford it, and they could not leave the grocery shop. So this engagement, here, in their village, was the one chance they would have to stand inside our union while we were still close to them. They were going to make it a day to remember.

Before I had left Australia, my brothers and I had worked out a set of code words for my phone calls home, so I could tell them how things were going without spelling it out. If I liked her, I was to say the flight had been smooth. If I did not, the flight had been rough.

So when I rang the day after I arrived, to tell them I had landed safely, and my brothers asked how my flight had been, I told them it had been magnificent. In fact, I said, I was getting engaged in under two weeks. Then I said to them, do you remember the vision? Dina had two sisters. I told them plainly that I was looking at their wives.

Philip tried to remind me, a little nervously, that he was already engaged, and due to be married in six weeks to a girl back home. I told him that he was the one who had seen the vision, not me, and that if he truly believed it had come from God, he had better get on his knees and ask God about his own future, because I had a strong feeling he was about to make a serious mistake.
There is one more thing you need to know about that engagement, and it had happened six months before I had ever heard Dina's name.

I had been in a shopping centre on the Gold Coast, buying clothes, and as I was passing a jewellery shop, a beautiful ring caught my eye through the window. I felt compelled to buy it. I said to myself, This ring will fit whoever my wife turns out to be. I put it away and very nearly forgot about it, until the day six months later when I packed it into my luggage and carried it to Italy, to a girl I had not yet met, whose finger it was always going to fit.

Our engagement fell on the twelfth of May, which that year was Mother's Day, and that made the search for flowers nearly impossible. I wanted red roses, and I wanted one white rose in the very middle of them, and on Mother's Day in Italy there is not a red rose left standing in any florist in the land. We went from shop to shop until we finally found one with two dozen left. But not a single white one. The florist, seeing my disappointment, suggested we take a walk around the village and find a white rose growing in somebody's garden.

So, hand in hand, Dina and I set off to find a white rose. As we were looking, we noticed a beautiful white rose bush in the front garden of an elderly lady's home. We knocked on her door and explained that we were about to get engaged, and asked if we might pick just one white rose for the moment. She smiled and told us to take as many as we liked, the whole bush if we wanted. I picked two, just in case, and we thanked her and went on our way.

Dina asked me why I wanted a white one so badly. I told her. Among all the girls in the whole world, every one of them a red rose, I had found my one special one, and she was the white one, set apart, pure, in the middle of all the rest. That was why I had walked the streets of her village hunting for a single white rose when two dozen red ones were already in my hand. She was amazed, and she put her arms around me.

The engagement itself looked more like a wedding than an engagement. Dina's parents gave everything they had, because this was their one chance to be present at their daughter's union. There is a tradition in Italy that the family of the bride buys an engagement ring for the groom as well, so when we exchanged our rings, it truly felt as though we were being married. When I slipped the ring onto Dina's finger, it fit perfectly, and she said it felt like Cinderella's slipper. We all knew Dina's family would not be in Australia for the real wedding, and so the whole evening was filled with that knowledge, and it made the night both tender and sad. A great many tears were shed. At one point I went over to the bouquet, took out a single red rose, carried it to my mother-in-law, and told her, "Today, you have become as my own mother." We embraced, and we wept, and then the cake came out.

What a cake. The Sicilians know how to make a cake. But I will tell you the one comic tragedy of that beautiful night. I was so caught up in all the emotion of it, the speeches and the toasts and the champagne and the tears, that by the time I thought to look for a slice, the waiters had already cleared the tables, and I never got so much as a single bite of my own engagement cake. If I were to make a tradition out of it, I would call it a sign of good fortune, because everything else about that night could not possibly have gone any better.

The deepest joy of that night was that Dina's parents were there to share it with us. On one of the most important days of our lives, her mother and her father stood beside us and gave us their blessing, and behind them the whole family gave theirs too. We knew they would not be with us in Australia for the wedding, and so this was the night they laid their hands, and their love, upon our union. Blessed by her parents, blessed by the family, and blessed by God.

Dina came from a place where the stone houses cling to the side of the mountain. On that mountain stood a small church, and it shone there like a lamp in the dark. Its story began far across the ocean, in Argentina, in a time when that whole nation seemed to be on fire with God.

Revival was sweeping through the towns and the families. Hearts were waking up. Lives were being handed over to Jesus. Among the people it touched was Dina's grandfather, on her mother's side, a man named Francesco. Like many Italians before him, he had sailed to Argentina looking for a future. He went looking for opportunity, and he came home carrying something far greater. He came home carrying the gospel.

When he returned to Sicily, he brought a faith with him that could not be hidden. His words carried conviction. His life carried the proof of it. One by one, his family listened. One by one, they believed, until a whole household had received Jesus. But the flame was never meant to stay inside one home. He bought a little house halfway up the mountain, knocked out the walls inside it, and turned it into a church. It stands there to this day. It was more than stone and timber and mortar. It became an outpost of hope, a light shining out over the country around it. The gospel that had crossed an ocean now had a home, calling people in.

When my father-in-law, Antonino, came of age, and married into that family, the church passed into his hands. He did not inherit an easy position or a comfortable life. He inherited a mission, and he carried it faithfully for the next fifty years.

By day he worked as a labourer. His hands grew rough, his body grew tired, and his clothes carried the marks of honest work. But when evening came, his real labour went on. He visited homes. He spoke to his neighbours. He opened the Scriptures and told anyone who would listen about Jesus. On Sundays he stood before the congregation and led the services. Week after week, season after season, he watched over that little church in the middle of the village.

Higher up, at the very top of the mountain, stood the Catholic church, high above the village, looking down over every house below it. The villagers did not want to offend their own church, so they would not walk into his. He understood that, and rather than trying to bring them in, he thought of a way to bring the gospel out to them. He set up a few speakers outside his church, so that when he preached, the whole town could hear the sermon right from their own homes, without having to move a step. Then, when the service was over, he would make the short walk back home, and as he went, the villagers would be sitting on their chairs outside their doors or on their balconies, and one after another they would greet him and thank him, telling him how great the sermon was. He may not have had a packed church. But in God's eyes, he was preaching to the multitude.

He was not a man who only spoke about prayer. He lived it. There were calluses on his knees from the years he spent before God. While others slept, he prayed. When trouble came, he prayed. When the answers seemed far away, he prayed still. He obeyed what the Scripture says, and prayed without ceasing. Prayer was not an event in his life. It was the breath of it.

The church was precious to him. He poured his own money into it, determined that the house of God would stay beautiful and cared for. Every wall, every room, every small detail bore the mark of his devotion. From the top of that mountain, the church went on shining.

Then, at the age of seventy-five, he was told it was time to stop. For a man who had given his strength, his years, and his heart to the work, stepping aside was one of the deepest disappointments of his life. Yet even when his position changed, his calling did not. No one could retire the fire God had placed in him.

His greatest congregation was always his own family. He taught his children the ways of God, and made certain they understood that faith was not something kept for Sundays. It was the road they were to walk every day. They were raised in holiness, with the things of God placed firmly in their hands.

Beside him stood my mother-in-law, Angelina, a righteous and faithful woman, who lived with that same quiet strength. Everything she did was meant to honour Jesus and to make the gospel beautiful to those who watched her life. Together the two of them became a living answer to everyone who ever tried to belittle the faith. Their character spoke where arguments failed. Their home became a testimony. Their children became the evidence. They were more than caretakers of a church. They were guardians of a flame.

I often wish people like them could live forever. Men and women of courage, whose faith has been tested by hardship and made stronger through prayer, who do not chase recognition but quietly change generations. Yet I thank God that my father-in-law is still alive. Whenever we speak, he has a word from God for me. He encourages me to pray, to read the Bible, and to stay faithful. Though the years have passed, the fire in him has not faded.

And when I look at my wife, I can see the fruit of the home that raised her. She is diligent, righteous, and faithful, because she was brought up in the purity of the gospel. The same flame that crossed an ocean, climbed a Sicilian mountain, and burned in a little church now lives in the next generation. That is the wonder of a faithful life.
