It never ends with one person.

Years ago, one man sailed to Argentina in search of a future. God met him there and sent him home with eternity in his heart. He returned with the gospel. A family received Jesus. A church rose on a mountain. A young man took up the call and carried it for fifty years. Children were raised in holiness. Grandchildren inherited the story, and the light kept travelling. The world may never know how many prayers were spoken in the dark, how many tears fell on those callused knees, or how many souls found hope, because one family refused to let the flame die. But heaven knows. The little church on the mountain was never merely a building. It was an altar to obedience. It declared that one surrendered life can reach across oceans, climb mountains, and transform generations.

And still today the baton moves forward. The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness has not overcome it. The church may stand on a mountain in Sicily, but its light now shines wherever the family carries the name of Jesus, even to the ends of the earth.

In the first few days after I arrived, Dina took me up the mountain to the church. Some time later I wanted to spend time alone with God there, so they gave me the keys, and I went up by myself and let myself in. The moment I stepped inside, the weight of the Holy Spirit came down on me so strongly that I wept and could not stop. There was no mistaking it. It was the presence of God.

Dina told me afterwards that every single person who had ever set foot in that church came out baptised in the Holy Spirit, and she asked me how it had been for me when I went in. I told her the power of God had fallen on me so strongly that I could not stop crying. She laughed, and she said, "It happens to everyone."

The three weeks I spent on that island were never only about Dina. God had said, through Philip's vision ten years before, that there would be three brides for the three of us, and now that I had found mine, I understood that I had been sent to find the others as well. Dina had two younger sisters, Romina and Natalie, and I had come to believe, in my spirit, that I was looking at the wives of my brothers Andrew and Philip. But it was one thing to believe it, and another thing to say it to two young women who had not asked to be part of any vision.
I began with Romina.

There was a couple Dina's family loved, Carmelo and Liliana, who lived in a town called Scordia, a good two hours away, and we were invited to visit them. Romina came along with us, partly to keep us proper company, for in that village a man and his bride to be did not travel about on their own. The drive was meant to take two hours. With the traffic, it took us three.

Somewhere on that long road, Romina opened up to me. She told me, a little shyly, that there had been a young man from Germany she had cared for, that she had carried feelings for him for some time. But since the day I had arrived, she said, and since she had watched what God was doing in front of her own eyes, those feelings had quietly left her, and she no longer felt anything for him at all. I took that as my opening. I told her about my brother Andrew, the kind of man he was, and I told her about the vision Philip had been given years before, the three brides in white that God had promised the three of us. I watched something settle over her as she listened, something between wonder and surrender. She did not argue. She began, instead, to dream.
I should tell you about the sweets, because my family has never let me forget them.

Dina's mother had sent us off to Carmelo and Liliana's with a beautiful tray of Sicilian pastries, wrapped up carefully as a gift. Now, three hours in a hot car is a long time to sit beside a tray of fresh Sicilian pastries. By the time we were halfway there, we had, between us, eaten rather more of that gift than we were ever meant to. There was nothing for it but to find a solution. We stopped at a pasticceria along the way, bought enough fresh pastries to fill the gaps we had made, arranged them all back into the tray, and wrapped the whole thing up again so that no one would ever know the difference. Carmelo and Liliana received their gift none the wiser, and I have carried the secret of that tray for more than thirty years.

In truth, the pastries were only a small part of it. The Sicilians fed me as though I were a returning son the entire time I was there, and I never once had the heart to say no. By the time I flew home, twenty-one days later, I had gained eight kilograms.
Natalie was harder to win.

Where Romina had softened, Natalie held her ground. She did not want to hear about an arranged marriage at all. She wanted what every young woman dreams of, to be courted, to be chased, to live a love story of her own, and an arrangement spoken about over a dinner table was the very opposite of all that. So I did not push her. I simply told her, as I had told Romina, about Philip, and about the vision God had given him as a young man, the three brides God Himself had promised. I watched her come to the thing slowly, on her own. She began to understand that this was not two families arranging a convenient match. The one arranging it was God. The matchmaker was heaven itself. God did not leave her to take my word for it. He gave Natalie a dream of her own, and in that dream she was shown plainly that Philip was to be her husband, so that her certainty came not from me but from heaven. There was one more thing, too. She already knew Philip's face. In the very first letter I had ever sent to Dina, I had enclosed photos of myself with my brothers standing beside me, and Natalie had studied those photos long before any of this began.
So there it was. Three sisters, three brothers, one vision, drawing together exactly as God had said it would, ten years after He first showed it to a teenage boy.
Now I had to bring Dina home.

The custom in her village was clear and old. The groom would return to his own country, prepare the wedding, and the bride would follow only in the last week before the day itself, arriving alone, staying in a hotel until the morning she was to be married. That was how it had always been done. But I could not make peace with it. The thought of Dina making that enormous journey by herself, halfway around the world, sitting for all those hours beside whatever stranger the seat beside her happened to hold, was more than I could bear. I wanted to bring her home with me, at my side, where I could watch over her.
When I told Dina, she said she would be happy to come with me, if only her father would allow it. But she did not believe for a moment that he would.

That evening, at the dinner table, I asked if I might say something. I told them, with all the respect I had, that I understood and honoured their traditions. But I was not at peace with the idea of Dina travelling all that way on her own. The world was not always a safe place for a young woman alone. I asked her father, plainly, whether he would give me his permission to bring his daughter home with me, so that I could be with her, protect her, attend to her, and guide her through the airports if anything happened along the way.
The table went quiet. Then her father spoke.

"I knew this day would come," he said, "when I would have to let my daughter go. It was prophesied over her that she would leave for a far country, that her life would follow the pattern of Rebecca, who left everything she knew to cross a great distance and marry a man she had been promised to. I have had good reports of you from your pastor. I know that you are the one. I trust Dina. And if Dina is happy to go with you, then I give you my consent."
I had been expecting that answer. I was not shocked, only amazed at what God was doing. Her mother understood what it meant faster than I did, and the moment it landed, the tears came.
"That means," she said, "Dina is leaving in less than ten days."

She thought it could not possibly be done. An Australian visa, she said, took three months at the very least. Beyond the visa, I think the speed of it had simply caught her in the heart, the realisation that her husband had just released their daughter to the other side of the earth, and that the parting was no longer a distant idea but a thing with a date on it.

It was then that I told him the rest of what I believed God was doing. "Since you believe in dreams and visions and prophecies," I said, "let me tell you about my brother Philip." I told him about the vision Philip had been given years before, the three brides for the three brothers, and what it might mean for their other two daughters. Dina's mother very nearly came out of her chair.
"Did you come here," she cried, somewhere between laughing and weeping, "to take all three of my daughters?"
I told her the truth. I had come for one. But two more young men were coming behind me.

She did not know whether to laugh or to cry, and so she did both. For years, I learned, the people of that town had quietly mocked this family for raising their daughters so carefully, so set apart, so pure. There were those who had said that girls kept that sheltered would never find husbands at all. Here was God, answering all of it at once, sending three brothers across the world for three daughters, turning the whole of that mockery on its head.
There remained one impossible thing. The visa.

The next day I asked Dina's father to drive us into Messina, to a travel agency there. The manager listened to what we needed, and then he asked whether Dina already held an Australian visa. She did not. He shook his head. These things take months, he told us. The Australian consulate was in Rome, and we would need to travel there and begin the process in person, and even then there were no guarantees.
I did not argue with him. I prayed, quietly, on the inside. Lord, now would be a very good time for You to step in.

In the middle of his own explanation of why it could not be done, the manager stopped. Something changed in his face. "Give me your passport," he said to Dina. He called out to another agent in the other room, a colleague of his who happened to be travelling to Rome the very next morning. When the man came in, the manager handed him Dina's passport and said, "You're going to Rome tomorrow. See if you can get a visa on this passport."
The agent looked at it and said, simply, "I'll try."
Dina's father turned to me, and he was not unkind, but he was honest. "You will need a miracle for this," he said.
"Then get ready," I told him, "to see one."

Two days later, the telephone rang in the grocery shop. It was the manager, asking Dina to come into Messina. When we arrived, he handed her back her passport, and there, inside it, was the Australian visa. A process that should have taken three months had taken two days. The whole family rejoiced, and Dina's father looked at me, and at the passport, and said, "Hand of God. Hand of God." There was nothing else to say.

Then there was the ticket to pay for. I had set money aside for Dina's fare, but her parents would not hear of me paying it. After Dina came back to Sicily, her parents had bought the grocery shop, and she had worked there that year and dropped her savings into a money box, never once counting it. Her parents insisted her fare come out of that. So she broke it open, not knowing what was inside, and when it was counted, it came to the exact price of the ticket. Not close to it. The exact amount. That is the sort of God I was serving in those days, a God who had kept the coins in a girl's money box matched to the cost of the very seat that would carry her to her husband.

Dina had an older brother who also carried the name Moses. He had left Sicily at eighteen to become a policeman, and he lived now in Rome with his wife, Franchita, and their little boy, Antonio, who was six. Franchita was eight months along, carrying their second child. Dina's mother had one request to soften the parting. Would we stop in Rome on the way to Australia, and stay three days with her son, so that the family could be together a little longer before the distance swallowed us. Of course we would.

Our last Sunday in Sicily was the nineteenth of May, and our final meeting in Dina's father's church before we left. I knew what I wanted to ask for. I had grown up understanding that the blessing of a patriarch is worth more than gold or silver, and I did not want to leave without it. So after the meeting, I asked Dina's father if he would bless us, as a father blesses his children, for all the generations that would come after us.

He came round to the front of the pulpit, and the whole family gathered in close around us. He laid his hands on our heads and began to pour out the blessing over us, the way a father pours it over his own children. We stood there absorbing every word as though it were liquid gold from heaven. I felt as though the frame of our whole future was being built in those words, piece by piece. What sealed it for me was the way he finished. "I can only pronounce this blessing as a man," he said. "But may Almighty God Himself pour His oil upon you, from His heavenly kingdom, in the name of Jesus. Amen." In that moment I knew that we were sealed, and that we were sent.

A day later we drove to the airport at Catania. The whole family came to see us off, her mother and her father, her sisters, and even Carmelo and Liliana, who had made the trip in from Scordia to say goodbye. That was when it truly landed on all of us, that Dina was leaving, not for a visit, but for the far side of the earth. The tears came, and they did not stop. Handkerchiefs came out all around. There were hugs and kisses, and long embraces that no one wanted to be the first to end, the ache of a family letting one of its own go so far away, and underneath the ache, the quiet joy of sending her out under the blessing of God. Then we boarded, and Sicily fell away beneath us, and one hour later we came down in Rome.

Brother Moses was waiting for us at the airport, a big man, tall as a tower, and the moment he saw Dina he threw his arms around her and held her for a long time, this brother she loved and was about to leave for the other side of the world. Then he turned to me, and welcomed me warmly as the man who was soon to marry his sister. He drove us the forty-five minutes to his home, where Franchita and little Antonio were waiting with the door open and the table already set. They welcomed us as though we had always belonged there. The first two days were like something out of a dream. He showed us his city, and what a city it is. We stood beneath the Colosseum. We walked through the Vatican. We threw our coins into the Trevi Fountain. We wandered the old streets with coffee and warm pastries, and once we even boarded the wrong train and laughed our way back. For two days it felt like a honeymoon we had not planned, the four of us happy together in one of the most beautiful cities in the world.

On the third night, at three in the morning, brother Moses woke Dina. Franchita had begun to bleed badly, and he was taking her to the hospital. He returned alone in the grey hours of the morning, and he was weeping. They had lost the baby. A little boy. They had already chosen his name. David.

There was nothing anyone could say in a moment like that, so we did not try to speak. We put our arms around him, and we called on the name of Jesus over him, and we held a grieving father in the dark while the city woke up outside the window as though nothing in the world had changed. It was the first sorrow I tasted in that new family, and I did not yet understand how much a man can love people he has only just met, nor how completely their grief can become your own.

That same evening, we had to leave for Australia. Here is the measure of the man. Brother Moses, who had lost a son only hours before, would not hear of anyone else taking us to the airport. He drove us there himself. We held on to each other at the gate, all of us in tears, the joy of our wedding still ahead of us and the grief of a lost child standing side by side and refusing to let go of one another.

Dina and I boarded the plane, and we flew at last toward home. She was leaving everything she had ever known, her mother and father, her sisters, her village of brightly painted houses climbing the mountainside above the sea, to cross the whole earth and make her life beside me in a new country. She had visited Australia once before, the year before this, so the land itself was not a stranger to her.

There is something about that earlier visit I have to tell you, because only God could have arranged it. On that holiday, her aunt had taken her by bus up to the Gold Coast. Dina and her aunt were upstairs on a double-decker bus, in the very front seats, right up against the window. So, as the bus made its way through the Gold Coast, along the highway near the ocean, the whole of it was laid out before her like a screen at the cinema, sliding by frame by frame. The tall towers, the houses on the water, the palm trees, the beauty of the place presented to her front on. The road she was travelling was the road into the city, and it ran right past my own street, only a few houses down from where I lived. Looking out over it all, she said aloud to her aunt, "Blessed are the people who live here. It is such a beautiful place." She did not know that the man she would one day marry was there, just below her, as she said it. God had driven her past her own future and let her bless it, a full year before she understood that it was hers.

But this time she was not coming as a visitor. This time she was leaving home for good, the way Rebecca had, exactly as it had been spoken over her. When the doors of the aircraft opened on the other side of the world, and the warm Australian air came in, Dina set her feet down in the land that would hold the rest of her life. She had arrived in the far country. She had come home.

We landed in Brisbane on the twenty-first of May 1991, and a small crowd of family and friends was waiting at the airport to welcome us. It was a warm and excited welcome, everyone crowding in to meet my fiancée at last, and Dina was glad to meet every one of them, and excited to see her new life begin.

The airport gave us one more thing that day, though I did not learn of it until later. My brother Philip was standing in the welcome party, and Philip, at that time, was engaged to be married. He had an Italian girl from near our own town on the Gold Coast, a wedding date already set, and relatives who had booked their flights from overseas to come to it. But Philip had been carrying a question in him that he had never been able to settle. Ten years earlier he had seen three brides in a vision, promised to the three of us, and he did not know whether the girl he had chosen for himself was truly the one God had chosen for him, or whether he had run ahead of the promise and picked his own. He had been weighing that choice for a long time, his own will against God's design, unable to lay it down.

Then Dina walked through the doors. In that instant the vision came alive in front of him, and the question he had carried for ten years answered itself. He knew, with a certainty he said came straight from the Lord, that God's design was real and that he had almost settled for his own. He chose the promise over the plan he had made. By the time we all got home, he told us it was done. He had broken it off. It was a hard thing, and it looked an unkind thing, and I would not stand here and defend the manner of it. But I will say this much: the young woman herself admitted, later, that she had felt the very same, that something in her had known it too.

It left us looking at something none of us had arranged. All those relatives had booked to fly across the world for Philip's wedding, and now there was no wedding for them to attend. Only then did we see what God had quietly done. He had gone ahead of us and opened a window, a whole gathering of our family already booked and on their way, and we had only to step into it. So we set our own wedding for the week Philip's had been meant to take place. They had booked their seats for one wedding, and God had them arrive for another.

Ten days after we arrived, on the thirty-first of May, we were married at the city registry. It was the legal side of things, quiet and quick, a signature and a witness and a few words from an official, the marriage made real in the eyes of the law. We did it that fast for a reason. I wanted to put Dina's parents at rest. They had let their daughter travel to the far side of the earth with a young man they barely knew, and I wanted them to see that I was no charlatan, that I had meant every word I said, and that their daughter was truly and honourably my wife. It mattered to their town, too. In that watching village there were some only too glad to seize on any slip, any hint of misconduct, and use it to drag the gospel down. I did not want to hand them a single thing to talk about, no whisper of a young couple living in the same country before they were properly wed. I would not be the one to put a mark on a pastor's house. Marrying at the registry straight away settled all of it. The wedding, the real one, the one before God and the whole church, we set for the twentieth of July.

What I wanted to give Dina was a day that might make up, even a little, for everything her family could not be there to give her. I had promised myself she would not feel like a girl alone in a strange country marrying into a strange family. She would feel like a bride. We would surround her with people and music, and I would give her a day she would remember with joy.

There was one thing more I did, quietly, for the same reason. When we were in Rome, I had asked Dina's brother Moses, the policeman, if he would give me the badge he wore on his police uniform. I wanted to wear it on the coat of my wedding suit, over my heart, so that when Dina stood before me and made her vows, she would see it there on my chest, and know that her family was present with us in spirit, even though almost none of them could be there.

That is very nearly what it was. It was one of the happiest days of my life, from the morning to the very end of the night. If a few small things went sideways along the way, and one or two of them did, they have only ever made me smile in the years since. They are the sort of thing you laugh about at anniversaries. They never once touched the joy of the day itself.

The week before the wedding, the house filled right up. All of Dina's Sydney relatives had driven up for it, and from the other side of the world came mine. Dina's family did not stay with us, they had taken rooms at a hotel on the coast, but they were at the house through the days, and they had come with work to do. Aunt Ninetta and her daughter Mary, a cousin as dear to Dina as a sister, made wedding dresses for a living, and they had made every dress for our day, Dina's gown and the little white dresses for the girls, so they went carefully over each one, fitting them and setting them right. One of those little girls was my brother David's daughter, Aurelie, and one of the two boys was my sister's son, Daniel. Aurelie's dress had been sewn all the way over in Sydney from measurements posted to them, without the child ever standing in the room, so they were especially anxious that it should sit perfectly. Everything had to look just so, and they saw to it that it did. My bride, and every child who would walk in ahead of her, would wear gowns made by her own family's hands.

With my brothers still living at home, we fitted our own household in however we could. I took the unit downstairs, underneath my mother's house, sharing its two bedrooms with the twins, and Dina slept upstairs, in my mother's own room, for we did not sleep under the same roof as a couple until we were married in church. My mother had taught us something about that, and it had settled deep in me. She used to say that the first night belonged to God, that keeping ourselves until then was a way of telling Him we were not animals in a hurry to have our fill of one another, but a man and a woman who wanted to give the first fruit of ourselves to our Maker. Dina and I had talked it over and agreed together that this was how it would be. There was a kindness in it, too, beyond the honour to God. It meant a young bride could come to that day without a weight of expectation pressing on her, free simply to get to know the man she was marrying, in God's good time and not before. It was a full house, and a happy one, and it was in that week, before any of the wedding-day stories, that the first of them happened.

My brother David rang me from the Brisbane airport. He asked where I was, and I told him I was at home, where else would I be. He told me he was standing in the terminal with his whole family, and with our aunt Elvira, just off a twenty-four-hour flight from Belgium, all of them waiting for me to come and collect them, exactly as we had arranged. I laughed, certain it was a prank. It was not a prank. I had simply got the day wrong. I had it in my head that they were arriving the following day, and I had gone about my business without a care, while they stood in an empty arrivals hall, worn out, with nobody there to meet them. I told him to hold on, I would be an hour.

We had already arranged for my brother-in-law to come along in his own car to help me collect them, since one car would never hold all those people and their luggage. So when I heard I had the days wrong, I simply told him it was today, not tomorrow, and that I would go on ahead right away and he could come at his own pace. He was, to put it kindly, a careful and unhurried driver, and I was in no mood to crawl behind him with my brother's family standing exhausted in an airport.

I got into my car and prayed a prayer that tells you everything about the man I was in those days. I asked God to keep the police off me, to keep me clear of the radars, so I could get to the airport fast. I look back on that prayer now and I have to smile, and wince a little at the same time. In those days I had a habit of treating God as though He were there mainly for my convenience, a God who would happily bend His own rules to get me out of a tight spot, because He was fond of me. The astonishing thing, the thing I can only lay at the feet of how much He loved me, is how often He seemed to do exactly that.

The limit on that highway was a hundred kilometres an hour. I was doing a hundred and fifty. About halfway there I came over a rise and saw, far too late, five police cars pulled up along the left-hand side of the road, my side, the side heading into Brisbane, for in Australia we drive on the left. They were stopping cars for random breath tests. Before I understood what I was looking at I was already sailing past the whole line of them at fifty over the limit. I was certain they would pull out and come after me, and I slowed right down, saying out loud to myself, I'm done, I'm done. Nobody came. Not one of them moved. It was as though my car had turned to glass and every officer there had looked straight through it. I counted my blessings and drove the rest of the way at exactly the speed the law allowed.

I do not tell that to boast, and I would never tell a young man to pray that prayer. I tell it because it is true, and because it is a small, clear picture of the God I thought I knew in those years. A God who ran on ahead of me and cleared my road and bent the rules to keep me out of trouble, because I was His and He was fond of me. It would be many years before I learned that He is far greater and far deeper than my errands, and that His love is not the same thing as His approval. But that is a lesson for much further along in this book. On that morning, He simply let a foolish, speeding, overjoyed young man reach the airport in one piece.

When I found them, my brother-in-law had come to help carry so many people and their luggage, and we drove them home. Elvira was my mother's sister, and my mother had not seen her in ten years. Nobody had told my mother she was coming. When the two of them laid eyes on each other there were the kind of tears only ten years apart can make. It was the first time any of my mother's sisters had ever set foot in Australia, and it would be the only time. Elvira could not get over the place. The whole way from the airport she kept saying it, over and over, that we were living in paradise.

The night before the wedding, my brother-in-law had a good idea. He offered to have me stay over at his place, so that I would not see the bride while she was getting ready, and could get myself ready there in peace. I thought it wise, and I did.

On the morning of the wedding I was up before almost anyone. I had organised a limousine to collect Dina, and I wanted to be at the church early to set the whole place up myself. Much of it was ready to go, because the day before, the family had all sat together making paper flowers by the handful to help me decorate the church. I taught a good many of them how to fold and shape the paper, and we made piles of them. There were fresh flower arrangements too, and I had arranged for all of it, the paper flowers and the fresh ones both, to be carried on to the reception room afterwards, so that nothing beautiful would go to waste. I had never planned a wedding in my life, and I dare say it showed, but I put my heart into it. I hung the ribbons and set out the flowers. I did the best I could, and I was proud of it. I had also organised a long red carpet to run down the centre of the church, so that when Dina came in, her white dress against the deep red would look beautiful. What I had not counted on was the material. It was a strange, slippery material, and laid over that shiny timber floor it was like ice. So I wrote a note and had it sent across to Dina, warning her to walk very carefully on that carpet, because it was slippery. I did not know until she walked in whether the note had reached her at all, though she told me afterwards that it had. Then I went back to my brother-in-law's, dressed, and drove straight to the church.

Two friends of mine had offered to capture the day for us. One, a young man who had waited tables at the restaurant I was managing, was studying photography and offered to take the photos for nothing, for the practice. He had shown me some of his earlier work and it was good, so I had gladly said yes. Another friend offered to film it. I was grateful to them both, and thought no more about it. It was two less things to worry over.

Then it was time, and I took my place at the front, and the music began, a beautiful song the two of us had chosen for her entrance. My heart was pounding in my chest. From where I stood I watched the children come out of the limousine and start up toward the church, five little girls in white and two little boys, walking ahead of the bride. The people helping Dina kept her covered, so that I could not catch a glimpse of her, not until she stood at the front door of the church. Then the entrance music swelled, and there she was, and my tears began to roll down my face before I could do a thing to stop them. Down the aisle came the gift God had prepared for me before the day I was born. She was radiant in a beautiful white gown that her aunt Ninetta had made for her in Sydney, and the little girls wore dresses from the same hands. The whole entourage looked royal. She was walked down to me on the arm of her uncle, aunt Ninetta's husband, who was a brother of Dina's own mother, so that it was her mother's own blood who gave her away in her mother's place.

My own pastor and Pastor Foti, the pastor from the Sydney camp, married us together. It was Pastor Foti who had us exchange our vows, and I made mine to Dina as a promise I swore I would never break. My whole family stood there to see it, every one of them, apart from my father. My joy was so complete I can hardly put it into words, and it seemed to be over almost as soon as it began. Before I knew it the limousine was back at the door to carry us home, and we were finished by lunchtime.

The whole family came back to my mother's house together, cheering, with champagne, and we had a bite to eat, all of us packed happily into the one house. The reception itself was not until half past five.

By the afternoon I had come down with a headache, so I went downstairs to lie down for a while, and Dina rested upstairs in my mother's room. I fell asleep. When I woke and climbed the stairs, I got a shock. The house, which had been full of my entire family only a little while before, was empty. Every one of them had gone on ahead to the reception without a word. I knocked on my mother's door, and Dina came out, just waking herself, and the two of us understood that we were the only people left in the house. It was only then that I remembered I had forgotten to book a car to come and collect us. There was no limousine, and no one left to drive us anywhere. I went down to the garage to see if any car had been left behind, and thank God my mother's had. Dina settled herself into the front seat in her great white gown, and I drove my own bride to our own wedding reception. We had to stop at a few sets of traffic lights along the way, and each time, the people in the car alongside us would look across and see a bride sitting in the front seat, and the two of us would burst out laughing.

When we pulled up at the reception room they were all there waiting for us, some outside, some in. As we walked in, our own family band struck up to welcome us. David on his trombone, Gesuina on her accordion, Philip on saxophone, Andrew on trumpet, and my brother-in-law on the guitar. For a few minutes, on the Gold Coast, we were living a glimpse of what our church in Belgium had been, the same joy, the same music, the same family lifting it up.

The tables were set out in a great U shape. Dina and I sat at the short table in the middle that joined the two long sides, and there were just six of us there. My mother sat next to me, with her sister Elvira beside her. Dina was on my left, and beside her sat her aunt Ninetta and her uncle, up from Sydney. Down one arm of the U sat the rest of Dina's family, and down the other, facing them across the room, sat mine.

It was at the reception that the day played its last two tricks on us. About half an hour in, my friend with the video camera came over, crestfallen, to tell me the battery had died, and that by the time he drove home and back the whole thing would be over. I told him to leave it, not to worry, that we would remember this day for the rest of our lives whether it was on film or not. Then, later, the other truth came out. My friend the photographer, who had worked away so carefully all day, moving us this way and that, had never had a single reel of film in his camera. Not one photo of the wedding survived. Between the two of them, the empty camera and the dead battery, all that was left of our whole wedding day were the odd snapshots the guests had taken here and there. I remember Dina's face when we understood. She smiled, and held that smile in place with everything she had, so that she would not cry. In the end, I did not mind. Some days are meant to be kept in the heart rather than in a box.

There was one more moment I will never forget, and it came before the cake. Two of Dina's people, her cousin Frank, who was a bank manager, and Angelo, the husband of her cousin Mary, drew me aside into a private room. They were not churchgoers, and I have always believed God arranged for them to be there and to say what they said. They put it to me plainly. Dina was living up on the Gold Coast now, far from the rest of them, they said, but they were only an hour away in Sydney, and if they ever found out that I had mistreated Dina or wronged her, they would come, and it would not be pleasant for me. They were watching. I laughed, and I told them there was no need for any of it. I loved Dina with all my heart, and they could watch me all they liked, for all they would ever see or hear was the love I had for her. I thanked them, too, because what they had just done showed me how much they loved her, and that only made me love them more. We hugged, and I could see they were glad they had said their piece, and gladder still of my answer.

For a honeymoon, my niece Lidya, my sister's daughter, gave us a gift of two nights at a beautiful hotel right there in Surfers Paradise, the one that is called the Crowne Plaza now, with a revolving restaurant up on its roof where we ate the night after the wedding. When she had asked where we wanted to go, I had thought about it and decided we should simply stay. All of Australia comes to the Gold Coast for its holidays, I reasoned, so why go anywhere else? This way we could stay close to all the relatives who had travelled so far, and go on enjoying them by day, while the two of us kept our nights to ourselves.
It was the wrong decision, and it is worth telling you why, because it taught me the first real lesson of my married life.

I have told you already that I was raised in the thick of people, and that my wedding gave me the very thing my heart loved most, everyone I loved gathered into one place. I did not want it to end. I wanted to soak up every last minute of it. So when our two families arranged to come together again the day after the wedding, for a lunch at a community centre, I thought it a splendid idea. More time with everyone. Staying in Surfers had never been the mistake. Dina was glad to stay close by, just the two of us. The mistake was that I kept us among the family when I should have taken my bride away.

Dina did not tell me at first. I only saw that something was troubling her joy, some shadow she was trying to keep off her face so as not to spoil mine. Later she told me what it was. The day after our wedding she had to sit in a room full of family, both sides, hers and mine, and feel their eyes on her, the big knowing smiles, the sense that every one of them was picturing the same thing and thinking they knew what our first night together had been. She felt exposed. What had been sacred to her, her union with me, her dignity as a new wife, was being quietly passed around a room like common gossip, and she had no way to escape it. She had hoped, without ever pressing me, that we might simply have gone away, the two of us, and seen everyone another time, when we were next in Sydney or they came up to us.

It had never once entered my head. In my hunger to keep everyone close, I had not thought to protect the one person I had just promised to protect above all others. It grieves me still, all these years later, to think of her sitting in that room carrying something heavy and alone, keeping it off her face for my sake, while I sat happily beside her, not seeing it. If only I had known. If only I had thought for one moment to ask myself how the day looked through her eyes instead of mine, I would have taken her away without a second thought, and spared her all of it. I would have stood between her and that whole room. That is all a husband is for, and on that day I did not know it yet.

That was my first lesson as a husband, and I have never forgotten it. To love Dina was not enough. I had to learn to climb inside her mind and feel a thing the way she felt it, from where she stood and not from where I stood. It is a lesson God has gone on teaching me all my married life.

There is one image from that lunch, though, that I keep. Both families took the paper flowers we had all made together for the church, and the fresh flowers besides, and built a great heart on a stand, with the letters M and D joined in the middle of it. Two families from opposite ends of the earth, most of them meeting for the first time, bent over a pile of flowers, making one heart out of them. Whatever I still had to learn about my wife, that heart was true. It was the sign of the thing God had done, two houses made one, and my name and hers set side by side in the centre of it.
There is one more thing I have to tell you before I close this chapter, because without it the story is only half told.

Ten years before any of this, in a quiet lounge room on the Gold Coast, in the middle of the worst season our family had ever known, my brother Philip had picked up his guitar, and the Spirit of God had come over him, and he had seen three young women from behind, dressed in white, and heard the Lord say, I am preparing three sisters for you three brothers. We had tucked that promise away because we were too wounded and too young to do anything else with it.
Now I watched it come true with my own eyes.

I had married Dina. Within eighteen months, both of my brothers had crossed the world to Sicily and married her two sisters. Philip married Natalie, the sister who had wanted to be courted rather than arranged, until she understood that the one arranging it was God, on the twenty-third of February 1992, at Scaletta in Sicily. On the very day of Philip's wedding, at the very same reception, my brother Andrew became engaged to Romina, so that the guests found themselves at two celebrations at once, a wedding and an engagement under one roof, the promise unfolding two sisters at a time in front of their eyes. Andrew married Romina later that same year, on the sixth of October, on the Gold Coast in Australia. Three brothers. Three sisters. Three weddings. One vision, seen a decade earlier by a heartbroken young man strumming a guitar, who could not see the faces of the brides God was showing him because God had not finished painting them yet.

Six months before I went down to Sydney for the camp, an old lady we knew, who lived directly across the road from my mother, passed away. I went to her family and asked whether I could buy her house, and they set a price within my reach, low enough that I could borrow against it and carry the repayments on my own. So I bought it. I rented it out on a one-year lease and thought no more about it.
I see it clearly now. First the ring, and then the house. Both sat waiting, in the dark, for a life God already knew was coming.

So when Dina and I began our married life, the tenants still had half a year to run on their lease, and so, for the time being, we moved into the small granny flat at the back of my mother's house to wait the lease out. We had little to spare and the whole of a life ahead of us to build.
Because Dina had paid for her ticket, the money I had set aside for it was left free, and it was just enough to pay for our wedding.

The day the lease ended, we crossed the road from my mother's house and into the first home of our married life. We did not have much to fill it with, but Dina had a way of turning bare rooms into a place you never wanted to leave. She turned that house into a warm country home. And the best part was that she was in it, and that made me feel like the richest man in the world.

Around that time, the Italian pastor whose church we had belonged to went back to Belgium to live, and took his family with him. It left our little Italian community without a shepherd, and something in me could not let it simply scatter. So Dina and I started our own Italian church. We held it in the very community centre where we had gathered the day after our wedding, and we drew in the family and all our Italian friends, and we began.

I can see now what I was really doing. I was trying to rebuild what my father had built and lost. I did not want our memories of Belgium to end on something sour, a great church pulled down and a family broken. I wanted to gather it all up again and hand my family and my future children the thing I had grown up inside. We kept it going for a year and a half. I preached the love of God, and I meant it. I gathered my family in and did my best to feed them from the Word. But if I am honest, I did not feel God was in it, not the way I had told myself He was. My purpose was not quite the right one. What was driving me was not my father's fire for the lost. It was the instinct of a man who wanted his family under one roof again. But a good instinct is not the same thing as a calling. I had grown up watching God's fire burn in my father's church, I knew exactly what it looked like, and this was not it.

It was a pastor in Surfers Paradise who helped me see it, a man named Richard Nugent, whom I had come to confide in. When I told him honestly how things stood, he did not flatter me. He said that if I was pouring my strength into something that had no life left in it, I should come and pour it into what he and his people were doing instead, and run alongside them. There was a great relief in hearing it said plainly. So I closed our Italian church, and our entire family joined his, the Surfers Paradise Assembly of God, as it was known in those days, and we settled in there to serve, and it is the church we have belonged to ever since, right up until now.
Then, on the twenty-eighth of August 1992, a little over a year after Dina and I married, our first child was born. A son. We named him Joshua.

I have told you already that I became a father once before, at seventeen, when I found myself with a mother and two younger brothers looking to me for everything. That fatherhood had been handed to me by a disaster. I had not chosen it. It had fallen on me, and I had carried it because they were my family, and I was not going to leave them stranded. But this, this was different. This was a fatherhood given to me as a gift, a son we had longed for, placed in my arms, mine to love rather than mine to rescue. I held him and I understood that God had let me become a father twice. Once by necessity, and now, at last, by choice.

There is a thing the Bible does with the name Joshua that was not lost on a family like mine, where every name carried a story. Joshua was the one who stayed at Moses's side, the young man who never left him, and who went on after him. That was reason enough for me to love the name for a son of my own.

I had wanted the name Joshua for as long as I could remember, a Joshua to follow after my own name. But when I said the name to Dina, she went quiet, and then she told me something she had kept hidden in her heart for an appointed time. Her own father had longed all his life for a Joshua, a son to come after his own son Moses, Dina's brother, just as in the Bible. But that Joshua had never come. So Dina had made her father a promise. If ever she married and God gave her a boy, and if her husband would allow it, she would call him Joshua, and make her father's wish come true at last. Neither of us had told the other. We had each carried that name toward our marriage from opposite sides of the world, she for her father, I for mine, and when the time came to choose it, there was nothing to decide. It had been chosen for us already, on both sides of the family, before we ever met. I did not plan my life around that. But I have never been able to look at my son's name beside my own without feeling that God has a sense of these things, and that He arranges them long before we notice.
I made myself a quiet promise over that boy, and I will keep it until I die.
My own father, for all that he was a great man, had not managed to live out the very thing he preached. That failure shaped me more than all his great words put together.

So when I held Joshua, the promise took its shape. I would be a captain who never left his ship. Whatever came, whatever it cost me, I would not step off the deck of my own family. My children would never have to stand where I had stood at seventeen, looking at the place a father is meant to be and finding it empty. My father had handed me a faith I would never let go of, and for that I will thank him for the rest of my life. But I wanted to give my children that same faith and one thing more besides: a father who was still there in the morning, and the next morning, and every morning after that, no matter what.

The favour that had run through my whole life, the buses, the marriage across the world, the three sisters for the three brothers, had not stopped. It had simply turned domestic. It looked, now, like a wife, a son, a home of our own, and a future to build in it, and I thanked God for every piece of it.

There was a reason that promise to Joshua went so deep in me, and it goes back to a gate, and to a spirit that came onto me behind it when I was a boy, one I would not be free of for a very long time.

When I was nine years old, and my brothers Philip and Andrew were eight, the Italian government made an offer to the Italian families living in Belgium. They would take the children to Italy for a month in the summer, to colonies set up for that purpose, so that we would learn the language of our own people. The whole thing was free. My mother took the offer.

To get us to go, she painted us a picture of it. She told us we were going on a long train journey, far away, to somewhere beautiful, and that we would have a wonderful time. Every time we asked her what would be there, she gave us more of it. Were there horses? Yes, beautiful horses. Were there merry-go-rounds? Yes, merry-go-rounds. Mum, is there chocolate ice cream there? Yes, she said, you can eat all the ice cream you want. Little by little, out of her promises, we built a paradise in our minds, and we wanted to go, and it did not hurt that it was somewhere other than where we were.

My mother was with us all day on the train. After a long day of travelling we fell asleep. When we woke, she was gone. There were other women with us, telling us not to worry, that we would be there soon.

When we arrived, there were no horses and no merry-go-rounds. There was a vast stretch of land near the beach with two army barracks standing on it, and nothing else. We looked around for everything we had been promised, and it was not there. We were frightened, and we were certain our mother had tricked us and left us behind. If I am honest, I believe that is where it began in me. That is where a gate closed that would stay closed for a very long time.

The dormitory had two hundred beds in it. The windows had no curtains. They had been painted over, thinly, some of them blue, some of them green, so that only a dim light could come through. My little brothers cried, but I told them not to be afraid, because I was there with them. The women spoke only Italian, and we couldn't understand them properly. One day one of them said something to Andrew. He did not understand her, so he answered no. She took it as defiance, and she began to smack him. He cried, and I cried with him, trying to tell her that he had meant yes, that he simply had not understood the question. Every time we asked when we could go home, they told us tomorrow. Tomorrow never came. It went on like that for a month.

It was not all fear. We did learn some Italian, and some songs, and there were days with games and things to entertain us. But there were things about the place that I have never forgotten. All the boys had to shower together in one huge room, and I hated it. And because the colony was right on the beach, there was always sand in the glasses we drank our water from.

They brought us into a Catholic church, too, to have mass. It must have been a Catholic colony. We had always been taught that people should never worship statues, and so when we walked in and saw them standing everywhere, we were afraid. To me it was like a cemetery. They told us to kiss the ring of the priest. I would sooner have died than do it. They must have seen the fear in my face, because they never made me.
The next year, she sent us back.

This time we knew exactly what was waiting for us. We would go often to the gate and look out through it, because on the outside it was a beautiful place, a tourist place. Out beyond the gate there was a great arena, rows of seats built up all the way around a huge pool of water in the middle. It was some kind of sea park. From where we stood we could see the dolphins leaping up out of that pool, right over the top of it, and we would watch them and long to be out there.

That was the year my brother David married, and he came near the colony on his honeymoon. He asked whether he could take us out, even for a while. They told him no, that it was not allowed, for security. We stood at the gate and begged him to get us out. All we were allowed was to speak to him and his new wife, and to my sister and her husband, through the bars of the gate. He promised us it would not be long now, that soon it would be time to go home, that we were not to worry. We cried. We cried so often in that place.
I did not have a name for what that gate put into me. I carried it out of childhood and into my own manhood without ever knowing it was there.

It showed itself when Joshua was small, on the first day I took him to kindergarten. When the moment came for me to leave, my son turned around and looked at me, and his face said the thing I could not bear. You are not going to leave me here, are you? I was behind that gate again, all at once, a small boy watching the people who loved him walk away. I started to cry. No, my love, I told him. Daddy is not going to leave you. I knelt down and I explained it to him as gently as I could, that I would come back, that he could play with his friends, that I would not be far. I spent a long time over it. When I got home I was still in tears. Dina asked me what had happened. I told her that if she wanted Joshua to go to kindergarten, she would have to be the one to take him, because I could not stand to see him cry behind a gate. My own past had devastated me. But Joshua himself made it easy on me in the weeks that followed. He came to love his kindergarten, and once he understood how it worked, that I was only ever just around the corner and always came back for him, he was happy to go. The gate was never his wound. It was only ever mine.

It was not until a few years later that it finally came out of me. I was telling this whole story to some friends who understood deliverance, and as I told it I began to weep, and I could not stop. One of them told me, gently, to let it go, that the spirit had come up as I spoke and it was time to be free of it. Until that moment I had never known there was such a thing as a spirit of abandonment, or that it had been living down in me the whole time. But it had, since I was nine years old, behind that gate. There, telling the story with the tears running down my face, I let it go, and it left me. And I know that it left me. I will tell you how I know, but that part of the story belongs further on, in a chapter still to come.

We were not finished building, though. Dina and I are both creative people, good with our hands, and we had always loved houses. That first home across from my mother we had shaped into a little cottage, and we were happy in it. But a couple of years on, we heard that a new estate was going up nearby, and since the two of us loved nothing better than walking through display homes for decorating ideas, we went to look. I said to Dina, plainly, as we drove in, that we were only looking, that she was not to fall in love with anything, because we were staying where we were in Mermaid Beach.

We walked through the first display house and did not like it. The rooms were small, the design too closed in. We were open-plan people, we told the agent who met us at the door. He said he had one he was sure we would love, and he took us through it, and he was right. We loved it at once, big and open and full of light, just the size we liked. Then he told us the catch. That house was already sold. But this design, the one we had just fallen for, was being built only once more, on the block directly across the road. That was the last of it. We loved that block too, the wide frontage, the shape of it.

We told him again that we were only looking. He asked why we did not simply buy it. All it would take, he said, was a thousand dollars to hold it. I had the thousand dollars. But I had not so much as put our own house up for sale, and the mortgage would climb a great deal, and so I was pulling back even as I stood there loving the place. Then he made me an offer I could not refuse. Bring the thousand, he said, and I will hold the block for you. Take the weekend to decide, and if you are still not sure, I will give you your money back. There was nothing to lose in that.

Dina looked at me as if to say, what are you doing, you are the one who said we were only looking. I went to the bank, drew out the money, gave it to the agent, signed, and drove home to start doing my sums. That weekend I brought in an agent to tell us what our little two-bedroom cottage might fetch, and once we had settled on terms with her, we put the cottage on the market. Needless to say, we bought the new house. We waited six months for it to be built, which worked out perfectly, because it took us just about that long to sell the cottage. By the time the new house was finished, the old one was gone, and we moved straight in.

We poured ourselves into that home. Dina made beautiful curtains with her own hands. I found a second-hand dining suite, sanded it back, polished it, and gave it a whitewashed look. People walking past used to say it was the best-looking house in the street. In those days, to us, it looked like a palace.

There was one thing in that house that meant more to me than all the rest. When my parents had divorced, and everything they owned was divided between them, there were three things that could not be split, three beautiful pieces we had carried all the way from the apartment in Belgium. A huge crystal chandelier, a golden standing lampshade, and a Louis the Fifteenth golden clock, a replica my father had bought on one of our holidays in Italy during the years we lived in Belgium. Since they could not be divided, we shared them out among us. I took the chandelier. Andrew took the lampshade. Philip took the clock. I had been there, a boy at my father's side, on the day he bought every one of them, and they had never left me.

That chandelier hung right in the middle of the lounge room of our new house, shining exactly as it had on the first day my father brought it home. It was more than a beautiful thing to me. It was a piece of everything we once had, and a piece of my own broken childhood, carried out of the wreckage of my family and hung, whole and shining, over the beginning of my own.

I thought I could see the whole shape of our life from there. A home, a marriage, a son, and room to grow. I did not yet understand that our family was still being added to, and not only here on earth.

Because there was another child coming to us. A daughter. Before she was ever born, before Dina ever carried her, she was chosen, in a place I would be shown one night in a way I have never been able to fully explain, and have never once doubted. But that is the next chapter, and it is the most important one I will ever tell.

When Celeste was small, she loved for me to tell her stories at bedtime. I kept a rotation of them going, the old stories my own mother had told me when I was a boy, stories out of the Bible, and ones I invented myself as I went.

Then one night, something in one of those stories set her wondering about how she had come to be, and she asked me. Dad, how did I get here? So I opened myself up and relied on God to show me how it happened. And that was when it began.
This one did not come the way the others came.

You know the wonder of how life begins at conception. A great multitude sets out together, each one carrying the whole of a child that might be, and they run toward the single hidden place where life is waiting. Only one arrives. Only one breaks through and is welcomed in, and out of all the countless children that might have been, that one is chosen, and begins.

That is how the words of this story came to me. Out of all the words I might have spoken, one would rise and press forward and break through, the living one, the chosen one, and take its place, and then the next, each arriving the way a child arrives, out of millions, exactly itself and no other. I was not inventing this story. It was being conceived in me, word by word, and I knew, as it came, that it had been given to me, whole and alive, by God.
Before you were born, I said, your mother and I were called up to heaven to choose you.
It was late at night, and we were fast asleep, when a bright light woke us. It was shining in through the window, brighter than the moon, brighter than anything.

We got up and went to the window to see what could be shining so, and I pulled back the curtains, and oh, what a sight was waiting for us. There, floating just outside, was a great white horse with enormous wings, folded softly at its sides. And sitting high on its back was a beautiful angel. He had hair like shining gold, and armour that glittered and gleamed, and he smiled at us the kindest, warmest smile you ever saw. He looked straight at us, and he lifted his hand, and he beckoned us to come to him.

And then, in the most wonderful way, the angel drew us right through the window and set us gently onto the great horse with him. He told us not to worry about your brother Joshua, fast asleep in his little room, because his very own angel was watching over him and would keep him safe. Then, because he had somewhere wonderful to take us, the huge wings opened wide, and up, up, up we went.

Up we flew, higher and higher, and everything below grew smaller and smaller, the houses like little toys, the streets like ribbons, the whole wide world shrinking away beneath us, until there was nothing all around but stars, thousands and thousands of them, flashing and sparkling past us as we flew. And then, ahead of us, we saw it: a great golden gate, shining like a giant pearl in the dark. It swung open as we came near, and we passed straight through. The angel brought the horse gently down, and we landed softly at the foot of a great white palace, taller than any building on earth. We had arrived. We were in heaven.

Another angel was waiting there to meet us, and he led us inside. And oh, Celeste, it was magnificent. The hall was vast, an enormous place, grander than anywhere we had ever been, with mighty pillars of gold and white rising up all around us, and the ceiling so high, so very high, that it looked as though the roof touched the sky itself. Then the angel asked us a question. Did we want a little boy, or a little girl? We told him we already had our boy, your brother Joshua, and now, oh how we would love a little girl. And there before us, in the middle of that great hall, rose two grand staircases, one curving up on the left, and one on the right. The one on the left was made of blue marble, and that was the way to the boys. The one on the right was made of pink marble, and that was the way to the girls, and that was the way the angel sent us.

Up the pink staircase we climbed, and at the very top another angel was waiting for us. This one was a girl angel, with beautiful long flowing hair and a beautiful pink dress. She reached out and opened a great door, a giant door, taller than a house, all gold and white and gleaming. And when that great door swung open, oh, Celeste, what we saw took our breath away.

And when we stepped in, what do you think we saw? A great room, filled from end to end with little cots. And in every single cot lay a tiny baby girl, hundreds and hundreds of them, all sleeping softly, all of them waiting, ready to be sent down to earth. Somewhere in that room, the angel told us, was the one who was meant for us, and we were allowed to walk among them and find the one we preferred.

Then we saw it. One special cot, right in the very middle, lifted up higher than all the rest. And over that one cot hung a soft veil, drifting down from high above, so that we could not see the baby who lay beneath it. But the moment we saw it, something tugged at our hearts and pulled us towards her, even before we had seen her face. And we asked the angel, please, may we see the little girl in that cot?
And the angel said no. That one, she told us, was very, very special. She had been set apart for something, and she could not be chosen.

But our hearts would not let go. We begged her. Please, just one look. Just one little moment. Just to see her face. And at last the angel smiled, and she gave in. She lifted the veil, just for a tiny moment, and let us peep.

And that one tiny moment was all it took. The moment we saw that little face, we knew. We did not want any other baby in all that room, nor in all of heaven, nor anywhere in the whole wide world. We wanted her, and only her.

The angel told us to choose another. She pointed us on to the other cots, the other babies, but we would not move an inch. She could see it in our faces, that our hearts were set fast on the one baby we were not allowed to have. And when she saw that we would never give up, she said that she would go and ask the Lord Himself. And that was when Jesus came into the room.

And oh, when Jesus came into the room, we could hardly believe our eyes. It was Jesus Himself, the Lord Himself, come to see us. We were so amazed we could barely breathe. He looked at us, and He smiled, and then He spoke to us gently, the way you say a hard thing to someone you love.
You don't know what you are asking for.
We still did not stop to weigh the words. We wanted her. We begged Him for her, both of us together, the way we had begged the angel, and we told Him that she was the one and there could be no other.

Then He told us why she had been set apart. This little one, He said, was going to rescue many of the others, the children who would not be raised in love, the ones who would be mistreated and rejected, the ones who would end up with no mummy and no daddy. She had been kept aside for that.

Yes, He said, you may have her. But you must promise Me something. You must promise to love her, and to teach her about Me, and to keep her close to Me always, and never let anything steal her heart away from Me.
And we promised. Oh, we promised with all our hearts. We told Him we would love her, and teach her His ways, and give our whole lives to looking after her.

Then Jesus told us one more thing. I am giving her to you, He said, but I will never take My hand off her. She will always be Mine. And if anything bad ever tried to take her away from Me, I would come quickly and snatch her back, and hold her tight in My arms, and never let her go, because she is My little girl, and I love her so, so, so much.
He gave her to us.
And I asked Jesus, what is her name? And He said, I cannot tell you her name. All I can tell you is that it starts with the letter C. But if you guess it, I will let you know.
This was her favourite part. Because now I would start to guess, and Jesus would answer me, and she would wait, and wait, with her eyes shining.
Is it Celine? No.
Is it Carolina? No.
Is it Camilla? No.
Is it Claire? No.
And then, just before I said it, I would stop. No, Jesus, I would say. Don't tell me it is my very favourite name. Is it Celeste? And Jesus would say, yes. Yes, it is.
And Celeste would burst out laughing, laughing and hugging me with all her joy, and she would say, tell me the story again, Daddy.

And then, I would tell her, Jesus said it was time for us to go home. He told us that in nine months she would be in our arms at last. So the angel took us back the same way we had come, up onto the great winged horse, out through the shining gate, down and down through the stars, all the way home to our own house and our own bed, with the wonderful promise that she was coming.
And nine months later, just as He promised, she came.

I thought I was giving my daughter a beautiful story about herself. I did not understand that I was sitting at the edge of her bed prophesying her future. I was reciting her life to her, over and over, in her own bedroom. Everything that story held was true, and everything it held was still to come.

When Celeste was born, Dina's parents were here in Australia with us. Her mother was there in the room beside me when our little girl came into the world, and all of us were overjoyed to see this new one added to the family. For the first few months I gave my in-laws all the time with her they could want, and I held back a little myself, because I knew they would soon have to return to Sicily, and only God knew when they would next have the chance to hold her. Once they had gone home, though, I began to come to know her properly. I stood over her one afternoon, simply watching her sleep in her cot, when all at once she woke, and looked up, and saw me, and gave me a smile that went straight to the deepest part of my heart. In that moment I knew. She had me. No one on this earth would ever love her the way that I would. She was my baby girl.

It started one day when Dina found her in tears. There was nothing wrong with her, nothing that had happened to her that day, so Dina sat down on the bed beside her and asked her what was the matter. Celeste said, I feel hurt for my friend. I feel that she is crying right now. Dina understood what was happening. The gift was coming to life in her. She explained to Celeste that when she felt like that, it was God showing her that her friend was in need of prayer, and she taught her how to pray for them. The two of them sat there together and prayed, until Celeste looked up and said that her heart felt better now.

Dina knew that girl, and knew her mother. The next week she saw the mother at school, and asked her whether anything bad had happened to her daughter on that day the week before. The mother said that it had. The little girl had climbed up on the chicken coop, and fallen, and hit her head, and they had taken her to hospital.

Dina came home and told me what the mother had said. That confirmation made us realise that Celeste had received the spirit of intercession. She had felt that child's hurt at the very same hour it happened, and was taught to take it to God in prayer.

I had stood once with Joshua in my arms and promised myself that I would be a father who never left, who came when he was needed, who stayed at the wheel no matter what. Celeste was the child who took me at my word. She was Daddy's girl.

In the story, we had given God our word to raise her for Him and to keep her close to Him, and by His grace, and with everything Dina and I had, we kept it. She grew up in the church and in the faith, with her face turned towards God from the time she was small. By the time she was a young woman she had given herself to her youth group and to the people in it, carrying others to the Lord.

She was tuned to other people's feelings in a way I have rarely seen in anyone, let alone in a child. She could read a room the moment she stepped into it. She was tuned to mine most of all. She kept her father inside her circle at all times, watching to see that I was happy, and if something in me shifted, even a little, she was onto it straight away and would not rest until she knew what it was. I was the same with her. Whatever she needed, I was there.

I remember the day she came and begged me to let her have her hair chemically straightened. She had been struggling with her hair for years and had begun to believe she would never win. Dina and I told her yes, she could have it done, when she turned thirteen. From that moment she counted the weeks. She would check with us again and again to make sure we had not changed our minds.

When the day finally came, I took her to the hairdresser myself. It cost a great deal of money in those days to have it done, and I did not care in the slightest. I wanted my daughter to have her day.

I left her there and came back three or four hours later. She turned around and looked at me, and I looked at her, and all I could say was, oh my, look at the beautiful girl you have just become. I watched the joy rise straight up through her. Her confidence arrived with it, all at once, and from that day she was Queen Celeste. She wanted photos taken. She wanted the world to know that she had arrived.

Not long after, her aunt Romina was starting a new business making photos and albums, and she needed a model, someone she could photograph so that people could see the quality of her work. She had wanted to use her own daughter, Jasmine, but Jasmine wanted nothing to do with it. So she asked Celeste. Celeste did not think about it twice. She said yes, and they made a whole album of her, and she stood in front of that camera taking shot after shot like a model, completely at home, exactly where she wanted to be. Celeste had become a young lady and the whole world was going to know about it.
Those photos are the ones we hold closest to our hearts now.
When she was a little older, there was an afternoon I have never forgotten.

She came to me one day and asked whether she could go to the cinema with a boy she knew. I wanted to know more about him than she had told me. She reassured me that he was a friend, only a friend, and that there was nothing more to it than that. So I agreed. I drove her there myself and told her to telephone me when the film was over, and she said that she would.
I had been home barely half an hour when the telephone rang. It was Celeste, asking me to come and get her. I asked whether she was all right. She said that she was, but that I should come now.

She got into the car furious. She told me she could not believe that boy. At school, when they had made the plan, she had settled it plainly with him, that they were going only as friends, and that there was to be no touching, and he had made her feel that was all he wanted too. But ten minutes into the film, while her hand was resting on the arm of the seat, he reached across and started touching her fingers. So she turned to him and said, you are not a man of your word, you will never be my friend. Then she stood up and walked out.

I sat there in the driver's seat listening to her, and I do not think I have ever been more proud of my daughter than I was in that moment. Everything Dina and I had tried to put into her was standing up on its own two feet. She was becoming exactly the person we had promised God we would raise. That made her father very proud.

I do not want to leave you with a picture of a girl who never put a foot wrong, because that was not Celeste, and she would not thank me for it. She made her mistakes. She loved this world, and most of all she loved the people in it. She had an enormous character, open and outspoken and loud. Her laugh carried. You could hear it right across a room and well beyond it, and once she started the rest of us would go with her. She was sharp, and she was very funny, and we laughed and we laughed. Wherever that girl was, she brought fun into the room with her.

I watched the promise come true in her. The child chosen behind a veil grew into a girl who lived exactly as He had said she would: set apart, tender towards the lost, always with someone else on her heart. She was everything we had been promised, and more than we had ever known to ask for.

In August of 1999 we took the children to Sicily for a holiday. Celeste was four years old. One day I was running on the beach when I felt a pain deep in my leg. It did not ease. It grew worse, until I could not stay on my feet. I was taken to a hospital there in Sicily. Even though they did an ultrasound, the doctors could not work out what it was. They guessed it was a torn muscle. In the end they sent me back to my in-laws' house to rest, and there I stayed, in bed, for the better part of a month, before it was time to fly home to Australia.

I flew all the way back with that pain still in my leg, not knowing what I was carrying. I could not walk. Dina had to push me through the airport in a wheelchair, with the two children beside her and the hand luggage as well. As soon as we arrived home in Australia, Dina took me to see our doctor. His face changed. He suspected a blood clot, and he sent me immediately to hospital. There the tests were done, and they revealed what I had been carrying all that time. A thrombosis, deep in my leg. I could have died at any moment on that long flight home. The tests revealed something else as well. I had Factor V Leiden, a mutation in the gene that helps control clotting. It meant my blood would clot too easily, when it should not, over and over, for the rest of my life. They put me on a medication called warfarin to thin my blood, and it left me weak.

The doctors told me I had to stop working. I had spent my whole working life on my feet in a kitchen, long hours, hard hours, and now I was told that the very work I knew was the thing most likely to kill me. But how does a man simply stop? I still had a mortgage to pay. My children were in private school at King's Christian College. I turned it over and over, looking for a way through, and there was none. So I did the only thing left to do. I went on welfare, and we scraped by on next to nothing, and I did not know how we were going to make it.

Then one night I had a dream. In the dream, my neighbour from across the road came and knocked on my door, and told me that he had just sold his house for double what he had paid for it. That was all. Then I woke, and I lay there knowing, the way you sometimes just know, that God had said something to me in it. I woke Dina and I told her, I think God wants us to buy another house. I think prices are about to go up, and if we buy now, we can sell later, and it will carry us through.

But I did not want to run ahead of God on the strength of a dream alone. So Dina and I laid it before Him plainly. I would go to the bank and tell them our plan, that we would rent out the home we were living in and buy another one to move into. If the bank agreed, we would know it was God, and we would go ahead. If they said no, we would know it was not, and we would let it go. With no job, and living on welfare, I knew the chances of a bank agreeing to such a thing were almost none. It was the kind of plan a bank turns down without a second thought. But the bank said yes. So we went looking, and we found a house across the road. We bought it. All it really needed was a fresh coat of paint. My brother Philip tiled it, Dina made beautiful curtains, and we dressed it with our own furniture. By the time we had finished, the place looked like a display house. For ten years the house prices on the coast had not moved. But after we bought, just as the dream had foretold, they went through the roof. At the end of that year, I set a little desk out on the driveway, and beside it a sign I had made myself. Private Sale.

People came through all week to look. Then, at the end of one day, I was just about to pack up the desk and go inside when a four-wheel drive pulled up in the driveway. A man leaned out and asked, "Have I made it in time to see the place?" I told him yes, of course, come in. He went through that house like the wind. When he came back out, he said, "This is exactly what I have been looking for. How much do you want?" I told him the price, and that very week, we sold it.
