That was the week we became debt free. The mortgage that would have taken me another twenty years to pay, the one I could no longer even work to service, God cleared in a single year. I had gone from a hospital bed, told to stop working, certain we would lose everything, to a man who owed nothing to anyone. I could not have done it. I did not do it. God did it, in one year. He intervened in our desperation and lifted us higher than we could ever have done on our own.
The year before she died, my mother went into a nursing home. She was eighty-three, and she could not care for herself any longer.

Not one of us wanted that. We all offered her to come and live with us. She would not hear of it. She did not want to be a burden on anybody's house, and more than that, she did not want to be a burden on anybody's marriage. We told her that she was not a burden, that she never could be, that she was the reason any of us had anything at all. It made no difference. That was the type of woman she was. She had spent her whole life carrying other people and she was not about to let anybody carry her.

She was comfortable in a place like that, with nurses in it, and sisters of charity walking up and down the corridors. I have often thought about that. I believe it gave her back something of the convent she had walked out of as a young woman in Italy, the quiet, the routine, the sight of women in habits going about their work.

It was a good home, a modern one, with a hairdressing salon, a residents' convenience shop, and a restaurant, and every comfort an old person could want. I would tell her to go and have her hair done. She would say no. She did not want to spend her money. She was keeping her money for her children, to leave to us when she went. I would tell her that whatever she had saved, divided among the five of us, would hardly buy any one of us anything worth having, and that what we wanted was for her to spend it on herself and enjoy the rest of her life, now that she was here with us. But no argument of mine was going to shift her. I knew exactly what she was doing. She was still trying to provide for us from a nursing home bed.

So I went to the manager of the home, and I made an arrangement with her. Whatever my mother wanted, she was to have, and it was to go quietly onto a bill that came to me each month, and my mother was never to be told. The manager agreed to it.

Then I went to my mother and I told her some very good news. The government, I said, had brought in a new law. Everyone living in a nursing home was now to have whatever they wanted for nothing. If she wanted her hair done, it was free. If she wanted to buy chocolate from the shop, it was free. Anything at all that she wanted was free.

She was overjoyed. She thought it was the most wonderful country in the world. She was so taken with it that she sat down and wrote to her sisters in Belgium, telling them to come out to Australia, that everything here was free, that we were blessed by God, and that they should come and enjoy the rest of their lives with her.

My aunt Antonia telephoned me not long after. Moses, she said, what on earth is this letter your mother has sent me? So I explained the whole thing to her, the money she would not spend, the manager, the new law that did not exist. My aunt started to laugh. What a good boy you are, she said, to let your mother live the rest of her life thinking that everything is free. She was still laughing when we said goodbye. Two of us, on opposite sides of the world, glad to keep the same happy secret for a woman we both loved.

By then her memory had begun to fail her. She knew exactly who we were, every one of us, she never lost that. It was the past that was going. So I made it my work to give it back to her, a little at a time. Every visit I would bring her something else about her own life.

I would remind her that she had been a pastor's wife. That she and my father had built a church for the Lord in Belgium. That they had run a great bus company. I would tell her about her sister, and her brother, and her mother and father, and the convent. Some days she would look at me and say, really? Oh, glory to God. Other days her face would change and she would say, oh yes, I remember.
Then she would ask me, did God really do all of that through me?
Yes, Mum, I would tell her. He did. You were a great woman of God.
Glory to God, she would say again. Glory to God.
There was one question she came back to more than any other. Moses, she would say, I remember having two husbands. Did I have two husbands? I remember a good one, and then a bad one.
No, Mum, I would tell her. You only had one husband, and he was a good one. He was a beautiful man. He loved the Lord. The two of you did such a beautiful work for God together in Belgium.
Then she would ask me how he died, and I would tell her that he died of old age. She would sit with that for a moment and then she would say, oh, what a shame that I cannot remember.
You two were just beautiful together, Mum. And when I said it, her gaze would lift, and her eyes would go soft and faraway, as if she were looking at something lovely that only she could see.

I make no apology for any of it. I did not want that woman going over the worst thing that ever happened to her every afternoon, finding the wound again and again with nothing left in her to heal it. All I wanted was for my mother to remember beautiful things. To have a smile on her face. To spend her last year thinking about what God had done for her, and nothing else.

She was never left on her own in there. My brothers and my sister went in to see her whenever they could, as often as they could manage it. The home was not far from my house, so I went every day to see her.

The home was very close to Celeste's school. In fact, it was on the very next block. So I asked Celeste whether she might go there after school and sit with her grandmother in her room, and pray with her, until I could get there myself. She did it. Nearly every day she went in after school and sat with my mother for half an hour or so, talking to her and praying for her, and I would arrive and find the two of them together.
My mother used to say it to me. Moses, your daughter is something else. She prays for me. She cares for me.

I would often take her in little things that she liked, some small delicacy or other. I even bought her a small refrigerator and put it in her room, so that there was somewhere to keep her ice cream. She wanted her ice cream every day, and her chocolate with it. Diabetes does not run in our family, thank God.

The day before she passed away, Dina and I went in to see her, and we brought her downstairs to the restaurant. I asked her what she wanted to eat. She said that she had already eaten, and that she was happy just to sit with us and talk while we had our meal. I would not have it. I told her to go and choose something from the display. She looked along it, and she saw a bunch of grapes, and she pointed at them and said, all right, I will have some grapes. What she did not know was that they were only there for decoration. They were plastic. I started to laugh, and I told her they were plastic, and then she started to laugh with me, and I promised her that when I came in the next day at lunchtime I would bring her fresh grapes. She smiled at me and said, all right.
The next day, on the second of April 2011, in the morning, my mother had her breakfast and brushed her teeth and went back to bed. She coughed three times, and she passed into the hands of Jesus.

I was not there. All I had was a telephone call from one of the nurses at seven o'clock that morning. Moses, she said, come quickly to the nursing home. Your mother has just passed away. I stood there with the telephone in my hand and I cried, instantly. No, no, no. We were eating together only yesterday. How can she be gone? She was fine.
It cut me that she had gone without one of her own family beside her. But I knew Jesus was there. That was the only comfort I had that morning, and it had to be enough.
The nurse kept saying it, over and over, all the way through the call. I am sorry. I am sorry, Moses.
I never brought her those grapes.

We buried her in the lawn cemetery where my father lies. We could not get a place beside him. We took the nearest one we could find, over near the chapel. My brother David came out from Belgium for the funeral, so that all of us were together, every one of her children in the one place, the way she would have wanted it.
There is one more thing I did that day, and I have never forgotten it.

Her coffin was lying open in the chapel, with all the people gathered in front of it. I stood up before my brothers and my sister, and took off my coat. I told them that the responsibility for this family, the one I had carried since I was seventeen years old, was going with our mother. I laid the coat over her body as a symbol of what I had declared, and nobody moved it. It went with her when she was buried.

I had been the man of that house since I was a boy. I had carried my mother, and my brothers, and everything that fell on us the day my father walked out, for more than thirty years. That day I laid it down on her, in front of all of them, and I let it be buried with her.

She walked out of that convent with a hidden Bible under her cloak, because she wanted to know God for herself. She found Him, and spent the rest of her life serving Him. On the second of April 2011, while no one was watching, Jesus came, took her by the hand, and she went to be with Him.

blocks.title: The God I Thought I Knew

blocks.html: The last day I had my daughter began like any other.

That afternoon Dina and I had gone out to do some shopping, and when we came home and were unloading the car, Celeste came out to meet us. We carried everything inside and put it all away, and then she said, "Mum, Dad, I have something very important to tell you." We must not have stopped quickly enough, because she said it again. "Mum, Dad, are you listening?"

So we stopped, in the middle of the lounge room, and we gave her our full attention. There was something in the way she said it that told us this was not a small thing, that we needed to hear it properly.

She told us that when she had come home from school that afternoon, there had been music playing in Joshua's room. It was worldly music, and Joshua was not there, he had already gone to work, so she felt she should turn it off. Once she had, she felt the Lord telling her to put worship music on, so she went into her own room and put it on there. As she worshipped, the Lord said something to her, and she had been waiting for us to come home so she could pass it on.
He had told her to tell us that everything was going to be alright.

I want you to understand where we were standing when she said it. Our life, in that moment, was good. Our family was well. There was nothing in front of us that needed a word from heaven to put right. So we did not hear it the way we would come to hear it later. We took it the way you take a lovely thing your child carries home to you. Dina and I stored that word away in our hearts and minds, and I said to her, "That's great, Celeste. Thank God. Everything is going to be okay."

I did not know that I was agreeing to the hardest promise of my life. I did not know that my daughter had just brought me, on the last afternoon she would ever live, the one sentence I would need to survive the twelve years coming. She had done the thing she was put on this earth to do. She had carried a word from God to the people in front of her. Then she went out into the evening.

It was that Friday night, and it was raining. Dina and I were home, watching television, the most ordinary thing two people can be doing. Celeste had gone out with her friends. They were driving up into the hills, to the lookout on Panorama Drive, where people go to see the lights of the whole Gold Coast laid out beneath them. Her friends had talked her into going, and she had said yes for the most ordinary, most Celeste reason there was. It gave her a chance to get closer to a few of the girls she did not usually spend time with, the ones she had quietly set her heart on bringing to the Lord. Even a drive to a lookout on a wet Friday night was, to her, a chance to do the only work she truly cared about.

I was not there for what came next. I have had to learn it the way you are learning it now, afterward, from others, piecing it together from what they were able to tell me. But this is what happened to my daughter while Dina and I sat in front of the television in the warm and the dry, with no idea that anything in the world was wrong.

There were five of them in the car. On the way they stopped at a McDonald's, and they all got out, and when they came back one of the girls who had been sitting in the back wanted the front, so everybody moved around. Celeste ended up in the back, on the side, by the window. She simply took the next seat that was free.

It was still early in the evening when the girl who was driving took a wrong turn, onto a road that fell away in a sharp descent, full of tight bends, and on the wet surface the car slid, swung across the road, and struck a tree. It was thrown side-on, and the side that met the tree was Celeste's. Her head struck it through the window beside her.

She never woke. From the very first moment she was unconscious. Of all the things I have asked God about that night, this is the one mercy I was given. My daughter was not afraid. She was not in pain. One moment she was laughing with her friends, and the next she was snatched by the Lord.
Then there was a knock at the door.

We went to answer it. There were police standing there. For a few seconds we did not understand what was happening. They told us there had been an accident, and that one of our children had been involved in it. We asked them which one. They said Celeste.

They told us she was not in a good way. She had been in a car accident, and she was fighting for her life. She was still alive. That was the word we caught hold of, because if she was alive, then God could still do what God had always done. Before we left with them, we rang our pastor, Richard, and told him what had happened, and asked him to pray, to pray that Celeste would make it. Then we went out into the rain and got into the back of the police car, and the whole way to the hospital we prayed. We did not stop. We had been praying for her life from the moment we heard her name, and we did not mean to stop until she was back in our arms.

We called my brothers. Andrew and Philip came, and brought their wives. Pastor Richard reached the hospital before any of us, and he came in drenched, soaked clean through from the rain, because he had not paused for anything, not even to shelter from it. They put us all in a room near the surgical theatre and told us to wait there. The surgeon would come out, they said, when there was something to tell us, whether she had made it, or whether she had not.

Joshua was still at work, doing the evening shift as a chef at the Radisson, and he did not yet know that his whole world had already changed. His uncle Phil went for him. He ran into the kitchen of the Radisson and told him to come quickly, that something had happened to his sister, and he brought him to us.

Then the surgeon came into the room. He was apologising before he had even finished crossing it. He told us he had done everything he could, but that they had lost her. What he said next I have never forgotten, because it was not the language of a doctor, it was the language of a father. He said, please believe me, I have three daughters of my own. I know what a daughter means to a father. Then he told us we could go in and see her.
I cannot describe what happened inside me except to say that my brain, my spirit and my soul collapsed all at once.
We went in. I felt faint on my own feet. She was lying there with a tube still in her mouth. Someone had laid a cloth over the right side of her face, and they asked us, gently, not to lift it.

I did not know if I could touch her. So I laid my head down on the bed beside her, next to where she lay, and I took her hand and held it against my face. I kept thinking the same thing, over and over. This is the end of it. The end of all the hugs. The end of all the kisses.

Two days before, she had been sitting at the kitchen bench, and I had come and stood beside her and kissed her on the cheek, over and over, twenty times at least. She turned and looked at me as though to ask why, but she never said a word. She simply sat there and soaked them up.
The end of holding each other. The end of all the joy, and all the jokes, and all the laughter that girl sent through our home and through our lives. All of it gone in one minute.
I stayed there like that, with her hand against my face, and I wept.

Everyone in that room was weeping. Somewhere behind me they were already making arrangements to bring Joshua in, so that he could see his sister one last time. Dina was beside me, unable to take hold of the nightmare we had both just fallen into. Pastor Richard, who had run through the rain to be there, could not find a single word to say. There were none to find. All he could do was rest his hand on Dina's back, and on mine, and leave it there.
We were all together that night, around her. My Celeste. Sixteen years old, three months short of seventeen, snatched by Jesus and taken home ahead of us all.

Underneath all of it, one thought kept turning over and over in me. How can anything be alright after this? Nothing is ever going to be alright again. Her words from that afternoon came back to me even as I stood there, everything is going to be alright, and the closest I could come to believing them was to look down at my girl and think: it is going to be alright for you, my love. But not for Daddy. Not for Daddy.

The morning after we lost her, the whole family came to our house to pray. We did not gather to grieve. We gathered to ask God to give her back. Every one of us in that house believed He could do it, because every one of us had been raised on a God who did.

While we were praying, my brother Philip received a word. Philip is the one who, years before, had seen three young women dressed in white and heard the Lord say that He was preparing three sisters for three brothers. So when Philip said that God had spoken, we listened. What he had been given was this.
I am God. If you want, I will bring Celeste back.
I cannot properly describe what went through me. Joy came up in me all at once. God was bringing my daughter back.
I telephoned my brother David in Belgium. We had already told him of her passing. I told him what God had said, and I asked him to pray, and to believe with us that God would do what He had spoken.
David said that he would. He said, Moses, I will pray, and I will believe that God will bring her back. Then he said, but brother, do you understand where she is right now?
I said yes. She is with Him.
He said, do you know how beautiful it is up there? The peace. The joy. The love. The beauty. The presence of God Himself. Do you really want her to come back here, into this corrupt world?
I froze with the telephone against my ear. Everything in me sank.
Because the choice had been put into my hands. God had not said that He was going to bring her back. He had said, if you want.

I began to ask Him why. Why did You say if? Why did You not simply do it Yourself, without laying it on me to choose? Why would You put a decision like that into the hands of a father who could hardly think straight?

I understand it now. He knew something about me that I did not know about myself in that moment. He knew that when it came to it, what she had would weigh more with me than what I wanted. He was not being cruel to me. He was giving me the dignity of loving my daughter properly.
So I did the only thing I could do. I did not say yes, and I did not say no. I gave the choice back to Him and left it in His hands, still hoping, with everything in me, that He would bring her back.

About a thousand people came to Celeste's funeral, from every corner of her short life and ours, all the year twelve students from her school and the youth she knew there, her own friends, our church family, our friends from work, our personal friends, and all of our family. A thousand people, for a girl of sixteen. I have thought about that number many times since. It is not something a person arranges. It is the measure of how many lives one young girl had already reached in the little time she was given.

Dina and I had made a decision together about that day. If we had to stand in front of a thousand grieving people, then we were going to let Celeste do, one last time, the only thing she had ever truly wanted to do. We were going to let her bring people to Jesus. Even now. Even from here. We wanted her to have, even in her leaving, the credit of more souls coming home because of her.
So we gave every person who came a copy of her last words. We had them printed, a message that spoke for her, the kind of thing she would have said if she could have stood up and said it herself.
I'm gone to be with Jesus. If you want to see me again, get to know Him. xoxoxo love Celeste xoxoxo.

My cousin John Iuliano, the son of my father's sister Palma, came up from Sydney to conduct the ceremony, and brought his wife Anne. John pastors a great church down there, and more than that, John knew. He knew Celeste, and he knew exactly what she came from. He knew that the girl in that coffin was a fourth-generation evangelist, the last link in a chain that ran all the way back through me, through my father and his churches in Belgium, to my grandfather and the first gospel preached in our village in Calabria. I do not believe there was another man alive who could have given her the honour, and the history, and the credit that John gave her that day. He stood her in her rightful place in a long line of people who had given their lives to the same Lord, and he did it justice.
As he preached, I sat there and I waited.

I want to be honest with you about what was happening in me, because the whole of this book has been leading to it, and I will not dress it up. With the casket open in front of me, I was believing God to raise my daughter. Not hoping. Believing. Every word John spoke lifted my expectation higher, until I was watching the coffin itself, watching her face, fully expecting to see Celeste open her eyes and sit up in front of all those people. It was the same prayer I had prayed since the knock at the door, only now it had come to its furthest edge. I was not asking whether God could do it. I knew He could. I was waiting for Him to do it. Here. Now. In front of everyone.

I had grown up on a God like that. A God who straightened a child's legs in front of a man who came to mock Him. A God who saved twins the size of a palm. A God who did not lose. Why would He lose now? Why would He lose her?

As John finished, I stood at the front, next to my daughter. I gave them a short message, and I asked anyone who wanted to give their life to Jesus to come to the front. We had gone out beforehand and bought every Bible we could find, so that we could put one into the hands of everyone who responded.
They came in their hundreds.

About five hundred people came forward that day to say yes to Jesus, next to Celeste's coffin. Five hundred. We handed out Bibles until we had none left to hand out. Two hundred and seventy of them, and then we simply ran out, because not even buying every Bible we could find had been enough for the size of what came. The harvest was bigger than anything we had thought to prepare for.

I want you to hold those two things in your mind at the same time, because I had to hold them in my body at the same time, standing in that one spot. In front of me, five hundred people were passing out of death into life; and in the box beside me, the one life I was begging God to raise was not rising.
The ceremony came to its close, and she had not moved.

I was crying out to God on the inside, where no one could hear me. Are you really not going to do this? They were getting ready to close the coffin. Something broke loose in me. I jumped to my feet and I ran to her, and I lifted her veil.

She lay there in Dina's wedding dress. Dina had wanted her to depart in it, the dress she had married me in, and so our daughter was dressed as a bride. There was a veil over her face, and I lifted it.

Dina asked me to make sure I wrote this next part down, because she does not want it forgotten. Celeste loved dressing up. She had been looking forward to her year twelve formal, and she had already decided exactly what she wanted, a red dress, a princess dress, and she talked about it. She never got to buy it. She never got to wear it. The only gown our daughter ever wore was her mother's wedding dress.

That dress carried more than either of us ever said out loud. I had received my bride in it, white as snow, pure and innocent. Now we were sending Celeste back to God in the very same dress, pure and innocent, exactly the way He had given her to us.

I have only understood since how much that veil holds. In the story I had told her so many times, the one about how she was chosen, she had lain beneath a veil in a room full of cots, set apart from all the others, lifted up in the centre, and an angel had drawn the veil aside for just a moment so that we could see her face and know she was ours. Now, at the other end of her life, I was lifting a veil again, looking at the same face, and this time I was not being given her. I was giving her back.
He did not raise her.

I looked at her, and I managed to give her a last kiss on her forehead, and in that moment, as they closed the coffin, I buried myself with her inside it. I do not know how else to say it. The real Moses, the man I actually was, went into that box with my daughter and the lid came down on the both of us. I walked away from that church certain of one thing, that no one was ever going to see the real Moses again. Whoever they saw from that day on would be a man walking around the outside of his own life, while the inside of it stayed sealed in that coffin, alongside a sixteen-year-old girl in a wedding dress.

They carried her coffin out then, down through the church toward the doors, and the young people lined the corridors on either side as it passed, her schoolmates and the youth, standing as a kind of guard for her. Every young man among them had tears running down his face. Many of them, I think, were meeting for the first time in their lives the thing none of us can outrun, how thin the thread is, how quickly a life that is here can be gone. She was teaching them even then, on her last day above the ground, the very thing she had spent her whole life trying to teach people: that this world is not the end of the story, and you had better know the One who is.
Only the family went out to the cemetery, and a few close friends. After a thousand people, it was a very small group of us standing on the grass.

We took her to the same lawn cemetery where my father lies, and where we had buried my own mother ten months before. There was still one place left in my mother's grave, and my brothers agreed that Celeste should have it. So my daughter was laid there above her grandmother, the two of them together in the one piece of ground. The old woman who had prayed her way out of a convent, and the young girl who had come in after school to sit with her and pray for her.
I would have given her the world. God gave her heaven instead, and heaven is where I will join her one day.
We buried her. Then I began to wait for her to come back.
I have to tell you what I believed in those first months, even though I understand now what it was. I believed, with everything in me, that Celeste was going to come out of that grave alive.

There was a church on my street, and outside it stood one of those signs that the churches change from week to week. One day, as I passed it, it read: And the water covered the earth a hundred and fifty days. I read those words and I knew that God was speaking to me. Noah had gone into the ark, and the flood had covered everything, and for a hundred and fifty days there was nothing but death and water in every direction. Then the waters went down, the ark came to rest, and Noah walked out onto dry ground into a world washed clean. A hundred and fifty days, and then deliverance.

That was her timeframe. That was God telling me how long. Celeste would lie in that coffin for a hundred and fifty days, exactly as Noah lay in the ark, and on the last of those days the ground would open, and God would lift her out of the earth, and give her back to me alive.
So I waited. I counted.

Once a man is waiting for a sign, he begins to find signs everywhere. I read them on number plates. A car pulled in front of me one day carrying a plate that said, simply, believe, and I did. I read them on billboards by the road. One of them, in large letters, said Get ready for your moment, and I took it as God speaking straight to me, telling me to be ready, that the day the ground would open was almost here. Everything my eyes fell upon seemed to be confirming that the miracle was still coming, that I had understood God correctly, that I had only to hold on until the count was finished.

One day I was lying down, looking out of my window and asking God to give me a sign, and there in the sky was a cloud that had formed into the shape of Jesus, clear and exact and unmistakable, with His arms open wide. I have never been more certain of anything I have seen with my own eyes. I reached for my phone to take a photo of it, to have the proof of it, and I pointed it and took the picture. But even as I took it, the cloud was already thinning and drifting apart, and the photo did not hold it. When I looked at what I had captured, there was nothing in it that anyone could describe. If I had shown it to another person, they would not have understood what they were looking at. What I had seen so clearly with my own eyes was for me alone, and then it was gone.

I filled a whole book in those days. Every dream, every sign, every number, every word I believed God was speaking to me. I wrote down how I felt in my soul as well, whatever was going on inside me that day. Page after page of a man trying to read the future of his daughter in the things around him.

Then the hundred and fiftieth day arrived. The day I had counted to. The day the ground was supposed to open and give her back to me. I waited through the whole of it. Nothing happened. The earth stayed shut, the coffin stayed where it was, and no hand reached down to lift her out. When that day ended the way all the others had ended, I gave up. This is the last sign, I had told myself. If nothing happens, I am done. Nothing had happened. I was done. I was so tired. Tired in a way I did not yet have the words for.

I can name it now, from this side of it. That was grief. It was the first part of grief, the part they call denial. My mind could not hold what had happened, so it built a hundred and fifty days of waiting to keep from holding it. I was not out of my senses. I was a father whose daughter had been alive on Friday afternoon and gone by Friday night, and a heart can only take in so much at one time. So mine took it in the only way it could. It told itself she was coming back.
She did not come back.
I stepped out of the waiting into something far longer and far quieter. That is the part of the story I have to tell you next.

blocks.label: Chapter Twenty-Five
blocks.title: A World I Did Not Want to Be In

blocks.html: The last of the hundred and fifty days went by, and the ground did not open.

There was no morning when the earth gave her back. There was no coffin lifted into the light, no daughter sitting up and calling me Daddy. There was only the count running out, and the silence after it, and me still standing there, a man who had promised himself a miracle and been handed a grave.

What began then is hard to put into words for anyone who has not lived inside it. I have called it my journey to live in a world I did not want to be in. For years, if you had asked me how I was, the truest answer I had was a single sentence that ran on underneath everything else I said. I just want to go. I never meant to act on it, and I never would have. It was only a weariness so deep that being where she was, wherever the dead in Christ are kept, seemed like the only rest left to me. I was tired of walking around in a life with a hole in the middle of it.

So I went through the motions of it. I got up. I went to church. I went to work. I built rooms onto my son's houses with my own hands, good rooms, straight and solid, built by a man who was not really there. On the outside I was moving. On the inside nothing moved at all.

At church they could see it, I think, though they were kind enough not to say so. When the pastor leaned over and asked me, the way he used to, whether I would give the thought at communion, or share something at the offering, I always said no. I had nothing to give. A man cannot pour out of a cup that has been emptied and cracked and left upside down to dry. So I sat in the pew, and I let the service happen around me, and I went home.
Underneath the motions, I was wrestling with God, though it was a quiet, worn-out kind of wrestling, with no strength left in it.

People kept telling me to stay active, and I knew that they were right. There was a treadmill sitting unused in the room outside our house, so I began to walk on it. I even turned it around to face north, towards the cemetery, because I had it in my head that God wanted me to walk in her direction.
What I did on that machine is not something I am proud of, but it is the truth, and it says more about the state I was in than anything else I could tell you.

I would walk, and I would speak to myself on God's behalf. I would pretend that He was angry with me, and that He had taken Celeste in order to punish me. Then I would say His part out loud, in His voice, as though He were standing behind me. You deserve this pain. You disobeyed Me your whole life, and you thought you would get away with it. Now it is time to pay.
I said that to myself, over and over, walking north towards my daughter's grave.

Then one day I did it again, and something in me broke open. I was enraged that nothing was happening, that no answer ever came, and I was crying and shouting and swearing at the top of my voice on that machine. When I had run out of everything else, I started up the same words again, ready to say His part back to myself one more time.

I do not know how to explain what happened next, except to say that it seemed He could not stand to listen to it any longer. The treadmill stopped. Not slowed. Stopped, all at once, underneath me, and I nearly went off the front of it.
Then I heard Him.
Stop that. You know that is not Me saying that. You are rehearsing the words of the enemy.
That machine did not work for ten days. I tried it, and nothing. On the tenth day I switched it on and it started up as though there had never been anything wrong with it.

I have thought about that many times since. He did not leave me to it. He stopped the machine underneath me, and He told me plainly whose words I had been repeating. It was not Him accusing me. It never had been. He would not let me go on putting the words of the enemy into His mouth.

The first thing I wrestled with was the promise. In the middle of the night there was only one conclusion a father in my condition could come to. We had failed somewhere, and He had taken her back, and it was our own doing.

So I went looking for it. I went through her whole life, year by year, turning over the way we had raised her, the things we had allowed and the things we had refused, every conversation I could remember, hunting for the place where we had broken our word to Him.

I never found it, because it was not there. She had grown up in His house with her face turned towards Him. She prayed for other people as though their troubles were her own. She gave herself to her youth group and to anyone in it who was hurting. She was, in every particular, the girl He had described to us in that room before she was ever born. The proof that we had kept our promise had been walking around in front of me the whole time. It was her.
It took me a long time to see the rest of it, and I want to set it down plainly, because someone will read this page with the same question sitting in their chest.

What I have come to believe is something else altogether. God could see something coming towards my daughter's life that I could not see, and He took her home before it ever reached her. There is a verse in Isaiah that says exactly that. The righteous perish, and no one takes it to heart; the devout are taken away, and no one understands that the righteous are taken away to be spared from evil. Isaiah, chapter fifty-seven, verse one.

Then there is the word He used. He did not say that He would take her away from me. He said that He would take her back. Back is a word that only makes sense if she was His to begin with. She was in that room, waiting, before Dina ever carried her. She was His, and He lent her to me, and He let me have sixteen years of her.
This is the thing I would say to any mother or father reading this. Our children are not our possessions. They are entrusted to us.

There is one more thing, and it has taken me the longest to understand. When we stood in that room and begged Him for her, He said, You don't know what you are asking for. He was not warning me about failure. He was warning me about the cost.

It was not unlike what Mary was told. She was given a son, and she was told at the same time that a sword would go through her own soul as well. The child was a gift, and the gift came with a wound in it, and she was told so before she ever understood what it meant.
We asked anyway. We asked because we had seen her face, and love reaches for a thing long before it understands it.
I would ask again. Knowing everything I know, sitting here with all of it behind me, I would stand in that room and beg Him for her again.

I read Paul writing to the Philippians about wanting to know Christ, and the power of His resurrection, and the fellowship of His suffering. I had wanted the first two all my life. I had never noticed that the third one was in the same sentence. Then I read the words of Jesus, In this world you will have trouble, and I understood at last that He had never promised me a life without a night like this one.

I used to think of the Titanic, the great ship they had said could not sink, and the iceberg waiting for it in the dark water, the thing under the surface that no one saw until it had already torn the ship open. That was how it felt. A life I had built and trusted, sure of its course, and then something underneath that I never saw coming, and all of it going down in the cold.

There was one fear in me deeper than all the others, so deep I could hardly look at it. It was the fear that I might never be able to trust God again. I knew that fear. I had met it once before, a long time ago, in a boy of seventeen whose father had preached that a good captain never leaves his ship, and who then stepped off the deck of his own family and disappeared. I had already learned, once, what it does to a heart when the one who is meant to hold you lets go. Now, in the worst of it, a terrible voice kept whispering that God had done the very same thing. That He, too, had left. That the Father I had given my whole life to had walked off the deck the moment the water came in.
I want to tell you about two lights in those years, because even in that dark, God did not leave me entirely without them.
The first was a child.

In 2019, on the fourth of August, my son Joshua and his wife Mallu had a baby boy, and they called him Caleb. He was my first grandson. There is a whole story in how that little boy came to be, in how his mother came into our lives, and in all that God would go on to build out of the two of them. I will tell it to you soon. For now it is enough to say that in the middle of my darkness, a child arrived. When they laid him in my arms, I felt something stir in me that I had long believed was gone, and Dina and I loved that little one from the first day he arrived. I have to be honest about the kind of joy it was. It was a circumstantial joy, the kind that comes with a happy circumstance and rises and falls along with it. It sat on top of the heaviness the way sunlight sits on the surface of deep water. It was warm, and it was real, and it could not reach the bottom of me, where the cold still was. But I thanked God for it. A drowning man is grateful for any light at all.

Mallu understood, without my ever having to explain, that there was a great empty space in our house where a daughter used to be. She never once held Caleb back from us. Whenever we wanted him to stay, she and Joshua let him come, and so that little boy and I grew close in a way I had not gone looking for. Wherever I was, he wanted to be. As he grew, I began to see something in him that stopped my breath. His heart was like hers. He was a child made for people, full of love, pulled towards them the way Celeste had always been pulled towards them. I had not expected to see that again in this life, and there it was, looking up at me.
The second light was stranger, and I still do not fully understand it.

In all those years when I had nothing to give, when I refused the pastor and sat empty in the pew, there was one thing I could not stop myself from doing. I kept telling people about Jesus. I did not plan it. I did not feel worthy of it. But I would find myself beside a stranger, and I would open my mouth, and out it would come, and somehow it was always Celeste who came out with it. I would use my own loss, the fragile, breakable shortness of our time here, to show a person that this life is not the whole of the story, and that they had better come to know the One who waits on the other side of it.

I remember sitting on a bench one day, waiting for Dina, next to an old man I had never met. I could not help myself. I told him about Celeste, and I told him that one day I was going to be with her again.
He said that he did not believe in any of that. He did not believe in life after death.
Then it came out that he had five sons, and that the youngest, the one he loved best, had been killed in a car accident.
I could see that he was identifying with my grief, and I could see something else with it. The two of us had lost a child each, and we were travelling in opposite directions with it.

Somewhere in that conversation I said to him that faith is believing in what you cannot see. I told him that he was already doing it, only in the wrong direction. He had decided, without any proof at all, that he would never see his son again, and he was living every day inside that belief. But if he chose to believe the other way, then there was a chance he would.
He looked at me and asked me how he was supposed to believe such a thing. He said that he simply could not.
I asked him whether I might pray for him, and he let me. It must have been something I said in that prayer, because the old man started to cry, and then he began to murmur it. I believe. I believe.
I said to him, do you? He said, yes, I do.

So I asked him whether he wanted to receive Jesus into his heart, and he said yes, still crying, and I led him through the prayer word by word, and then I put my arms around him and the two of us wept together on that bench.

His wife came out of the shop while it was happening and saw us, and she was alarmed, and asked me what had happened. So I told her. She started to cry herself. She told me that their whole family were Christians, every one of them, and that he was the only one who had never given his life to God. They had been praying for that man's salvation for fifty years.
How did you do it, she kept saying. How did you do it?
Jesus did it, I told her. He was ready.
I cannot describe the joy in that shopping centre. Fifty years of a family's prayers, answered on a bench, by a man who had nothing left in him.
It happened like that again and again, in shopping centres and waiting rooms and on benches, with people whose names I never learned. No one ever said no to me. Not once.

Dina used to come and find me, and she would take one look at my face and shake her head and smile. You've done it again, haven't you? I would smile back, and say yes, and introduce her to whoever it was I had just been sitting with.

I did not see it then for what it was. I see it now. Celeste's calling did not die with Celeste. The gift she had carried since before she was born, the drawing of lost people home to God, did not go into the ground with her. It kept working. It kept working through her hollowed-out, heavy-hearted father, in the very years when he could not feel God at all. Her harvest never stopped. He was still the God of miracles, even in the seasons when I could not feel His hand on me, and He was doing through my grief the exact thing my daughter had been set apart in heaven to do. I simply could not see it yet.

The heaviness was still there. A grandson had come, and strangers were giving their lives to God beside me on benches, and none of it shifted the weight. I had made my peace with the idea that it never would. I believed this was simply what was left of a man after a thing like this, and that I would carry it, bent under it, until the day I finally got to go.

I was wrong about that. The weight on me was real, but it was not only grief, and it did not have the right to stay. It had a name I had not yet learned, and the day was coming, in front of an ordinary television set, when I would learn it, and be free.

blocks.label: Chapter Twenty-Six
blocks.title: Whatever I Did to Your House

blocks.html: I want to tell you about a house and a church, because the two of them belong together, and because of what they showed me about God, who begins a work and finishes it His own way, a way beyond anything men could ever have done.

While Pastor Richard was still alive, a man in the church, a builder, had offered to build him his house. Time went by, and one day I realised that Dina and I had never once been to see it. I felt it was time we did, so we drove out to the address to see how the work was coming along.

When we pulled up, Pastor Richard was sitting on a little wall beside his driveway, at the front of the house, with his face in his hands. We came over and asked him what was wrong. He lifted his head and said, you can see the shell of the house is here. But my builder has taken the money and disappeared. Now I have a mortgage on a house I cannot live in, and rent to pay on the place we are staying in until it is finished, and there is nothing left.
I had a quick word with Dina. She nodded. Then I turned to him and said, Pastor Richard, go home. Leave it with me. I will take care of it.
He did not really understand what I meant. So I said it again. Go home, to your family, and do not come back here until I call you.

The moment he was gone I began making calls, right through my own family. Philip, Pastor Richard is in trouble, can you finish the tiling. Yes. Andrew, can you manage the carpet. Yes. My mother bought the garage door. My sister bought all the doors and the paint. I bought the windows, and the kitchen appliances, and the stove. The rest of them came to paint and to do whatever else needed doing. Every one of them said yes.
Within three weeks I called him back. When Pastor Richard walked into that house, it was finished. All of it. Done.
I am telling you this for a greater reason, because some years later that same man came to something much bigger, and it was the same story all over again.

Pastor Richard wanted a church in the middle of the city. He had a heart for people that most churches never reach, and he wanted to be where they were, in the centre of Surfers Paradise. He found the old Hoyts cinema complex, and it was an enormous thing. At street level was the cinema foyer, with shops all around it, and a grand staircase rising from it to the first floor. There the staircase opened onto a great foyer, the place where we now hold our receptions and our family lunches, and from that foyer two more staircases led up to the auditoriums above. Above all of that were two more levels of business offices, and part of one of them is the church office to this day. Beneath the whole building lay two levels of underground car park, and a lift serviced the whole of it, from the second basement all the way up to the fourth level. But getting it was not simple. The owner did not want to sell it as it was. His plan was to renovate it himself and sell it on at an astronomical price. Pastor Richard kept on at him, pleading with him to let it go, and after months of negotiations the owner finally gave in. Like the house, it was only a shell. It needed gutting and rebuilding from the inside out.
He stood before the church and told them the truth. We need four million Australian dollars to renovate this building.
Time passed, and nothing moved. Four million dollars is a number that stops a person before he has even begun. So one day I went up to his office, and I told him my plan.

Pastor Richard's dream was to knock down the wall between two of the auditoriums and make one enormous auditorium out of the pair, but the quote just to bring that wall down was four hundred thousand dollars. So I told him we would move into the biggest of the three auditoriums first, just as it was, so that at least we were in and holding services, and then, when the money came, we would knock down the wall and make the two into one.
He was reluctant. He said, no, Moses. This is far too big for us to do right now.

I said, Pastor Richard, it can be done. You know me. Whatever I did to your house, I can do to this. Only this time it will not be just my family. It will be the whole congregation. It had been prophesied that the resources were already in the house, the skills, the tradesmen, the gifts, all of it sitting right there among the people. Just give me the building, and go home.
In the end he gave in, the way he had in front of his house. All right, he said. Go for it. Start with the kitchen.
I said, no, Pastor Richard. Not just the kitchen. All of it.
He was hoping, but holding back a little, waiting to see whether the miracle of the two cinemas becoming one was really going to happen before he let himself believe in the rest.

The moment he gave me the go-ahead, I went to work. The first person who came to mind was our sound man, Steve McCallum. I asked him to price the sound equipment for me, and to tell me whether it could be hung from the ceiling.
That same day Steve went up into the roof to look. After a while he called down through the manhole. Moses, are you sure they want four hundred thousand dollars to bring this wall down?
I said, yes. That is what the quote said.
He said, I can see the truss running straight past this wall and leaning on the outside wall. I do not believe this wall is holding anything up. I believe it could come down.

Now, because I had worked for years in a pizza place, I had come to know a great many people, solicitors, architects, engineers, accountants. So I picked up the phone and rang an engineer friend of mine, to ask whether he knew where the old Hoyts cinema was, and whether he might come up one day and check the wall for us.
He started to laugh. Moses, he said, you would not believe it. I am walking past the front door of the building right now, as we speak. I can come in this minute if you like.
I met him at the door. He went up, and he asked Steve questions from inside the roof, and Steve took photos and showed them to him, and he confirmed it. This wall can come down.
There it was. Four hundred thousand dollars saved, in an afternoon.

That day Pastor Richard was away on his boat. There was a young man named Lucas in the office when the news came through, and he asked me if he could be the one to ring the pastor and tell him. I said, yes, you can. So he got on the phone and told Pastor Richard everything that had just happened, and then he asked him, can we smash it?
Pastor Richard said, wait. Wait, wait, wait until I get there.

Something happened before we knew anything at all about that wall, before the engineer, before we understood it was not holding the roof up. My brother Andrew came to me, sure of himself, and said, Moses, let me blow my trumpet. He wanted to sound it over the wall the way the priests did at Jericho, believing that God would bring it down the same way. He did not know a single thing about how it could be done. He simply knew that God would do it.

So we let him. We all gathered, and Andrew lifted the trumpet and sounded it straight at that wall. Nothing happened that day. Not a stone of it moved. But Andrew was not troubled. He believed he had heard from God, and as far as he was concerned, his part was simply to obey. God did bring it down, in the weeks that followed, block by block, by our own hands.

When that wall finally came down it was a victory that did more than open up a room. It put a great faith in all of us. Pastor Richard could hardly believe it, that God would use the ordinary people of his own church to do the very thing that needed doing. At last the two rooms were one, and you could see clear across the whole of it.

Next was the floor. A cinema floor is not flat. It slopes down toward the screen in steps, one for each row of seats, so that everyone can see over the heads in front of them. We had two of those stepped floors to join into one, and each cinema had been built at a different level, about a metre higher than the other. Rather than tear them out, we built a new floor up from the highest step, which brought the whole surface level. Then we built the new stage on top of that floor. In our connect group there was a retired builder, Alf Charnley. He gathered a team of builders and carpenters from among the congregation, and together they laid the floor and levelled it right through the building, as an offering to the Lord, as long as the church bought the timber. Another five hundred thousand dollars saved.

Then the air conditioning. To cool a whole building of that size had been quoted at eight hundred thousand dollars. There was a man in our connect group named Don, who worked in air conditioning. Don found the units, the motors and all the equipment that was needed for eighty thousand dollars, and he did the whole job himself as an offering to the Lord. So the air conditioning that had been priced at eight hundred thousand cost the church only eighty.
The day the crane came to lift those monstrous motors up onto the roof, they were so big that the police had to come and stop the traffic while it was done.

Then the tiling. My brother Philip laid three hundred square metres of it, and others in the congregation worked right alongside him. And then the painting, the whole of that vast place, done by the hands of the people themselves. Everyone worked as an offering to the Lord. No one asked for a cent for their labour. The only thing the church ever had to pay for was the materials.

Then the carpet, which had been quoted at three hundred thousand. I rang my cousin John in Sydney and asked him where he had got the carpet when he built his church. He said, Moses, do you not know we have a cousin, one of Aunt Iolanda's sons, who owns a Carpet Court? He will look after you. So I called Sam, and Sam said he had a representative on the Gold Coast who would take care of me. The man came and measured the area, and then he said, I will do it at cost price for you, forty thousand dollars, and I will put in ten thousand of my own, because I like what you people are doing here.
I want to tell you why he said that, because it is the heart of the whole thing.

When Dina and I first joined the church, Pastor Richard and his wife Erica had made a decision to open the church to the streets. They wanted a place where the drunks and the broken and the drug addicts could come in and find Jesus. He started an outreach ministry for them, and he called it Transformations. When he did it, half the church left him. The comfortable ones, the ones with money, said they did not want their children around people like that. As they walked out, they told him, see if those riff-raff are going to pay for your church.

It broke Pastor Richard's heart to see them go. But his heart broke more for the helpless and the broken out on the streets, and so, sadly, he let the others leave. The truth was, Pastor Richard had been a riff-raff himself once. He had been a drunk, worth nothing in the eyes of the world, until God came down into the gutter and lifted him out. He knew exactly what those broken people were worth, because he had been one of them, and he knew that whatever God had done for him, God could do for them. So he kept his eyes on the homeless and the rejected. Every Sunday he would tell his own story again. Now that he was in a position to lift the poor, he poured himself out for them without holding anything back. So when he bought that cinema, he did it believing that God loved the broken, and that the money was God's problem to see to, not his.
That is why the carpet man gave the price he gave. God moved like that over every single item we had to buy. One after another, the way opened.

The thing I had said to Pastor Richard at the very start turned out to be the key to all of it. If you ask the church for four million dollars, I told him, no one will be able to help you, because no one has that kind of money. But if we bring it to them one project at a time, everyone will pitch in, because they can see that it is achievable. That is exactly how it happened. Project by project, the whole place was furnished. We moved in only months later. And these were only the major jobs to finish a building of that size. There was more work than I could ever list, and willing hands at every turn to do it.

The day we opened, the joy that filled that building was out of this world. It was almost a dream. We had made it look like an entertainment centre, and it was a beautiful thing to see, and the glory of God came down into it. We have been there ever since.

That day took me all the way back to the opening of my father's church in Belgium, in 1971, when I was a boy of seven. I have told you about that day already, my mother cutting the ribbon with the tears running down her face, the crowds, the music, the glory of God filling the room. I had stood and watched it as a child, and it had never left me. This time I was a grown man, and I had been there to help build it.

The church has had three names in my time. It was the Surfers Paradise Assembly of God when Dina and I first walked into it. Some time later, Pastor Richard renamed it Surf City. When Pastor Richard passed away, on the seventh of October 2016, ten days before his seventieth birthday, his son-in-law Pastor Justin took the church on, and he calls it Presence, and that is its name to this day. Transformations is still going too, as a rehabilitation centre kept on in the original building, still doing the very thing Pastor Richard began, still gathering in the ones nobody else wanted.

We still owe four million dollars on our church building. I am not troubled by it. God is big, and four million dollars is nothing at all to Him. Though I do wish it were paid off, so that instead of giving all that money to the bank, we could pour it into the heart of our city to reach the lost.
The rich people may have left us, but God is still here. As long as we have Him, the rest will be taken care of.
There is one more thing I have to tell you, because it is the whole point of everything Pastor Richard built.

Pastor Justin, his son-in-law, the man who leads our church today, is one of the very ones that ministry saved. He was a third-generation pastor's child, the grandson and son of preachers, raised in the church. But after being raised in all of it, the world took hold of him, and he decided to craft a way of his own. He left everything his family had built into him and ended up on the opposite side of the truth, selling drugs, an addict himself, doing all the things a mother dreads for her son. He was deported from New Zealand for drug trafficking, and he had come to the end of himself, ready to take his own life, when his cousin urged him to come along to church. He came, and Jesus met him there, and he joined the Transformations ministry, the very outreach the comfortable ones had walked out over. In time he married Pastor Richard's daughter, Christine, whom we all know as Chrissy, and so the young man the streets had nearly taken became a son to the very pastor whose church had gone looking for him.

That broken young man is our pastor now. He picked up Pastor Richard's call, and he is running with it. I love his heart for the lost. It is the same heart Pastor Richard had, and the same heart that once came looking for me when my own church was failing. That is why I am there, at my age, still down on the floor beside them, to cheer them on and to encourage them, every one of them.

I have thought many times about why God let me be the man who stood in front of that house, and then in front of that cinema, and said, give it to me, I will finish it. I think it is because I know what it is to grow up inside a shell. My father built a great church once, in Belgium, and it stood like a tower, full and alive, until he lost all of it in one season of bankruptcy and sin. The building was never the shell. What he left as a shell was us. I grew up inside the empty place his leaving made, a family with the shape of a home but the middle gone out of it. I spent the rest of my life being handed hollow, half-finished things and being asked to make them whole again.

So when I saw Pastor Richard sitting on that little wall with his face in his hands, I knew exactly what I was looking at. This time, with the whole church behind me, and the hand of God on every part of it, we finished it. Nothing was left standing as a shell.
It began, of all places, with a video of myself.

Pastor Justin had asked me many times to either share a thought for communion or to speak for the offering, and for years I had always said no. It was never that I would not serve. I would do anything that needed doing quietly, out of the way. I baptised, I helped, I gave. What I would not do was stand up in front of the church and be seen and heard. Being on display was the one thing I could not bring myself to do. But there was one particular Sunday, and to this day I cannot tell you why, when the way he asked me made me think he was stuck, that he really did need somebody to do it. So I agreed.

I did it the way I did everything in those years, from the outside, going through the motions, saying the right words with nothing behind them. It was recorded, and afterwards it went up on the internet, and some days later I sat down with Dina and watched it back on our television at home.

I have watched a great many pastors on YouTube in my life, and I suppose that when I sat down to watch myself, some part of me was hoping to see one of them, to sound like them, to look like one of those men who seem to carry the anointing so easily. That is not what I saw. It was not the words that stopped me. It was my face. I looked at the man on the screen and I saw a sadness that had settled so deep into him that it had become the shape of his face, the set of his shoulders, the weight in his eyes. I thought to myself, if I were scrolling along looking for a word of encouragement, I would not even stop for this man. I would take one look at him and keep going. He looked like a man carrying something too heavy to put down. He looked like a man who had given up. That man was me, and I had not even known I looked like that. I had been wearing it so long that I had stopped feeling it as something I was wearing. It had simply become me.

It was not only that video. A few months before, I had baptised some young people in the tank at the church, and afterwards, when the photos came back, there I was in every one of them with the same face. We had just done one of the most beautiful things a church ever does, young people going down into the water and coming up new, and I stood there looking as though I were at a funeral. The coat was on me even there, even in the water, even in the middle of all that joy. I did not see it at the time.

Some time later, Dina and I started watching a preacher. He was quite an unconventional prophet, not at all the sort of man we were used to listening to, but there was something about him that raised our curiosity, and we kept watching. He began to teach from the book of Isaiah, from the sixty-first chapter, the third verse, in the King James Version. He read the words about those who mourn in Zion, and how God gives to them beauty for ashes, the oil of joy for mourning, the garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness.
Then he said something I had never heard anyone say, and it went through me like a current.

He said that Zion is the throne room of God, the place where His presence is. He said that mourning is natural, that God Himself makes room for the ones who mourn, that there is nothing wrong with grief and nothing shameful in it. But he said there was something else that could get into that room, something that did not belong there and was never meant to stay. He called it by the name the Bible gives it. The spirit of heaviness.
Then he explained how it works, and I sat very still, because he was describing my own life to me as though he had lived inside it.

He said the spirit of heaviness is a deceiver. It disguises itself as your grief. It hides underneath your sorrow and lets you believe that it is only sorrow, only the natural weight of what you have lost. So that when the grief itself has done its work, when enough time has passed that the sharpness should soften and the load should begin to lift, the spirit of heaviness quietly takes grief's place. It puts on grief's clothes. It convinces you that this is simply how things are now, that a man who has been through what you have been through is meant to walk bent over for the rest of his days, weighed down, joyless, waiting to die. It persuades you that the heaviness is the truth about you, and that you will wear it until they put you in the ground.
I thought of the man in the video. I thought of twelve years.

Then I am being fooled, I said, out loud, sitting there beside Dina. I have thought all this time that I was only grieving. But this is not all grief. This is that spirit, and it has been sitting on me, and I did not even know its name.

The preacher, on the screen, made a call. He said that if you recognised this thing on your own life, you did not have to carry it one more day. He said, come to the front, and we will evict it, right now, in the name of Jesus.

I was not in a building where I could walk to any front. I was in my own home, in front of a television. But something in me was up out of the chair before I had decided anything. I crossed the room, and I put both my hands flat against the television screen, against that preacher and his prayer, and I said the words after him, out loud, and I told the spirit of heaviness that it had no right to me, that it had trespassed long enough, and that in the name of Jesus it was going to leave.
It came out of me.

I do not have a better way to say it than that. Something that had been on me lifted off me and was gone, and I knew the very instant it happened. What came up out of me next was the strangest thing of all, and the sweetest. I began to laugh. Not a small laugh. A great, loud, helpless laugh, rolling up from somewhere so far down inside me that I had forgotten it was there. I laughed and I laughed. Dina was right there beside me, and she did not need anything explained to her. She could see it happening. She knew that the second coat was being lifted off her husband by God's own hands. It's gone, I kept telling her, laughing, wiping my eyes. It's gone. I feel like a heavy coat has been lifted off my shoulders. It's gone.
I want you to see what happened in that room, because it is the thing this whole book has been walking towards, and it is not the thing I once demanded.

For twelve years I had waited for a resurrection. I had stood at a graveside believing the ground would open. I had counted a hundred and fifty days, like Noah in the ark, certain that a coffin would be lifted out of the earth and a girl would sit up and call me Daddy. That resurrection never came. God, in a wisdom I did not understand then and do not fully understand now, did not give it.

But there was a body in the ground that did come up. It was mine. Twelve years before, I had bent over my daughter's coffin and told you that I buried myself in there with her, that the real Moses was sealed inside that box and no one would ever see him again. Here, in an ordinary lounge room, in front of a television set, with my hands on a pane of glass and tears and laughter running together down my face, the real Moses came up out of the grave I had put him in. The man I had buried with Celeste was raised. Not her body. Mine. That was the resurrection God had been waiting all along to give me, and it was not the one I had gone looking for.

Other people saw it too, though they had no name for what they were seeing. Some time after that day, I was asked to baptise again, at that same tank where the photos had once caught me looking so sad. This time was not like the last. The joy of the Lord had filled me so full that it simply poured out of me, and I could not have hidden it if I had tried. Afterwards, some of the people who had been there both times came up to me. They said, we have to ask you something. The last time you baptised, you looked so depressed that we were worried about you. Today you cannot stop smiling. What has happened to you? I told them, I am not forcing this. I could not force it if I wanted to. The truth of the Lord has filled me, and I am happy, really happy, for the first time in longer than I can say. They looked almost shocked, because they could see that it was true. They had watched a coat come off a man, even if they did not have the words for it.

Isaiah had said it plainly, and I had read it a hundred times without it once reaching me. The garment of praise for the spirit of heaviness. God took the heavy coat off my shoulders, the one I had worn so long that I had come to think it was my own skin, and He put something else on me in its place.
I have thought since about the two coats.

Ten months before I lost Celeste, I stood in a chapel and took my own coat off my shoulders and laid it on my mother in her coffin, and buried with her the responsibility I had carried since I was seventeen years old. I walked out of that chapel lighter than I had been in thirty years, only to take on the heaviest coat I would ever carry, ten months later.

I chose neither of them. The first was put on me by a father who walked out. The second came out of a loss allowed by a Father I could not see, whose plans were far beyond anything I could have conceived. Getting that second one off me took twelve years, and it was not my doing either. God arranged every piece of it. A pastor who needed someone to speak. A video I did not want to watch. A preacher on a television screen in my own lounge room, on the day I was finally ready to hear him. He built that moment for me, and He waited for it, and when it came He took the coat off my shoulders Himself.

Because what He gave me was not simply relief. It was not the lifting of a weight and nothing more. He gave me joy. I need you to understand what kind of joy, because I have already told you about another kind. When Caleb was born, I felt a joy that sat on the surface and could not reach the bottom of me, a joy that rose and fell with the day. This was not that. What God put into me that day went all the way down, into the cold place at the very bottom where nothing had reached in twelve years, and it stayed there. A deep joy. An unmovable joy. A joy that does not depend on my circumstances, that does not lift when things are good and drain away when they are hard, because it was never built on things being good in the first place. It was His gift, and He does not take His gifts back.

To comfort all who mourn, and provide for those who grieve in Zion, to bestow on them a crown of beauty instead of ashes, the oil of joy instead of mourning, and a garment of praise instead of a spirit of despair.
That is the oil of joy for mourning, the other half of what Isaiah had promised, and God poured it into me until the mourning finally had somewhere to go.

There is more to that verse, and He gave me the rest of it as a promise for my children. They shall be called trees of righteousness, the planting of the Lord, that he might be glorified. My children, and my children's children, planted by His own hand. Not saplings that might not take. Trees.

That was the beginning of my breakthrough. In the days that followed, people who knew nothing of what had happened to me in that room began to say the same thing over me, again and again, as though God were making certain I heard it. He is not finished with you. God is not finished with you yet.

In those days Dina and I still sat right at the back of the church. One morning a prophet came the whole way down and stood in front of the two of us and said that God was about to use us, that we were made for such a time as this.

Another time a song leader came down off the platform to find us. She told us that while she had been singing she had seen a light come straight down through the roof and shine on the two of us, and that she could not carry on without coming to tell us. God was highlighting us, she said.
They were all right. God was not finished with us.
Let me show you one of the things He was not finished doing.

I promised you, back in the darkest part of this story, that there was a whole tale behind my grandson Caleb, behind his mother, behind everything God would build out of them, and that I would tell it when the time came. The time has come.

My son Joshua had grown into a handsome man, if I may say so myself. He had inherited the blue eyes and the strong personality that ran all the way back through the bloodline. I could almost take the very words that were once used to describe my grandfather, before he was saved, and lay them on him, but I will not, because Jesus has washed our bloodline with His own blood, and what came down to Joshua came down cleansed. He had turned out to be a strong man of God. In his young adult years he served as a youth leader in the church we still call home to this day. Late in 2016 he bought his first house, and he moved in as soon as we had finished renovating it.

Joshua had come out of a relationship, and he was on his own. One Australia Day our church held an outing, and the young people were out in the sun playing volleyball. Joshua looked up and saw a girl he did not know standing near the game, a beautiful Brazilian girl named Mallu. He went over and asked her to come and play on his team. She said yes.
I have to be honest about my own part in what happened next, because it says something about where I still was.

When I saw my son come out of his last relationship and go straight into another, I worried. I thought he might be filling a hole rather than falling in love, and I was not at all certain that he had ever dealt with the loss of his sister. So my worry was not for Joshua. It was for this girl.
Some time later, we were all invited to Joshua's house for a party.
Somewhere in that afternoon I asked Mallu how many children she wanted. She said eight. I turned to Dina and said quietly, give her three and she will change her mind. Dina chuckled.
Later on I took Mallu aside, and I said it plainly.

I told her that we had lost a daughter, and that what I was about to say to her I was saying as a father to a daughter. Be careful with Joshua, I said. He is not steady at the moment. He is like a lion that will lie down beside his meal, play with it, and then get up and walk away from it. Go carefully.

She reminds me of that conversation to this day. What she remembers is not the warning itself. It is that a man she barely knew was trying to protect her, and that he was not trying to pull her away from his own son. I only wanted her to walk in with her eyes open.
Then my son proved me wrong. The lion I had warned her about lay down for good. He treated her with respect, he grew serious about her, and the fear I had carried for her quietly left me.

On the twenty-second of November 2017, he took her to a quiet restaurant, just the two of them, and there he asked her to be his wife. She said yes, and that evening he gave her the ring. The girl I had once taken aside to warn was going to marry my son, and I could not have been happier to be proven wrong.
On the fourth of May 2018, he married her with honour.

It was a beautiful wedding. Mallu looked like a princess. They were married on lovely grounds, in a little cottage church built of timber with a steeple on it, and the reception was held on the same grounds under a great marquee.
One of the things I will carry in my heart from that day is something smaller than any of it.

My nephew Joel, Philip and Natalie's firstborn, had a black Mercedes-Benz, and he had offered it as the bridal car, to bring Mallu from our house to the church. When the time came, something happened and Joel could not drive her after all. The car was still there, waiting outside our house, and I was the only one who could take the wheel.
So I drove my own future daughter-in-law to her wedding, in the back of a black Mercedes-Benz, up to the church where my son was anxiously waiting for her.

I had arranged beforehand with Pastor Justin, who was marrying them, for a moment in the service to be set aside for me, and it came after the rings had been exchanged, while the two of them were still standing at the altar. I gave them the old blessing, the one God gave to Aaron to speak over His people.
The Lord bless you and keep you; the Lord make his face shine on you and be gracious to you; the Lord turn his face toward you and give you peace.
I did not only say the words. I opened them up as I went, one at a time, and told them what each one carries in the Hebrew, because every one of them is heavier than it looks in English.
To bless is barak, and it means to bend the knee. It is a picture of God stooping down to put something good into the hands of someone far smaller than Himself.
To keep is shamar, a shepherd's word. It means to guard, to watch over, to put a hedge around a thing so that nothing can get at it.
To make His face shine is ya'er panav, the light of a face. It is what happens to a face when someone it loves walks into the room.
To be gracious is chanan, to stoop and give a gift that was never earned and could never be repaid.
