To turn His face toward you is yissa panav, to lift the face and look straight at a person, holding nothing back and looking nowhere else.
Peace is shalom, which is not the absence of trouble. It is wholeness. Nothing missing and nothing broken.

While I was speaking those words over them I felt the anointing come down on the two of them, the very same way I had felt it on the mountain in Sicily, on the day my father-in-law laid his hands on Dina and me and blessed us. It was the same weight, the same presence, come down all these years later on the far side of the world. In that moment I understood something. The blessing had passed into my hands. I had become the patriarch, or should I say the priest of my bloodline.
It is still on them to this day, and it will be on them and on our generations until the Lord returns.
By this time, Joshua had bought his second home, and the two of them moved in and made a home of their own.
Then the children began to come.

Caleb came first, on the fourth of August 2019, the grandson I have already told you about, the little light I could not yet feel all the way to the bottom of me. After him came a girl, Bella, on the twenty-ninth of June 2021. Then two came at once, twins, Chloe and Matteo, on the sixteenth of December 2024. Last of all, on the third of May 2026, came the youngest, Sofia.
Five beautiful grandchildren by the time this book goes to print.

Joshua's house, quiet not many years before, was suddenly full of children and noise and running feet and small hands reaching up. God had taken the one son He had given me and built a whole world around us, and He had done most of it in the very years I was too heavy to watch it happening. I had thought I was only a drowning man. All the while, up on the shore where I could not see, God was raising a family that would one day fill my later years with more joy than I know how to hold.

This is the place to tell you what I promised you earlier, back when I first spoke of the gate. I said I knew the spirit of abandonment had left me, and that I would tell you further on how I knew. Here is how. After Caleb, my first grandson, was born, I often took him to kindergarten in his early years. And even though I remembered the gate, it did not wound me. I would kneel down to his level and explain to him that he was there to enjoy himself, and that when the afternoon came, Nonno would be back to get him. And just like his dad, he would walk out and enjoy the day with his friends. The thing that had lived in me since I was nine years old was gone.

Out of all of it I learned one thing I want to pass on, because it is the thing nobody did for me. Tell the children the truth. Tell them exactly what is happening. Do not dress it up in horses and merry-go-rounds. Tell them the plain truth, and then reassure them, that you are coming back for them, that they are going to have a wonderful time with their friends, and that it will not be long. A child can bear almost anything if he knows the truth and knows you are coming back. It is the not knowing, and the deception, that closes the gate.
Then there are the names.
My name is Moses. My son's name is Joshua. My first grandson's name is Caleb.

I will not pretend that came to me as a surprise. I knew what those three names were from the beginning. I had grown up on that story, and when Joshua was born I knew what I was looking at, and when Caleb was born I knew it again. What I could not do, for a very long time, was believe it applied to me.

In the Bible, Moses led God's people out of slavery and through the wilderness towards the land God had promised them. A whole generation came out with him. But at the edge of that land their courage failed, and God said that generation would die in the wilderness and never enter it. Only two men believed Him and were allowed to cross over. Their names were Joshua and Caleb. When Moses's own journey came to its end, it was Joshua who rose up in his place and led the people in.
Moses. Joshua. Caleb.

I should say plainly what happened to the first of those three. Moses never walked into that land himself. God took him up a mountain at the end of his life and let him look right across it, and that was as far as he went. It was Joshua and Caleb who crossed over.

I had been through a wilderness of my own, one I would not wish on any man, and in the worst of it I had been certain I would die out there and never see the far side of anything again. But the names under my own roof had been telling the true story all along. There is a promised land. There is a crossing over. It may be that I only ever stand at the edge of it and look. That is enough for me. My son and my grandson, and the little ones coming up behind them, will walk into all of it, carrying forward everything I once almost stopped believing.
There is one more thing to say about that land, and it is the thing that matters most.

The land Joshua and Caleb crossed into was a piece of ground. The one I am walking towards is not. I will not be looking at mine from the side of a mountain. I will go into it, and Dina with me, and Joshua and Mallu and all their children after them, and we will be together in it, every one of us, and nothing will be missing and nothing will be broken. And I will not have earned my way in. None of us could. The only reason any of us will cross over is that Jesus paid the price to bring us there, with His own blood, opening a door none of us could open for ourselves.

And here is the thing I did not understand for most of my life. My promised land is not a place at all. It is a Person. It is Jesus Himself. I have Him now, here, and He has never once left me. But one day I will see His face. I will feel His arms around me for real. He is the country I am crossing into. He is the merry-go-round. He is the horses. He is the chocolate ice cream. He is every good thing I was ever promised as a boy and told I would find, and to see Him face to face, and to be held by Him at last, is the whole of what I am walking towards. Everything I am, and everything I need, is in Him.
I have to take you back now.

Back many years, to before I lost Celeste, before the long years of heaviness, before any of what I have just walked you through. Back to when I was a younger man and my own life was still only beginning. There is a story I have kept until now, and I have kept it on purpose, because I do not think I could have made you feel what it means until you had seen everything else. It is the story of my father, and of how, in the end, he came home.

In the years after he left us, my father went to Sydney, and there he worked in a restaurant. The owner could hardly run the place himself, he was disabled, and he was often drunk, so a great deal of the running of it fell to my father. He was good at it. He worked hard and true to the cause, the way he always had. He was gone from us for a long time. Then, in 1988, he came back to the Gold Coast. He bought himself an apartment on the northern side of the coast and settled there.

I believe he came back because he had heard that the lady he had left us for was, by then, ready to leave her own husband. I do not say that to wound anyone. I say it because it is what I understood at the time, and because this is a book of the truth as I lived it. Whatever the reason, he came back, and he reached out to me.

I could have refused him. He had walked out on my mother, on all of us, when I was seventeen years old, and I had spent the years since being the father of a family that was never mine to father. I had every reason a man could want to close the door.

But I could not do it. I have turned it over many times, and the answer is always the same, and it is very simple. He was my father, and I loved him. Whatever he had done, that had not changed, and I did not have it in me to keep neglecting him. So I did not.
Before I did anything, I went to my mother.

I sat with her and I asked her plainly how she would feel if I began again with my father, if I let him back into my life. I was ready for her to be hurt. She was not. She told me that it was the godly thing to do, for us to be reconciled to him, that a son should not be cut off from his father. She was ready to forgive him. I do not think she had ever truly stopped being ready. What had changed was only that now, with him back within reach, she could finally show it. Forgiveness that has nowhere to go just sits inside a person, year after year. Hers had somewhere to go at last.

So we began to see him. He would come when the family was gathered, on our birthdays, or on special occasions, or on my sister's wedding anniversary, or whenever my brother David came out from Belgium and all of us, every one of my father's children, were together in the one place. He would come to my mother's house, where we gathered, and take his seat among us. Slowly, carefully, over those gatherings, something that had been broken between a father and his children for a very long time began to mend. It was not that my mother and father were coming back together. That was never what happened. It was that a father was being welcomed back by the children he had left, and my mother, who had already forgiven him, made room for him at the table.
Then one day he told us that he was going to marry the lady.

Up to that point, if I am honest, my forgiveness had not really cost me anything. It is easy to say you have forgiven a man while nothing is asked of you. It is another thing entirely when he stands in front of you and asks for your help, when the asking itself plays with the wound he made.

He asked me to come to the wedding. He also asked me for something else. He wanted his bridal car decorated the way it had always been done in our church, back in Belgium, in the country we had come from. There was a particular way of it: paper flowers made by hand, glued along ribbons, the ribbons run over the car to trace out its shape until the whole thing was dressed like something out of the old world. I was the only one left who still knew how to make those flowers. The knowledge had come down to me and stopped with me. Of everyone he knew, only my hands still held it.

I want you to understand what he was asking, and what I understood myself to be doing. He was asking me to take the one thing I had carried out of our old life, out of our church, out of the faith we had shared before everything fell apart, and to use it to bless his marriage to the woman our family had been broken over. To make beauty with my own hands for that.
All the way through it, I believed I was betraying my mother. That belief did not leave me for a moment. I sat and I made paper flowers, and I felt like a traitor with every single one.

But I made them anyway. I made them because I had come to a line I could not cross back over. I had called myself a Christian my whole life. I had stood and preached the faith to strangers. If the word meant anything at all, it could not only be something I said. It had to be something I did, in my own life, in the places where it cost me. A faith that cannot forgive a father is not a faith. It is only a collection of words. So I decided that I would rather betray my own feelings than betray the thing I claimed to believe.
I made the flowers. I dressed the car. I went to the wedding. Afterwards I made my peace with his new wife too, though I will not pretend to you that it was easy, because it was not.

There is something else that must be said, because it belongs to the truth of his life. When he married her, he sold the apartment he had bought when he first came home, the one place that was truly his own. He used the money to pay off the house she had built with her former husband. He poured what he had into a foundation another man had laid. I do not think he ever let himself see it that way. But he had given up the one solid thing that was his, to secure a house that could never really be his, and it is part of why, at the very end of his life, so little of what he had worked for turned out to be his to give. It was money that should, by any right, have come to us, his children. It never reached us.
There was a harder test still, and it came at my own wedding.

When it was my turn to marry, I wanted my father there. But I could not have him there at any price. I asked him to come on one condition, that he come alone, without his wife. I knew my father. If he brought her, he would not show any restraint. He would hold her and show his affection for her in front of the whole room, and I could not let my mother sit and watch that on the happiest day of my life, could not let her watch the woman who had taken her husband held close in front of everyone. Asking him to come alone was the only way I could protect her.
He would not come on that condition. So he did not come at all.

I would have liked to have my father at my wedding. But I had been handed a choice that no one should ever have to make, my mother's peace on that day or my father's presence, and I chose my mother. I have never once regretted it. Still, I noticed the empty place where he might have been.

Still, I was not fatherless on my wedding day. I knew, even as I stood there, that a far greater Father than mine was in that room. The God who had found me my beautiful bride, who had arranged every step of how she came to me before I ever knew her name, He was there, and He was the one who deserved all the glory. My earthly father had stepped away from the day. My heavenly Father had not, and never would. It was He who was giving me Dina, and a man who is handed his wife by the hand of God is not a man anyone should pity for an empty chair.

I think I understand now why he was the way he was, though I offer it only as a son's guess at his own father. I think he was a deeply insecure man inside that marriage. He knew, better than anyone, by the very sermons he had once preached, that in the eyes of God that union did not stand. So it seemed to me that he spent himself trying to prove on the outside what he could not settle on the inside. He would call her his wife, always his wife, rather than simply use her name. He worked hard, in front of everyone, to make it look settled and right and permanent. The louder a man insists on a thing, the more you can hear the doubt underneath it.

After I was married, and Dina and I had our Joshua, my father started a business. He bought a refrigerated truck. He would drive south to Sydney and fill the truck with Italian small goods, forty thousand dollars of it at a time, and then he would drive that truck two and a half thousand kilometres north to Cairns and sell every last piece of it to Italian families, by talking to people until one led him to the next. He would come home with eighty thousand dollars. It was a good business, in its way, and it was his own. Often his wife went with him.

But I could not look at that truck without something turning over in me. In Belgium my father had been a man of honour. He had built a great church and run a fleet of buses, and men had taken off their hats to him in the street. Now here he was, an old man driving small goods up and down the coast of Australia, going door to door with salami, calling on strangers to make a sale. He never once said that it grieved him, and I never said it to him. But I saw how far the captain had come down, and it grieved me for the both of us.
Then one day the telephone rang, and it was his wife, calling from Cairns. My father was in hospital. Could I come up, she asked, and drive the two of them, and the truck, back home.

I was the right person to ask. I had been born among buses, and driving had always been a part of me, and years before I had gone and earned my heavy vehicle licence, so a truck that size held no fear for me. They flew me up to Cairns, and by the time I arrived he was well enough to leave the hospital, though he had been warned not to drive for a while, which was the whole reason they needed me.

I should tell you why he had been in there, because it matters for what came after. Cairns sits in the tropics, where the heat presses down on you. Time and again, straight off the heat of the day, he would climb up into the cold of the refrigerated compartment of his truck, where the goods were kept, and then back out into the heat again. Out of the heat and into the cold, and back once more, over and over, all day long. His lungs had never been strong. You will remember the coal, the ten years he had spent a kilometre underground in the dark of the Belgian mines, breathing the black dust into himself shift after shift. I have told you already how, years later, when we first stood in the clean air of this country, that coal came up out of him in small black pieces, the good air drawing some of it up out of his chest. It never washed his lungs clean, though at the time we half hoped it would. The coal had gone deeper into him than any air could reach. Whatever came to the surface, the damage underneath never left. It had been waiting in him all along, from the very first shift he breathed it, and now, in the heat and the cold of that truck, it came for him at last. That stay in hospital was a small thing next to what was coming for him. Looking back, I can see that it was the beginning of his end.
But the drive home from Cairns was a stretch of days that, at the time, I would not have traded for anything.

He had me stop along the way at a few more of his clients, to sell off the last of what was in the truck, and so the miles went slowly, and there was time. Over those days I came to know his wife better, for the first time. Things between the two of them came up in front of me, the ordinary cracks that are in any marriage, and instead of pushing me away it did the opposite. It let me see a part of her that was real and honest. Somewhere on that road I found I could relax in that truck beside her, and she became, for those few days, simply a person telling me the truth about her life.

I remember one thing she said, with the flat country going by outside. Vittorio, she said, using my father's name, I married you because you promised to make me a queen. Instead I feel like a gypsy, going from town to town, selling out of the back of a truck. Then she looked out the window, and with the sarcasm plain in her voice she added, Yes. I really feel like a queen.
My father answered at once. This is how you get there, he said.
I hope so, she said. Before I die.
I have done it before, he answered. I can do it again.

Back home, life settled into something almost gentle. He would come by to see us, and to see Joshua, whom he loved, and he never came empty-handed. He always had small goods for us, and Dina, being Italian, loved all of it and was grateful for it.

There was one thing about it, though, that sat wrong with me. He would tell me to share it around, to take some to my brothers, to my sister, to my mother. But then he would lower his voice and tell me to say nothing to anyone. It took me a little while to understand what the secrecy was. It was his new life he was hiding it from. His new wife, and her side of things, were not to know that he was still quietly giving to his first family. Because that is what he was doing. After everything, he had never really let go of us. He was still sending his children, and even the wife he had divorced, some of that Italian food, so close to our own table, only now he had to do it in the dark, passing it through my hands where no one could see. Even his kindness had to be smuggled.

My mother lived just across the road from us. Sometimes, when she saw his truck parked outside my place, she would walk over and say hello. That was all. No scene, no bitterness, nothing anyone would notice from the street. Just a woman crossing a road to greet the man she had once built a whole life with. I cannot fully explain to you everything that was in those small hellos. I only know that after all that had happened, they could still happen at all, and that seemed to me like a small miracle set down in the middle of an ordinary street.

Somewhere in those years he said something to me that I have never forgotten. He told me that he believed God had never left him. But I came to see that his guilt would not let him rest in it. He would pray, and a part of him hoped God was listening, and then his own conscience would rise up and tell him otherwise. He would open the Bible, and it was like a mirror held up in front of him, and he could not bear to look into it for long. So it was not that he had turned his back on God. It was that he could not quite believe God would still want him. He carried that doubt for years. It was the very thing that was waiting, right to the end, to be answered.
Then came the call.

His wife rang. He was in hospital again, in Brisbane this time. The truck, the years of cold and heat, the coal that had waited in his lungs since he was a young man, all of it had finally caught up with him, and this time his lungs did not recover. For several weeks we drove back and forth to Brisbane to be with him. Dina and I went up, and so did my brothers and my sister. Andrew and Philip made the trip whenever they could, and Gesuina came as well. None of us wanted him lying up there without his own people around him. The man who had once left us was not going to be left.
The first time I walked in, he had a tube down his throat and could not speak. But he did not need to speak. I could see it plainly in his eyes. He was happy that I had come.

There was one thing I was able to give him in that hospital, and I am glad beyond words that I did. I told him that Dina was expecting again, that another child was on the way, that he was going to be a grandfather once more. I saw what that news did to him, the future arriving in a room that had been filling up with endings.

He would not live to meet her. The child Dina was carrying was Celeste, and she would be born the following May, one day after my father's own birthday, seven months after we laid him in the ground. He never held her. But he knew she was coming. I have kept this close ever since, as one of the quiet arrangements of God: that even as my father was finding his way home, the little girl whose loss would one day undo me, and in the undoing hand me back to God, was already on her way into the world, and she would come tied forever to his birthday. One of them going home as the other set out.

Over those weeks, in the times when the tube was out of his mouth and he could get a few words free, and in the notes he wrote on paper when he could not, he began to let something out that I do not think he had ever meant to say to me. He gave me to understand that the woman he was with had deceived him. That the life had not turned out to be the thing he had imagined when he left us for it, any more than it had turned out that way for her, and that he wanted to come home.

I saw it with my own eyes more than once. I would walk into his room and the two of them would be in the middle of an argument, a real one, sharp and low, and the instant they saw me it would stop and the room would go still. When he and I were alone, when she was not there, he would ask me the thing he most wanted. He would ask me to speak to my mother. To find out whether she would have him back, and if she would not, whether he might come and live in the granny flat at the house.

I do not know if you can feel the whole weight of that from where you are sitting, but I could barely hold it. The granny flat he was asking for was in the house I had bought, all those years before, to shelter my mother and the family after he had left us to fend for ourselves. He was asking, at the end of his life, to be taken in under the roof his own leaving had made me build. The captain who had stepped off the ship was asking, quietly, from a hospital bed, whether there was still a place for him back on board.
His last day, my mother came to see him.

I still do not fully know how it came about, or who arranged it, or whether anyone arranged it at all. I only know that at some point I looked up and down the corridor of that hospital, and there, at the far end of it, were my mother and my father. They were holding each other.

I have told you already, in this book, about a night many years later when I would weep as though something inside me had come apart. But this was the first time in my adult life that I cried like that, standing in a hospital hallway, watching my parents hold one another after everything, after all the years and all the wreckage. I did not know a person could feel what I felt in that moment. It was as though my own body, which had been broken along some deep seam since I was seventeen years old, was being quietly put back together while I watched. Everything the leaving had torn, that embrace was mending, right there in front of me, without a single word.
Soon after that, on that same day, he took a turn for the worse, and they put the tube back in, and he did not speak to us again.

On that last night, the word came that he was near the end, and we drove in to him through the dark. My brother David had flown home from Belgium a week before, because we had told him our father might not recover. It was David, my mother, Dina, and I together in the car. Somewhere along that road a shooting star fell across the sky ahead of us, one long bright line that seemed to cut the whole sky clean in two, from the very top of it to the bottom. My mother saw it. She drew in her breath, and she said, Oh no. Your father will die tonight. His star has fallen.

She was right. When we reached the hospital, the doctor took us aside and told us gently that this would be his last night. So we came together, all five of us, all his children, and gathered in around his bed. Gesuina was there, Andrew, Philip, David, and me. We prayed over him. David sang, a song about the Lord, and his voice filled that small room with sorrow. My father, who could no longer speak, made us understand the one thing he wanted. He wanted every one of his children to be holding his hand. So we did. All five of us took hold of him, and of one another, and the doctor told us quietly that he would have until midnight.
He had done one more thing before any of us arrived, and we knew nothing of it until it was over.

When he was gone, a nurse came to us with two pieces of paper in her hands, papers my father had written himself, in his own hand, while he still could. She did not simply hand them over. She looked at us gathered there and asked which one of us was Moses. My father had put my name on the paper, that it was to come into my hands and no one else's, and the nurse had taken that seriously. She wanted to be certain it reached me, and did not pass into his wife's hands first. One of the papers was an ordinary sheet. The other was only a serviette, whatever had been within his reach.
On the sheet he had written, and signed it, and dated it the twenty-second of September, 1994:
I, Vittorio Campisi, first of all want to return to the Lord, then to my family. From Coomera, take the Volvo, half of the money from the sale of the truck, my clothes and my gold jewellery.
On the serviette, in the same hand:

I, Vittorio Campisi, want to die first in the hands of my God, then in the hands of my children, and to be buried wherever they wish, and I ask forgiveness for all my mistakes. This paper in the hands of Moses. Take the Volvo, half the money of the truck, all my clothes and gold jewellery, to my children.

I have read a great many things in my life. I do not think I have ever read anything that undid me the way those two scraps of paper did. My father, the man who had preached that a good captain never leaves his ship and then left, had written down, with nearly the last strength in his hand, the order of his own homecoming. First back to the Lord. Then back to his family. He had asked forgiveness for all of it. He had asked to die in the hands of his God and the hands of his children. He had come home on paper before he could come home in the flesh, and he had made me the keeper of it.
When we showed those papers to his wife, after he had died, she denied them. She said that he had never written such a thing, that we had written it ourselves.

We did not fight her. I want you to hear that clearly, because it is the whole of what I learned from my father's life, turned around and lived out at his death. We let her have everything. The car. The money. The clothes. The gold. All of it. Not because it was fair, but because none of it mattered to us, not one piece. She could keep every material thing his hands had gathered in a lifetime of chasing them.

What she could not seem to understand, standing there and accusing us over a Volvo and a share of a truck, was that we had already been given the only part of him worth having. Our father had come back to God, his Saviour, and he had come back to his family. You cannot write that onto a piece of paper, and you cannot deny it, and you certainly cannot buy it. She could have the rest. We had him.

There was one thing she honoured out of everything he had asked. She let us bury him where we wanted. So we did. We laid him to rest in a beautiful lawn cemetery, close to our homes, close to us. It is the same ground where my daughter would one day be laid, and where, in time, all of our family will come to rest together.

The wanderer, the man who had spent his whole life on the road to somewhere else, was finally brought to a stop and laid down in the ground near the people who had loved him from the beginning and never quite managed to stop.

He preached, once, when I was a boy, that a good captain never leaves his ship, no matter what. Then he left. It was the great wound of my early life, and it became, much later, the shape of my worst fear about God Himself. But I have learned that a story is not finished in the middle. The Bible says that He who began a good work will carry it on to completion, and I have seen that it is true. What God begins, He brings to completion. My father left his ship. Then, at the very end, by the only light he had left, he found his way back to it. He came home. To his God, and to us.

That is what forgiveness is for. Not to settle the account, because the account can never be settled. It is to keep the door open, in the belief that one day the one who left comes walking back up the gangway. I kept the door open. My mother kept it open. He came home before the end.
I have to tell you about the hardest thing my heart ever tried to do, because if I leave it out, everything else I have written is only half the truth.

Somewhere in those years, underneath the heaviness, underneath the soul-winning and the signs and the long silence, something took shape between God and me that I could barely stand to look at. A thought took hold of me, in a voice I took for God's own, that God was asking me to forgive Him. That He was stooping down to His broken child and asking me to forgive Him for how deeply the loss of my daughter had hurt me.

I have thought about that a great deal in the years since. At the time I believed it truly was God, lowering Himself to ask such a thing of a man like me. The hurt was real. God knew, when He allowed the loss of my daughter, exactly what it would cost me. But the hurt was never the reason for it. He did not do it to wound me. He did it to take the path I had chosen for myself, the path of my own dreams, the life I had planned and built and expected to keep, and to bend it onto His path, the destiny He had marked out for me before I was ever born. The pain was the price of that turning. It was never its purpose.

So I came right to the edge of it. I almost forgave God. Then, here, at the very end, as I came to the end of telling you this whole story, God broke in and gave me to see something I had never seen before, and it stopped me where I stood. It came to me as a revelation, sudden and clear, and it undid the whole thing in an instant. He took me back to the garden, to the very beginning, to a tree, the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and the one thing the man and the woman were told was that they must not eat from it. The lie that talked them into it was not really about a piece of fruit. It was about a throne. You will be like God, the serpent told them, knowing good and evil. That was what the fruit promised. Not knowledge for its own sake, but the right to decide for themselves what is good and what is evil, to become their own god, to pull the true God down off His seat and climb into it in His place. That is the sin underneath all the other sins. It is the reach for the throne.

I saw, with a cold shock, what I had been on the very edge of doing. To forgive God would be to rule that He had done wrong, and then, out of my own great mercy, to pardon Him for it. It would be to sit in judgment over my own Maker. It would be the reach for that same throne, the oldest sin of all, wearing the gentle face of a grieving man's forgiveness.

So I turned the whole thing around, all the way around, until it was finally facing the right way. The voice I had heard in my grief, the one that seemed to be God asking my forgiveness, had never been God at all. It was the serpent, the same one from the garden, only now he had made his voice sound like God's. He had whispered that God was asking me to forgive Him, knowing that if I did, I would be climbing onto the throne to judge my own Maker. It was the very same lie he told at the tree. Bite, and you will be like God.

The revelation was the other thing entirely. The revelation was God. It was God who broke in and showed me the trick, God who took me back to the tree, God who stopped me at the very edge and would not let me fall. The voice had come to pull me up onto a seat that was never mine. The revelation came to put me safely back on the ground. I would not climb up. I went lower still.

I will never do it. Not now, not ever. I would sooner be the most broken man on the face of the earth, still trusting a God I cannot understand, than be a comfortable man who has made himself God's judge.

I do not forgive God. I ask God to forgive me. I ask Him to forgive me for the years I spent believing He had done me wrong. I ask Him to forgive me for putting Him on trial. I ask Him to forgive me for ever imagining that my own understanding was large enough to hold a verdict on the Almighty. Then I lay myself down. I put my face to the ground at the feet of my Maker, where a creature belongs before the One who made him, and I stay there. It is the safest place I have ever been.
Here is what I came to know, lying face down.

Whatever God does, He does not do it to hurt me. He does not deal in cruelty. Everything He allows, everything He withholds, everything He gives and everything He takes away, He is doing to bring His own plan to its completion, a plan that is good, and wise, and far larger than the small square of it that I can see from where I am standing. So I have stopped demanding to understand. I have stopped searching through my own pain for reasons, turning the stones over one by one, needing an explanation before I will trust Him. I have learned to do the opposite. I arrange myself around His plan. I trust it first, and let the understanding come, or not come, as He pleases.

He is still the God of miracles. I want to say that plainly, because I have not stopped believing it for a single moment, and this book is full of His miracles from its first page. But the miracles rest now on His will for my life, and not on my picture of what my life is meant to look like. The miracles are real. He is sovereign even when the miracle does not come. He sees the whole world, and the whole of time, from a height I will never climb to, and He can only pour into my life what belongs to His design for it. When the miracle comes, it is Him. When it does not, that is Him too, and I bow to the one exactly as I bow to the other.
This is the thing I did not know at the beginning, and it is the reason for the name on the front of this book.

For most of my life I served a God I thought I knew. He was a good God, a great God, the God who had lifted my family up out of a Belgian coal mine, and filled a church with miracles, and handed me a wife by His own hand, and set a daughter apart for me in heaven before she was ever born. I loved Him with everything in me. But somewhere inside me, without my ever once saying it out loud, I had also come to believe that this God owed me. That because I had given Him my life, He would keep that life in the shape I wanted it kept. That a man who had served God the way I had served Him would be spared the very worst. That was the God I thought I knew, and He was, in part, a god I had built myself, a god whose only task was to protect my own version of my own life.
That god died on a rainy Friday night, on a road above the coast.

The God who was left standing, the God I truly know now, is greater and more terrible and more tender than the one I lost. He does not owe me the ending I would have chosen. He does not exist to keep my life in the shape I picked for it. He is God, and I am not, and the whole distance between those two things is the distance I have spent this entire book learning to cross. I do not stand over Him any longer, weighing Him in my hands. I lie down in front of Him, and I trust Him. I have found, to my very great surprise, that this is not a defeat. It is the only rest I have ever known that the world cannot reach in and take away from me.
So let me ask you something, before I put down my pen.
Who is sitting on the throne of your life?

There is a seat inside every one of us, and someone is always on it. For most of my life I believed God was on mine, and He was not. I was. I had made myself the judge of what was good and what was evil, the one who decided how my life ought to go, and I called it faith. It took the loss of my daughter, and everything I have written in this book, for me to see it and to climb down.

If you find that anyone other than God is on the throne of your life, whether it is you, as it was me, or anything else you have set up there, then I want to give you the same way down that God gave me. It is a prayer. Pray it slowly, and pray it with your whole heart, because the words of it matter. Say them and mean them, both together, so that they are true, and so that the accuser has nothing he can lay a hand on. Say it out loud if you can. Words spoken have weight.
Father.
Begin there, with that one word, because to call Him Father is already to say that He is higher than you, and that you are His child, and not the other way around.

Father, I have sinned. I see now that I have put myself on the throne that belongs to You. Right now I repent of that sin, and I take myself down from it. It is not my opinion of what is good and evil that supports Your kingdom and Your creation. It is what You decree to be good and evil that determines the very foundations of Your kingdom. So from this day I give You the throne of my life. I submit myself to You. Be my God, and be my Father, and I will be Your child. Help me to come to You first for every decision I have to make, so that my whole life may be lived in worship to You. In the name of Your Son, Yeshua, amen.

If you have prayed that, and meant it, then the same God who raised Jesus from the dead, and who lifted me out of my own grave, has that very same resurrection power to lift you out of yours. He is now your Father too. He will finish what He has begun in you, exactly as He finished it in me, and in my father before me.
That is the God I know now. He is far greater than the one I once thought I knew. I pray, with all my heart, that you will come to know Him too.
Kept here so that none of it is lost.

Rosina Maria Antonia, my mother, was born on 27 June 1927.
Raphael was born on 28 September 1932. He married my aunt Maria, and they had four children, two girls and two boys: Rosella, Angelina, Salvatore, and Jean-Pierre.
Josephine was born on 1 July 1935. She married my uncle Guy, and they had four children: Rebecca, Daniel, Anni, and Marco.
Antonia was born on 20 June 1939. She married my uncle Jacque, and they had one son, Fredi.
The children of Vittorio and Rosina Campisi

Gesuina was born on 25 December 1948 in Fabrizia, Italy, and registered on 2 January 1949. She married Arthur Luigi D'Antoni (born 12 March 1950) on 12 October 1968. They had two children: a daughter, Lidya, born 8 January 1971, and then a younger son, Daniel, born in February 1981. Arthur once told me he learned to play the guitar so he could be near my sister in the church band.

David was born on 4 August 1952 in Charleroi, Belgium. He married Jacqueline Macaluso (born 13 March 1953), who had been saved only months before, on 14 July 1973. They had four daughters: Isabelle, born 7 August 1974; Christelle, born 13 October 1976; Sylvie, born 14 May 1978; and Aurelie, born 11 September 1988.

Moses, myself, was born on 26 November 1963 in Charleroi, Belgium. I married Dina Gerarda Squadrito (born 17 December 1963 in Messina, Sicily) at the courthouse on 30 May 1991, and our true union followed in church on the Gold Coast, Australia, on 20 July 1991. We had two children, Joshua and Celeste. Celeste was born on 14 May 1995 and moved to heaven on 24 February 2012. Joshua was born on 28 August 1992. He married Mallu (born 20 November 1992) on 4 May 2018, and they have given us our beautiful grandchildren: Caleb, born 4 August 2019; Bella, born 29 June 2021; the twins Chloe and Matteo, born 16 December 2024; and Sofia, born 3 May 2026.

Andrew was born on 13 December 1964 in Charleroi, Belgium. He married Romina Squadrito (born 30 September 1973 in Sicily) on the Gold Coast on 6 October 1992. They had two children: Jasmine, born 9 July 1995, and Emanuel, born 27 January 1997.

Philip was born on 13 December 1964 in Charleroi, Belgium. He married Natalina Squadrito (born 10 December 1970) at Scaletta, Sicily, on 23 February 1992. They had three sons: Joel, born 29 September 1996; Benjamin, born 30 November 2000; and Jeremiah, born 8 February 2008. Joel married Chelsea (born 7 September 1995), and they have a son, Luca, born 18 March 2025.

This is the account of our family as it stood on the day this book went to print. By the grace of God, the line is not finished. There will be more births, more marriages, and more names to add after these pages were closed, and every one of them will be another proof that God is still building what He began.

It is my hope that one day, far from now, one of the generations still to come will take up this pen and write the next chapters, carrying forward the design God began in us long before any of them were born.
Before I close, there are people I have to thank, because a book like this is never the work of one person alone.

First, and with all my heart, I thank my wife, Dina. Through every up and every down, she has been there, and she has never once let go. I have often said that I was like the Titanic heading straight for the iceberg, and that time and again it was Dina who sounded the alarm in time for me to turn and steer clear of it. She is a true woman of God, and whenever I could not see the way, it was she who shone the light of God to keep me on His path. Much of what is good in my life, and in this book, I owe to her.

I thank my son, Joshua. I began this book many years ago, and for a long time I kept adding to it, never quite able to call it finished. It was Joshua who came to me and told me, with love, that the time had come to lay down the pen and let the story be told. Without his encouragement, these pages might still be sitting unfinished. He helped me bring it home.

I thank my brother David, who gave me the small but precious pieces I could not have found alone, the dates and the places, set down correctly at last. I thank my uncle Davide, my father's younger brother, who sent me a copy of a page from my grandfather's own Bible, with the dates of all his children written by his own hand. I also thank my cousin John Iuliano, who confirmed for me that my father's father had planted seven churches across Calabria, and who, through ancestry research, traced a quarter of our bloodline back to the Monteleone line.
I also want to thank everyone who, in one way or another, helped me set down my recollection of this history more accurately. Every piece they offered helped me tell it the way it really happened.
Above all, the glory belongs to God. He wrote this story, not with ink, but with real people and real events across four generations. I only took a pen and wrote down on paper what He has done.
Moses Campisi
